examples: Isaiah 9:7: of the increase of the Messiah's government there will be no end.
Ephesians 3:21 speaks of glory to God "to all generations, forever and ever", showing the new age continues.
questions.other: Amillennialists say the "end of the ages" began with Christ but will be completed at his return. Futurists often read "the end of the age" in Matthew 24:3 as the end of the present church age.

questions.q: What did James mean by "the coming of the Lord is near" and "the judge is standing at the door"?
questions.short: James wrote to Jewish believers suffering under rich oppressors. He told them to be patient because the Lord's coming was near and the judge was at the door.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, James gives a clear time text. He writes to the twelve tribes in the dispersion (1:1). He warns rich landowners who withheld wages and killed the righteous: "Weep and howl for the miseries that are coming" (5:1). Then he tells believers, "Be patient until the coming of the Lord" (5:7) and "the coming of the Lord is near" (5:8). He adds, "The judge is standing at the door" (5:9). A judge at the door is about to enter. James wrote before AD 70, probably in the 40s or 50s. The judgment on the land and its oppressive leaders came in the Jewish war. The farmer's patience for the early and late rains fits a short wait.
examples: James, the brother of Jesus, was killed in Jerusalem in AD 62 (Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.1).
Matthew 24:33 uses the same image: "he is near, at the very gates."
questions.other: Most commentators say James uses "near" to urge readiness for Christ's final return, which could come at any time. Some critical scholars hold James expected a return in his lifetime that did not occur.

questions.q: Why did Revelation say its events "must shortly take place" and told John not to seal the book?
questions.short: Revelation opens and closes with nearness: "shortly", "the time is near", "I am coming quickly". Daniel sealed his book because it was far off; John did not.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, Revelation brackets its visions with time words. It shows "things which must shortly take place" (1:1). "The time is near" (1:3). The same phrases return at the close (22:6, 10). Jesus says, "I am coming quickly" (22:7, 12, 20). The contrast with Daniel is striking. Daniel was told to seal up his vision because it referred to "many days" in the future (Daniel 8:26; 12:4). Daniel's time span was about four centuries. John is told the opposite: do not seal the book, for the time is near. If four centuries was "far", two thousand years cannot be "near". So most of Revelation's judgments must have fallen soon after it was written.
examples: Daniel 8:26 sealed a vision fulfilled under Antiochus IV in 167 BC, about four centuries later.
Revelation 3:11 tells the church at Philadelphia, "I am coming quickly; hold fast."
questions.other: Futurists say "shortly" (en tachei) can mean "swiftly" when it happens, and "near" is from God's point of view (2 Peter 3:8). Idealists say the events are always near because the conflict runs through history. Historicists see the book unfolding from the first century on.

questions.q: Does "the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world" in Revelation 3:10 mean the whole planet?
questions.short: The word is oikoumene, "the inhabited world", often meaning the Roman Empire. The hour was "about to come" and was promised to a real church in Philadelphia.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, Revelation 3:10 is a local promise with a near time. Jesus tells the church in Philadelphia that he will keep them "from the hour of trial that is about to come upon the whole world". The Greek word for "world" here is oikoumene. Luke uses it when Caesar Augustus ordered a census of "all the world", meaning the Roman Empire (Luke 2:1). The word "about to" (mello) signals nearness. The trial would test "those who dwell on the earth" or "land". The promise only comforts the Philadelphians if the trial came in their lifetime. The years AD 64-70, with Nero's persecution, civil war in Rome and the Jewish war, fit this hour.
examples: Luke 2:1: Augustus taxed "all the world" (oikoumene), meaning his empire.
In AD 68-69 Rome had four emperors in one year, a crisis felt across the empire.
questions.other: Pre-tribulation futurists say Revelation 3:10 promises the church removal from a future worldwide tribulation. Others say "keep from" means protection through it. Idealists apply it to trials in every age.

questions.q: What does "in a very little while, he who is coming will come and will not delay" mean in Hebrews 10:37?
questions.short: Hebrews quotes Isaiah and Habakkuk to tell suffering believers that the wait would be very short. "A little while" in the New Testament means within the hearers' lifetime.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, Hebrews 10:37 is one of the strongest time texts. The writer urges believers not to throw away their confidence. He adds, "For yet a very little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay." He blends Isaiah 26:20 and Habakkuk 2:3. Elsewhere in the New Testament, "a little while" means a short time within the hearers' life. Jesus said, "Yet a little while I am with you" (John 7:33). He said, "A little while, and you will not see me" (John 16:16). James says life is a vapour that appears "for a little while" (4:14). In the same chapter Hebrews says believers "see the day approaching" (10:25). The writer expected the coming within his readers' days.
examples: John 16:16-19: "a little while" was the days between Jesus' death and resurrection.
Habakkuk 2:3 promised Babylon's judgment would "not delay"; Babylon fell in 539 BC.
questions.other: Futurists say the writer stresses certainty and readiness, and that God's "little while" may be long by human standards. Some see a near fulfilment in AD 70 and a final one at Christ's return.

questions.q: What is the doctrine of "imminency", and do the time texts support it?
questions.short: Imminency says Christ's return could happen at any moment but may not be soon. The fulfilled reading says the texts do not say "may" or "could"; they say "near" and "soon".
questions.answer: Dispensational writers define imminency this way: an important event is likely to happen, could happen soon, and may take place at any time, though not necessarily very soon. The fulfilled reading asks where the texts use such words of possibility. Revelation says "must shortly take place". James says "is near". Peter says "is at hand". Hebrews says "will not delay". These are statements, not possibilities. If the apostles had wanted to say "perhaps soon", Greek had words to do so. Reading words in their plain, normal sense is the stated goal of literal interpretation. On that rule, the time texts say a great event would happen within the first readers' lives.
examples: Jesus could speak of a long delay when he meant one: "after a long time the master returned" (Matthew 25:19).
Revelation 1:1 uses dei, "must", a word of certainty, not chance.
questions.other: Dispensationalists hold that imminency protects watchfulness: since no sign must come first, believers must always be ready (Titus 2:13). Post-tribulation futurists reject any-moment imminency but still see Christ's return as future.

questions.q: Why are the time texts the most important element in Bible prophecy?
questions.short: They anchor prophecy to real history. If they can be stretched or ignored, the Bible can be made to mean anything, and a Bible that means anything means nothing.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, the time texts are the key that unlocks the rest. Images in prophecy, like sun, moon, stars, beasts and clouds, are often symbolic. Readers can disagree about them. But words like "this generation", "near" and "about to" are plain words. They tell us when to look. If we fix the time first, the meaning of the images becomes clearer. If we ignore the time, the images can be applied to any nation, leader or disaster. That is why prophecy charts change every decade. Sound interpretation lets the clearest parts explain the harder parts. The time words are among the clearest parts.
examples: Many prophecy charts from the 1970s that named the Soviet Union, the Common Market of ten nations, and 1988 have since been withdrawn.
Matthew 24:34 sets the time frame for the images in Matthew 24:29-31.
questions.other: Futurists say the content of a prophecy, such as worldwide events and a visible return, also limits its timing, and that time words must be read in harmony with it. Most interpreters agree time words matter but weigh them differently.

questions.q: Why do grammar and historical setting decide when a prophecy is fulfilled?
questions.short: Without the setting, a passage can be made to fit any generation. The time Jesus gave is part of the meaning, not a detail to be set aside.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, almost any meaning can be read into a verse if its grammar and history are ignored. Jesus spoke to particular people, in a particular place, about particular events. When he said "you", "this generation" or "some standing here", those words set limits. If the time is missed, the Olivet Discourse can be applied to the fourteenth century, to 1948 or to the next war. That creates endless confusion. The chief problem for those who place Matthew 24-25 in our future is that they must set aside these limits. Sound interpretation asks first: who was speaking, to whom, when, and about what? Only then do we apply the passage to our own lives.
examples: Nehemiah 8:8: the Levites read the law and "gave the sense", helping people understand it.
Matthew 24:1-3 sets the scene: the disciples are looking at the temple buildings when they ask their question.
questions.other: Interpreters of every view affirm grammatical-historical reading. Futurists argue that the same method shows some events, like a worldwide visible return, could not have happened in AD 70. The debate is about which details carry the most weight.

questions.q: What did Jesus promise in Matthew 16:27-28?
questions.short: He said the Son of Man would come in his Father's glory with his angels to repay each person. Some standing there would not die before seeing him come in his kingdom.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, Matthew 16:27-28 joins a great coming to a short time limit. Verse 27 describes the Son of Man coming "in the glory of his Father with his angels" to "repay each person according to what he has done". Verse 28 begins "Truly I say to you" and says that "some of those standing here will not taste death" before they see this. "Some" implies that most would die, but a few would still be alive. So the event had to be far enough away that most hearers would be dead, yet near enough that some would live to see it. A coming two thousand years later does not fit. A coming one week later does not fit either.
examples: "Taste death" is a Hebrew way of saying "die" (compare Hebrews 2:9).
Of the twelve, tradition says only John lived long after AD 70.
questions.other: Many futurists say verse 27 is the second coming but verse 28 is a different event, often the transfiguration. Some amillennialists see the resurrection and Pentecost as the kingdom "coming with power". Critical scholars say Jesus expected the end soon and was wrong.

questions.q: Was the transfiguration the fulfilment of Matthew 16:28?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, no. The transfiguration came six days later, when all the disciples were still alive. "Some will not taste death" would then mean almost nothing.
questions.answer: Many link Matthew 16:28 to the transfiguration because it follows in the next verses (17:1-8). But the fulfilled reading sees a problem. Jesus said some standing there would not die before they saw the event. That wording implies that most of them would die first. The transfiguration took place "after six days". If it were the fulfilment, Jesus would be saying that most of his hearers would die within a week. Also, verse 27 speaks of coming with angels to repay each person for their deeds. No judgment or reward took place on the mountain. The transfiguration was a glimpse of Christ's glory, and Peter later remembered it that way. It was a preview, not the fulfilment.
examples: 2 Peter 1:16-18: Peter recalls the transfiguration as seeing Christ's majesty.
Henry Hammond (1653) argued the transfiguration cannot fulfil the verse because no reward to each person occurred.
questions.other: Many church fathers, including Chrysostom, and many modern commentators hold the transfiguration view. They say "some" refers to Peter, James and John, who alone went up the mountain, and that the vision was a foretaste of the kingdom's glory.

questions.q: Was Pentecost the fulfilment of Matthew 16:28?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, no. Pentecost came only months later, when nearly all the hearers were alive. It also lacked the judgment and reward of verse 27.
questions.answer: Some interpreters say the kingdom came "with power" at Pentecost (Acts 2). The fulfilled reading agrees that Pentecost was a great event of the kingdom. But it does not fit Jesus' words "some ... will not taste death". Pentecost came about a year after Jesus spoke. That would mean most of his hearers died within a year, which did not happen. Also, verse 27 speaks of a coming with angels to repay each person. Pentecost brought blessing and the Spirit, not judgment. Finding a fulfilment in such close events also does not help futurists. If they say Matthew 16:28 was fulfilled at Pentecost, they admit that "the Son of Man coming in his kingdom" can refer to an event other than the final return.
examples: Acts 2:1-4: the Spirit came about fifty days after the resurrection.
Of the twelve, only Judas had died by Pentecost.
questions.other: Some evangelical scholars, such as Gleason Archer, prefer the Pentecost view. They point to Mark 9:1, "the kingdom of God come with power", and Acts 1:8, "you will receive power", as clear links.

questions.q: If the transfiguration fulfilled Matthew 16:28, does that make the interpreter a preterist?
questions.short: In a sense, yes. Anyone who places the fulfilment in the past agrees that the "coming" in this verse is not the final return. The debate is then only which past event.
questions.answer: The fulfilled reading makes a simple point of logic. Some futurist writers say preterists read too much into Matthew 16:28. Yet they themselves say the verse was fulfilled at the transfiguration. That is a past fulfilment. So they agree with the preterist on the key question: the "coming of the Son of Man in his kingdom" here was not the second coming at the end of history. Once that is granted, the question is which past event best fits all the details. The details are a coming with angels, a judgment of each person, and a time when most hearers would be dead but some alive. The fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 fits these better than a week or a year later.
examples: A dispensational paper at a 1995 pre-tribulation study conference argued for the transfiguration view.
Luke 9:27 words it as seeing "the kingdom of God", showing the focus is the kingdom, not only the person.
questions.other: Futurists reply that calling one verse fulfilled does not make them preterists in the full sense. They see a preview of the kingdom in the transfiguration while holding that the final coming of verse 27 remains future.

questions.q: Which event fits "some standing here will not taste death"?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. It came about forty years later, when most of Jesus' hearers had died but some, like John, still lived.
questions.answer: The fulfilled reading looks for an event far enough away that most of the hearers would be dead, but not so far that all would be. The destruction of Jerusalem by Rome in AD 70 fits. It came about forty years after Jesus spoke. Peter, James son of Zebedee, Paul and James the Lord's brother had all died by then. John lived on. The event was a coming in judgment: Jesus had said the blood of the prophets would fall on that generation. It also marked the public end of the old order and showed that the Son of Man reigned. Older writers called it "the coming of Christ" in his kingly office to judge his enemies and separate the faithful.
examples: James son of Zebedee was killed about AD 44 (Acts 12:2).
Josephus, Jewish War 6.9.3, gives the huge toll of the siege and the captives taken.
questions.other: Futurists accept AD 70 as a real judgment but say it did not include a visible coming with angels or the judgment of every person. Some see AD 70 as a partial or typical fulfilment that points to a final one.

questions.q: Did respected older commentators link Matthew 16:28 to the fall of Jerusalem?
questions.short: Yes. Henry Hammond, John Lightfoot, John Gill and Henry Alford all connected it with AD 70. The Dutch scholar S. Greijdanus did the same for Luke 9:27.
questions.answer: The fulfilled reading is not alone in this view. Henry Hammond (1605-1660) wrote that the coming in Matthew 16:28 could not be the transfiguration, because no reward to each person happened there. He linked it with John 21:23 and Matthew 24 and saw the fall of the Jews as Christ's coming in his kingly office. John Lightfoot and John Gill gave similar comments. Henry Alford, a leading Greek scholar of the 1800s, said the passage referred to the destruction of Jerusalem and the full display of Christ's kingdom. Greijdanus argued that only Jerusalem's fall fits Luke 9:27: not the resurrection, Pentecost, the gospel's spread or the final judgment. He saw AD 70 as a preview of the last day.
examples: Henry Hammond, A Paraphrase and Annotations upon the New Testament (1653).
Herman Ridderbos, The Coming of the Kingdom, quotes Greijdanus on Luke 9:27.
questions.other: Other respected commentators, both older and modern, prefer the transfiguration or the resurrection-Pentecost view. Many modern scholars (for example R. T. France) also see AD 70 or Christ's enthronement as the main reference.

questions.q: What did Charles Spurgeon say about the plain meaning of Matthew 16:28?
questions.short: Spurgeon said a child reading the verse would think Jesus was to come while some hearers were alive, and he called that the plain meaning.
questions.answer: The fulfilled reading cites Spurgeon as an honest witness. In a sermon on this verse, the great Baptist preacher said that if a child read it, he would suppose Jesus Christ was to come, and some standing there would not die until he really did come. Spurgeon said he believed this was the plain meaning. Yet he did not accept the conclusion that the coming was the judgment of AD 70. Instead he used the text to urge readiness. The fulfilled reading values his honesty. It holds that a plain meaning a child can see should be accepted, even if it challenges our system. Jesus himself praised the Father for revealing truth to little children.
examples: Spurgeon preached on the text in a sermon titled "An Awful Premonition".
Matthew 11:25: truths are revealed to "little children".
questions.other: Spurgeon and many others saw the passage as fulfilled in a preview of glory, while reserving the full coming for the end. Others say the "plain meaning" must be balanced with the whole teaching of Scripture about Christ's final return.

questions.q: How does Mark 8:38-9:1 show who would see the coming in glory?
questions.short: Jesus spoke of being ashamed of people in "this adulterous and sinful generation" when he comes in glory. Then he said some there would see the kingdom come with power.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, Mark adds a key phrase. Jesus warns, "Whoever is ashamed of me and my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels" (8:38). The judgment is aimed at his own generation. Then he says, "Some standing here will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God come with power" (9:1). These two verses belong together. The coming in glory and the kingdom coming with power fall in the same time frame. So it is not a distant generation that will face his shame. It is Jesus' contemporaries who rejected him.
examples: Matthew 12:39: Jesus calls his hearers "an evil and adulterous generation".
Matthew 23:36: "all these things will come upon this generation."
questions.other: Many commentators say "this adulterous generation" describes the sinful world in every age, and Mark 9:1 refers to the transfiguration that follows. Others see the resurrection and the spread of the kingdom as the coming "with power".

questions.q: Why do skeptics use these time texts to say Jesus was wrong?
questions.short: They read the texts as promising Christ's final return within a generation. Since that did not happen, they say Jesus was mistaken and cannot be trusted.
questions.answer: The fulfilled reading takes this challenge seriously. The philosopher Bertrand Russell wrote in Why I Am Not a Christian (1927) that Jesus clearly thought his second coming would happen in the lifetime of many then living. Russell used this to question Jesus' wisdom. Other skeptics have said the same: Jesus promised a kingdom in his disciples' lifetime, and he was wrong. If Jesus was wrong about this, they ask, why trust his moral teaching? The fulfilled reading answers that the critics and the futurists share a mistake. Both assume the coming in these verses must be the final return. If instead it was a coming in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, Jesus was exactly right, and the critics' argument falls.
examples: Russell first gave his lecture "Why I Am Not a Christian" in London on 6 March 1927.
Albert Schweitzer, The Quest of the Historical Jesus (1906), argued that Jesus expected an immediate end.
questions.other: Many evangelical scholars answer critics differently: by prophetic foreshortening, by seeing partial fulfilment in AD 70 with final fulfilment later, or by pointing to the transfiguration. Some liberal scholars accept that Jesus was mistaken but still value his teaching.

questions.q: Was the gospel preached to the whole world before AD 70?
questions.short: Paul said it had been. He wrote that the gospel was bearing fruit "in all the world" and had been preached "to every creature under heaven" (Colossians 1:6, 23).
questions.answer: One skeptic argued that Matthew 24 could not have been fulfilled by AD 70, because the gospel had not reached the whole world. Some futurists make the same argument. The fulfilled reading answers from Scripture. Jesus said the gospel would be preached in "the whole world" (oikoumene) as a testimony to all nations, and then the end would come (Matthew 24:14). Paul, writing around AD 60, said the gospel was "bearing fruit in all the world" and had been "proclaimed to every creature under heaven". He told the Romans that their faith was spoken of "in all the world". The apostles' own words say the condition was met. "World" here means the known world of the Roman Empire and beyond.
examples: Acts 2:5-11 lists Jews "from every nation under heaven" present at Pentecost.
Romans 10:18: "their voice has gone out to all the earth."
questions.other: Futurists say Matthew 24:14 looks to a final worldwide mission, perhaps during the tribulation (Revelation 14:6). Many missions leaders link it to reaching every people group today. Others see both a first-century and an ongoing fulfilment.

questions.q: Does 2 Peter 3:4, "Where is the promise of his coming?", show that early Christians were disappointed?
questions.short: Peter predicted that scoffers would come in the last days. On the fulfilled reading, they mocked before AD 70, and Peter said the Lord was not slow but patient.
questions.answer: One skeptical writer said that in the second century Christians began to ask, "Where is the promise of his coming?" because Jesus had not returned. The fulfilled reading notes that Peter wrote this letter before his death, in the mid-60s. He said scoffers would come "in the last days", and they were part of his own time. The scoffers argued that "all things continue as they were". Peter answered that God once judged the world by water and would judge again. He said God is not slow, but patient, giving time to repent. Within a few years, the old order did end. So 2 Peter 3 is not evidence of failed hope. It is a warning given to its first readers.
examples: 2 Peter 1:14: Peter says the putting off of his body is "soon".
Jude 1:17-18 says the apostles foretold scoffers "in the last time", and Jude's readers were seeing them.
questions.other: Many scholars date 2 Peter later and see it as answering a delay in Christ's return. Most evangelicals accept Petrine authorship and see 2 Peter 3 as looking to the final day of the Lord and new creation, not AD 70.

questions.q: How did C. S. Lewis handle Matthew 24:34?
questions.short: Lewis called it "the most embarrassing verse in the Bible". He granted that Jesus said it, and suggested Jesus, in his human nature, did not know the timing.
questions.answer: The fulfilled reading notes that C. S. Lewis faced the critics honestly. In his essay "The World's Last Night" (1952), he stated the skeptic's case: the first Christians expected the second coming in their lifetime, because their Master told them so, and he was wrong. Lewis called Matthew 24:34 "the most embarrassing verse in the Bible". He pointed to Mark 13:32, where Jesus says even the Son does not know the day. Lewis held that Jesus, in his humanity, shared some limits of knowledge. The fulfilled reading respects Lewis but finds a simpler answer. Jesus knew the generation in which "all these things" would happen. Only the final day and hour he left unknown.
examples: Lewis, The World's Last Night and Other Essays (1960), collects the essay.
Mark 13:30 and 13:32 sit side by side: "this generation" and "that day or hour".
questions.other: Many evangelicals follow a version of Lewis's view, stressing Christ's human limits. Others say Jesus' words were right because AD 70 fulfilled verse 34 while verse 36 refers to the final day. Liberal scholars say Jesus was simply mistaken.

questions.q: How have some evangelical commentators tried to explain Matthew 16:28, and why do their answers fall short?
questions.short: They point to the transfiguration, Pentecost, or even the triumphal entry. On the fulfilled reading, none of these explains "some will not taste death".
questions.answer: The fulfilled reading surveys several popular answers. One reference work lists three options: the transfiguration, Pentecost and AD 70. It chooses Pentecost but does not explain how "some will not taste death" fits. Another says Jesus simply promised that some would see a foretaste of his glory. That changes Jesus' words instead of explaining them. Some study notes suggest the triumphal entry a few days later, without dealing with the time issue. Others skip verse 28 altogether. The common weakness is that each answer avoids the plain force of "some standing here". A good answer must explain why most hearers would die but some would live. AD 70 meets that test better than any event a few days or months away.
examples: Gleason Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties (1982), favours Pentecost.
R. A. Torrey, Difficulties in the Bible (1907), also discusses the text.
questions.other: These commentators reply that "some" may simply stress that not all would be present, not that most would die. They see a preview of the kingdom in the near event and the full coming at the end, avoiding any claim that Jesus erred.

questions.q: How could Jesus "come in glory with his angels" in AD 70 if no one saw him in the sky?
questions.short: In the Old Testament, God often "came" in judgment on nations without being physically seen. Jesus used this same language of himself.
questions.answer: Read covenantally, "coming" is a common Old Testament picture for God acting in history. Moses sang that the Lord "came from Sinai" with ten thousands of holy ones (Deuteronomy 33:2). Isaiah saw the Lord riding a swift cloud and coming to Egypt in judgment, fulfilled when Assyria struck Egypt (Isaiah 19:1). Micah said the Lord would come down and tread on the high places to judge Samaria (Micah 1:3-6). No one saw God's body on these occasions. They saw his judgment through armies and events. Jesus applies this divine language to himself. So his "coming in glory with angels" in AD 70 means that he acted as King and Judge through the Roman armies, as God once used Assyria and Babylon.
examples: Isaiah 10:5: God calls Assyria "the rod of my anger".
Matthew 22:7: in the parable, the king sends his armies and burns the city of those who refused his invitation.
questions.other: Futurists accept that God "came" in past judgments but argue that Jesus' coming is personal and visible (Acts 1:11; Revelation 1:7). They say the Old Testament comings were types of the final, bodily coming.

questions.q: Which Old Testament texts stand behind Matthew 16:27?
questions.short: Daniel 7:13-14 (the Son of Man), Psalms 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12 (God repays each person), and Zechariah 14:5 (the Lord comes with his holy ones).
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, Jesus builds Matthew 16:27 from Old Testament pictures of God himself. The "Son of Man" coming in glory comes from Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man receives a kingdom. The promise that he will "repay each person according to his deeds" echoes Psalms 62:12, Proverbs 24:12 and Jeremiah 17:10, where God is the judge. The angels recall Zechariah 14:5: "The Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with him." Jude 14-15 quotes a similar line about the Lord coming with myriads of holy ones to judge the ungodly. By using these texts, Jesus claims the role of Israel's God as Judge. The point is his authority to judge, not the timing of a physical descent.
examples: Jude 1:14-15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9 on the Lord coming with ten thousands of his holy ones.
Craig Keener's IVP Bible Background Commentary notes these Old Testament sources.
questions.other: Futurists agree on these sources but read them as pointing to the final, visible return and final judgment. Some see Zechariah 14 as a future battle at Jerusalem. Most scholars agree that Jesus is applying divine roles to himself.

questions.q: Does the New Testament speak of comings of Christ other than the final return?
questions.short: Yes. Christ warned the church at Ephesus, "I will come to you and remove your lampstand", and Pergamum, "I will come to you soon." These were comings in judgment on local churches.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, not every "coming" of Christ is his final return. To the church at Ephesus, Jesus said, "Repent ... or else I will come to you and remove your lampstand" (Revelation 2:5). To Pergamum he said, "Repent, or I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth" (2:16). To Sardis, "I will come like a thief" (3:3). These comings depended on whether those churches repented. They could not be the single final return of Christ to the whole world. They were acts of judgment in history. This shows that "coming" language can describe Christ acting from heaven within history, which supports reading his coming against Jerusalem the same way.
examples: John 14:18, 23: Jesus says "I will come to you" of his presence by the Spirit.
The church at Ephesus did later decline; the city is now an uninhabited ruin.
questions.other: Most interpreters of all views agree that Revelation 2-3 speaks of conditional, historical comings. Futurists say this does not change the meaning of passages that clearly describe the final, visible coming, such as Acts 1:11 and 1 Thessalonians 4:16.

questions.q: Does the fulfilled reading of Matthew 16:28 deny that Christ will return bodily in the future?
questions.short: No. The partial-preterist reading holds that AD 70 was a coming in judgment, while Christ's final bodily return, the resurrection and the last judgment are still ahead.
questions.answer: The fulfilled reading of these texts is usually a partial preterist one. It holds that the coming in Matthew 16:28 and the events of Matthew 24:4-34 were fulfilled in AD 70. But it also affirms the creeds: Christ "will come again to judge the living and the dead". Acts 1:11 says Jesus will come back in the same way he went. Paul speaks of a future resurrection of the dead when Christ comes (1 Corinthians 15:22-26). The scholar Greijdanus called AD 70 "a precursor" of the judgment on the last day. So AD 70 is a real coming in history that points forward to the final coming. Seeing one fulfilled gives confidence that the other will be too.
examples: The Apostles' Creed: "From there he will come to judge the living and the dead."
1 Corinthians 15:24-26: the last enemy to be destroyed is death.
questions.other: Full preterists hold that all comings, including the resurrection, were fulfilled in AD 70; most churches reject this as outside the creeds. Futurists say the partial-preterist line between AD 70 and the final return is drawn in the wrong place.

questions.q: What "house" did Jesus mean when he said, "Your house is left to you desolate" (Matthew 23:38)?
questions.short: He meant the temple in Jerusalem. The very next verse shows Jesus leaving the temple while the disciples point to its buildings.
questions.answer: Read in context, the "house" is the temple. Jesus speaks the words inside the temple courts at the end of his woes on the scribes and Pharisees. Then Matthew says Jesus "went out from the temple" and the disciples showed him its buildings (Matthew 24:1). The movement is deliberate. Earlier Jesus called the temple "my house" (Matthew 21:13) and "my Father's house" (John 2:16). Now he calls it "your house". The change of owner signals that God is withdrawing his presence. This echoes Jeremiah, who warned that God would make his house like Shiloh if the people did not listen (Jeremiah 7:12-14; 22:5). On the fulfilled reading, Jesus' departure from the temple is an acted sign of the judgment he then describes in Matthew 24.
examples: Ezekiel saw the glory of God leave the first temple and move east to the Mount of Olives before Babylon destroyed it in 586 BC (Ezekiel 10:18-19; 11:23). Jesus leaves the second temple and sits on the same mountain (Matthew 24:3).
"My house" (Matthew 21:13) becomes "your house" (Matthew 23:38) within three chapters.
questions.other: Almost all interpreters agree the house is the temple, or Jerusalem with its temple. Futurists accept that this verse points to AD 70, but they argue that later parts of Matthew 24 jump ahead to a final temple and a still-future crisis. Some also read "house" as the nation or the ruling family.

questions.q: Why does this reading say the stone temple was always meant to be temporary?
questions.short: Because Jesus presented his own body as the true temple. The stone building was a shadow that pointed to him and to the people built on him.
questions.answer: In John 2:19-21, Jesus says, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." John explains that he spoke of the temple of his body. After the resurrection, the disciples understood. On this reading, the building in Jerusalem was a pointer. It showed that God wanted to live among his people. When God's Son "tabernacled" among us (John 1:14), the reality had come. Hebrews calls the earthly sanctuary "a copy and shadow" of the heavenly one (Hebrews 8:5). A shadow is useful until the body arrives. To hold on to the stone temple as permanent would, on this view, treat the shadow as more important than Christ. So the temple's fall in AD 70 did not defeat God's plan. It completed a transition God had planned from the start.
examples: Jesus told the Samaritan woman that true worship would soon not depend on Jerusalem or Mount Gerizim (John 4:21-23).
Stephen reminded the council that "the Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands" (Acts 7:48-50, quoting Isaiah 66:1-2).
questions.other: Most Christians agree Christ is the true temple. Dispensational writers still expect a future physical temple, either as part of God's dealings with Israel in the tribulation or as a millennial memorial. They say the temple's typology in Christ does not cancel specific prophecies about a literal building in the land.

questions.q: Why is the question "when?" so important for understanding Matthew 24?
questions.short: Because Jesus gave a clear time limit: all these things would happen before "this generation" passed. The time text controls how we read the signs.
questions.answer: The disciples' first question was "When will these things be?" (Matthew 24:3). Jesus answered with a sign list and a time statement: "This generation will not pass away until all these things take place" (Matthew 24:34). On the fulfilled reading, the time statement is the key that unlocks the passage. If we know when, we can test the events against history. That makes the prophecy checkable, not endlessly movable. The same approach applies to Revelation, which says its events "must soon take place" and that "the time is near" (Revelation 1:1, 3). Starting with the clearer Gospel discourse before the symbol-heavy Revelation is also sound method. Moving from clear texts to harder texts is a basic rule of reading Scripture.
examples: Daniel 9:2 shows Daniel reading Jeremiah's "seventy years" as a real, countable period, not a vague one.
Deuteronomy 18:22 gives a test for a prophet: does the word come to pass? A time-bound prophecy can be tested.
questions.other: Futurists agree timing matters but read the time words differently. Some take "generation" as the generation that sees the final signs. Others take it as the Jewish race. Many amillennial and historic premillennial scholars see a near fulfillment in AD 70 and a far fulfillment at the end of history within the same discourse.

questions.q: Could a future rebuilt temple be the one Jesus said would be torn down in Matthew 24:2?
questions.short: Not on this reading. Jesus pointed to the stones in front of him: "not one stone here" will be left. A future building would have different stones.
questions.answer: Jesus said, "Do you not see all these things? Truly, not one stone here will be left on another" (Matthew 24:2). The words "these things" and "here" point to the buildings the disciples had just shown him. The disciples could not have thought of another temple while looking at the one that stood before them. Jesus gave no hint that he had a future structure in mind. On the fulfilled reading, a temple built in our time, whatever its purpose, would have nothing to do with this prophecy. History records that the Romans burned and pulled down the temple in AD 70. Josephus says Titus ordered the whole city and temple razed, except a few towers and part of the western wall (Jewish War 7.1.1).
examples: Mark 13:1 records a disciple saying, "Teacher, look at these stones and buildings!" Jesus answers about those same stones.
Luke 19:44 adds that enemies would not leave one stone on another "in you", meaning Jerusalem itself.
questions.other: Futurists usually agree Matthew 24:2 was fulfilled in AD 70. They see a change of focus at verse 4 or verse 15 to a future temple. Some note the Western Wall still stands, but most explain it was a retaining wall of the platform, not part of the temple building itself.

questions.q: Why did judgment fall so heavily on the generation of Jesus' day?
questions.short: Because that generation had the Messiah in its midst and rejected him. Jesus said the guilt of the past would come to a head in their time.
questions.answer: Every generation must decide about Jesus. But only one generation saw him in the flesh and handed him over to be crucified (John 1:11; Acts 3:14-15). Jesus said they were filling up "the measure of your fathers" (Matthew 23:32). The blood of the prophets, from Abel to Zechariah, would be charged to them (Matthew 23:35-36). On the covenantal reading, this follows an Old Testament pattern. God bore long with Israel, sent prophets, and finally brought covenant judgment when the sin was full (2 Chronicles 36:15-16). Judgment here is national and covenantal, not a statement that every person was lost. Thousands of Jewish people in that same generation believed and were saved (Acts 2:41; 21:20). The warning was given so that people could repent and escape.
examples: 2 Chronicles 36:15-16: God sent messengers "early and often", but the people mocked them until there was "no remedy". Babylon then came in 586 BC.
Genesis 15:16: the sin of the Amorites was "not yet full". God judges when the measure is full.
questions.other: Most Christians accept that AD 70 was a judgment connected with rejecting Jesus. Many today stress that the New Testament blames specific leaders and a specific generation, never Jewish people in all ages. Dispensationalists add that Israel's national rejection is temporary and that a future national turning remains (Romans 11:25-26).

questions.q: How does Matthew describe "this generation" before the Olivet Discourse?
questions.short: As the people Jesus was speaking to: the leaders and crowds who rejected John and Jesus and asked for signs. The phrase points at them every time.
questions.answer: Matthew paints a clear portrait. John the Baptist called the leaders a "brood of vipers" fleeing coming wrath (Matthew 3:7). Jesus compared "this generation" to children who would not dance or mourn, because they rejected both John and himself (Matthew 11:16-19). When the leaders asked for a sign, he called them "an evil and adulterous generation" (Matthew 12:39). He said Nineveh and the Queen of the South would condemn "this generation" at the judgment (Matthew 12:41-42). In chapter 23 he says they are sons of those who killed the prophets and will kill and flog the messengers he sends (Matthew 23:31-34). On this reading, all these lines describe one group of living people. Matthew 24:34 should not suddenly change who is meant.
examples: Matthew 11:20-24: Jesus names the towns of that day, Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, as the places that saw his works and did not repent.
Matthew 3:7 and 12:34 both use "brood of vipers" for the same leaders, years apart.
questions.other: Interpreters agree that in Matthew 11, 12 and 23 the phrase refers to Jesus' contemporaries. The debate is about Matthew 24:34 only. Some futurists argue that the context of signs changes the meaning there. Others take "generation" as a moral class: an evil kind of people that lasts until the end.

questions.q: What does the parable of the returning unclean spirit say about that generation (Matthew 12:43-45)?
questions.short: It warns that the generation would end worse than it began. A house swept but left empty becomes home to worse spirits. Jesus applied it to "this evil generation".
questions.answer: Jesus told of an unclean spirit that leaves a man, finds the house swept and empty, and returns with seven worse spirits. "The last state of that man is worse than the first." Then he added, "So also will it be with this evil generation" (Matthew 12:45). On the fulfilled reading, this traces the path of that generation. John's preaching and Jesus' ministry brought a moment of cleansing. But the people who refused the King were left empty. Josephus describes the years before AD 70 as full of faction, murder and false prophets inside Jerusalem (Jewish War 5.10.5). The "last state" was the war and siege. The parable is a warning, not a curse on a people. It shows what happens when grace is refused.
examples: Josephus wrote that he did not think any other city ever suffered such things, or any generation was more fruitful in wickedness (Jewish War 5.10.5).
Luke 11:24-26 places the same parable right after the leaders said Jesus cast out demons by Beelzebul.
questions.other: Many commentators read the parable as a general warning about empty reform in any life. Others agree it applies first to Jesus' contemporaries. Christians today stress care here: Revelation's phrase "synagogue of Satan" (Revelation 2:9) targets specific local opponents who slandered believers, not Jewish people as a whole.

questions.q: When did Jesus say the kingdom would be taken from the leaders and given to others (Matthew 21:43-45)?
questions.short: In their own time. The chief priests and Pharisees knew he was speaking about them, so the transfer was not two thousand years away.
questions.answer: After the parable of the tenants, Jesus said, "The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits" (Matthew 21:43). Matthew adds that the chief priests and Pharisees "perceived that he was speaking about them" (Matthew 21:45). The parable ends with the owner coming and destroying the tenants (Matthew 21:40-41). The next parable has a king who sends troops and burns the city of those who refused his wedding feast (Matthew 22:7). On the covenantal reading, these scenes point to AD 70. The "people producing fruit" is the church of believing Jews and Gentiles (1 Peter 2:9). The stone that crushes (Matthew 21:44) echoes Daniel 2:34-35, where the kingdom stone breaks the old powers.
examples: Matthew 22:7: "The king was angry. He sent his armies, destroyed those murderers and burned their city." Jerusalem burned in AD 70.
1 Peter 2:9 gives the church Israel's titles from Exodus 19:6: a royal priesthood and a holy nation.
questions.other: Most interpreters agree the parable targets the leaders of that day. Dispensationalists say the kingdom is taken from that generation of leaders, not from Israel forever, and will be restored at Christ's return (Acts 1:6-7; Romans 11). Covenant theologians say the true Israel continues in the church with its Jewish remnant.

questions.q: Does "this generation" mean any people, in any age, who share the same evil traits?
questions.short: This reading says no. Jesus tied the judgment to a specific group he was addressing, and the leaders understood he meant them.
questions.answer: Some writers, such as Dave Hunt, have suggested that anyone at any time with the same evil tendencies would belong to that "generation of vipers". The fulfilled reading answers that this makes the phrase timeless and almost empty. Jesus said, "All these things will come upon this generation" (Matthew 23:36). He then said, "This generation will not pass away until all these things take place" (Matthew 24:34). A time limit does not make sense if the group never ends. There is also a moral risk. Making the phrase timeless can turn a judgment on one generation into a charge against Jewish people in every age. That is not what the text says. Christians in every age are warned from the passage, but the prophecy itself was aimed at one generation.
examples: Matthew 23:36 and 24:34 both begin "Truly I say to you": a solemn statement to the listeners in front of him.
Acts 2:40: Peter urged his hearers, "Save yourselves from this crooked generation." He meant people then alive.
questions.other: Some scholars hold that "generation" (genea) can carry a moral sense, "this kind of people", as in Psalms 12:7 or Philippians 2:15. On that view the evil kind lasts until Christ returns. Others answer that even the moral sense in the Gospels is always applied to people living at the time.

questions.q: How do Matthew 23:36 and 24:34 work together?
questions.short: They act like bookends. Both say "this generation" and both start with "Truly I say to you". The events between them fall within that time frame.
questions.answer: Matthew 23:36 says, "Truly, all these things will come upon this generation." Matthew 24:34 says, "Truly, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place." The disciples' questions in 24:3 were raised by what Jesus had just said in chapter 23. So the two chapters belong together. On the fulfilled reading, the two time statements frame the signs that sit between them. If 23:36 means Jesus' contemporaries, and nearly everyone agrees it does, then 24:34 should mean the same people. To change the meaning in the second verse, a reader needs a clear signal in the text. This reading finds none. The Old Covenant order would end with the fall of the temple, which was the sign of the "end of the age".
examples: The parallel accounts keep the same frame: Mark 13:30 and Luke 21:32 repeat the generation statement.
Luke 11:50-51 says the blood of the prophets "will be required of this generation", using the same idea as Matthew 23:36.
questions.other: Many scholars accept the link but see two answers in the discourse. On this view Matthew 24:4-35 covers AD 70 and 24:36-25:46 covers the final return ("that day"). Dispensationalists usually take "all these things" in 24:34 to mean the end-time signs, so "this generation" is the one that sees them.

questions.q: How is the phrase "this generation" used elsewhere in the Gospels?
questions.short: In every other Gospel use it means the people alive when Jesus spoke. The fulfilled reading asks why Matthew 24:34 should be the single exception.
questions.answer: The phrase appears more than a dozen times in the Gospels. Jesus compares "this generation" to children in the market (Matthew 11:16; Luke 7:31). He says no sign will be given to "this generation" except Jonah (Matthew 12:39-41; Mark 8:12; Luke 11:29-30). The Queen of the South will condemn it (Luke 11:31). The blood of the prophets will be charged to it (Luke 11:50-51). The Son of Man must be rejected by it (Luke 17:25). In each case the meaning is plain: the people living then. On this reading, the rule is simple. Let Scripture interpret Scripture. When a phrase has one steady meaning in all its uses, the reader should not give it a new meaning in one verse to fit a system.
examples: Luke 17:25: "He must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation." That happened in AD 30 or 33, not in a future age.
Mark 8:12: "Why does this generation seek a sign?" was said to Pharisees standing in front of him.
questions.other: Some futurists answer that context can change a word's meaning. They argue that the signs in Matthew 24 never happened in full in the first century, so the phrase must mean a later generation. Others accept the normal meaning and say "all these things" refers only to the events before the coming, not the coming itself.

questions.q: Why does it matter that Jesus said "this" generation and not "that" generation?
questions.short: "This" points to what is near, "that" to what is far. Matthew uses "that day" for distant time. Jesus chose "this" for the generation listening.
questions.answer: In Greek, as in English, "this" (houtos) points to something present or near. "That" (ekeinos) points to something more distant. Matthew uses both carefully. He writes "to this day" for his own time (Matthew 27:8; 28:15). He uses "on that day" for the future judgment (Matthew 7:22) and "that day and hour" for the unknown time (Matthew 24:36). If Jesus had meant a far-off group, he could have said, "That generation will not pass away." On the fulfilled reading, the choice of "this" is a deliberate signal. It ties the prophecy to the people who heard it. The change from "this" in verse 34 to "that day" in verse 36 is one reason some see a shift of subject there.
examples: Matthew 27:8: the potter's field is called the Field of Blood "to this day", meaning Matthew's own time.
Matthew 24:36: "concerning that day and hour no one knows"; the far demonstrative appears right after verse 34.
questions.other: Futurist scholars reply that "this" can point to the generation just described in the text, the one that "sees all these things" (Matthew 24:33). They say the demonstrative refers back to the signs, not to the listeners. Others answer that verse 33 itself says "you" will see them.

questions.q: What does the repeated word "you" in the Olivet Discourse tell us?
questions.short: It shows Jesus was speaking to his disciples about their own future. "You will hear", "they will deliver you", "when you see" all point to the listeners.
questions.answer: In the discourse Jesus says: "See that no one leads you astray" (Matthew 24:4). "You will hear of wars" (24:6). "They will deliver you up and kill you" (24:9). "When you see the abomination" (24:15). "Pray that your flight may not be in winter" (24:20). "When you see all these things" (24:33). Luke adds that they would be brought before kings and governors (Luke 21:12-13). On the fulfilled reading, a listener on the Mount of Olives would conclude that these events would happen in his lifetime. If Jesus meant a far future, we would expect "when they see" and "they will deliver them". The book of Acts then shows these very things happening to the same disciples. The plain sense of "you" agrees with the plain sense of "this generation".
examples: Acts 4:3 and 5:40: Peter and John are arrested and flogged, as Matthew 10:17 and 24:9 foretold.
Acts 25:23: Paul stands before King Agrippa and Governor Festus, as Luke 21:12 foretold.
questions.other: Futurists answer that the disciples stand for later believers, or for the Jewish remnant of the end time. They note that prophets often addressed people as though they would see events that came later. Moderate readers say the "you" fits AD 70 in the first part and believers in all ages in the second part.

questions.q: Does "Zechariah, whom you murdered" (Matthew 23:35) prove that "you" can mean people long dead?
questions.short: This reading says no. Jesus treats the living generation as sharing their fathers' guilt, and says the judgment will fall on them. The "you" still means his listeners.
questions.answer: Some futurists, such as Stanley Toussaint, argue that since Zechariah died centuries earlier, "you" in Matthew 24 can also mean people who are not contemporaries. The fulfilled reading answers in three steps. First, Jesus addresses the living leaders. They are "filling up" their fathers' measure (Matthew 23:32). They are one with their fathers in guilt, as they themselves admit by building the prophets' tombs (Matthew 23:29-31). Second, Jesus says the penalty "will come upon this generation" (23:36). The punishment falls on the living, not on the dead. Third, "may" is not "must". Showing that "you" can stretch in one special case does not prove it stretches in the discourse. The burden of proof lies with the reader who changes the plain meaning. The text names the living as the ones judged.
examples: Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20-22). He is the last martyr in the Hebrew Bible's order, as Abel is the first.
Nehemiah 9:33-34 shows a later generation confessing "we have acted wickedly" for their fathers' sins: shared corporate guilt.
questions.other: Futurists hold that the corporate "you" shows a prophet can speak to a nation across time. On that view the disciples in Matthew 24 represent the faithful of the end time. Scholars debate whether Zechariah son of Barachiah is the priest of 2 Chronicles 24, the prophet Zechariah, or someone else.

questions.q: How did earlier Bible commentators read "this generation" in Matthew 24:34?
questions.short: Many saw it as Jesus' own generation, with fulfillment in the fall of Jerusalem. This view was common long before modern dispensationalism.
questions.answer: A range of respected commentators read the phrase as Jesus' contemporaries. John Lightfoot (1658) said the verses before 24:34 speak of Jerusalem's ruin and that John and some rabbis lived to see it. Thomas Newton (1754) wondered how anyone could split the discourse when verse 34 is so plain. John Gill (1746-48) saw it as full proof that the whole section concerns the end of the Jewish state. In modern times D. A. Carson and William Lane said the phrase can only with great difficulty mean anything else, and R. T. France agreed. On this reading, the agreement of these careful scholars shows that the first-century view is not a new or fringe idea. Many of them still believed in a future bodily return of Christ.
examples: Eusebius (Church History 3.5-3.8, about AD 325) described the fall of Jerusalem as fulfilling Jesus' prophecy, quoting Josephus at length.
John Calvin, on Matthew 24:34, said Jesus meant the destruction of the city would come within the lifetime of his hearers.
questions.other: Several of these scholars, including Carson, still read Matthew 24:36 onward as the final return. Dispensational writers point to other commentators, such as some church fathers, who read the discourse as about the end of the world. They note that a majority view does not settle meaning.

questions.q: Does Matthew 23:39, "You will not see me until you say, Blessed is he who comes", promise a future national conversion of Israel?
questions.short: On this reading, "until" states a condition, not a promise. They will see him as Savior only when they welcome him. It does not say when, or that all will.
questions.answer: Some futurists read Matthew 23:39 as a promise that Israel as a nation will one day repent. The fulfilled reading notes that the verse begins with "for", linking it to the abandoned house in 23:38. R. T. France points out that the Greek expresses a possibility, not a firm prediction. Matthew often uses "until" in this conditional way. "You will not get out until you pay the last penny" (Matthew 5:26). The servant was jailed "until he should pay" (Matthew 18:30, 34). Men vowed not to eat "until they had killed Paul", and that never happened (Acts 23:12). In the years after Pentecost thousands of Jewish people did confess Jesus as the one who comes in the Lord's name (Acts 2:41; 4:4). The door was open. Those who refused faced him as judge.
examples: Acts 3:19-21: Peter urged Jerusalem to repent "so that times of refreshing may come": a conditional offer.
Psalms 118:26 is the source of "Blessed is he who comes"; the crowds used it at the triumphal entry (Matthew 21:9).
questions.other: Many scholars, both futurist and non-futurist, see hope in this verse. They link it with Romans 11:25-26 and Zechariah 12:10, expecting a large turning of Jewish people to Christ before his return. Postmillennialists and some amillennialists also expect such a turning, while denying a rebuilt temple.

questions.q: Was there still hope for Jewish people after Jesus declared the temple desolate?
questions.short: Yes. The gospel went "to the Jew first", and thousands believed. The hope was in Christ and his new temple, the church, not in a restored building.
questions.answer: Jesus' sentence on the temple was not a sentence on every Jewish person. Peter preached in Jerusalem, and about three thousand believed in one day (Acts 2:41). Soon the men alone numbered about five thousand (Acts 4:4). Later James told Paul that "many thousands" of Jewish believers lived in Judea (Acts 21:20). Paul himself was a Jewish believer and called himself proof that God had not rejected his people (Romans 11:1). On the covenantal reading, the door to God was not closed. It was moved. The new meeting place is Christ, and the new house is the people of God made of believing Jews and Gentiles (Ephesians 2:19-22). Scholars such as P. W. L. Walker note that Matthew never speaks of the judged temple being restored.
examples: Acts 6:7: "a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith", even from the temple's own staff.
Romans 1:16: the gospel is God's power "to the Jew first and also to the Greek".
questions.other: All Christian views agree that Jewish people are welcome in Christ now. Dispensationalists and many premillennialists add a future national restoration in the land with a central place for Jerusalem. Many amillennialists and postmillennialists expect a future large-scale conversion but not a return to temple worship.

questions.q: What harm do failed end-time predictions do?
questions.short: They damage trust in the Bible and in the church. People who were told the end would come on a date often conclude that prophecy itself is false.
questions.answer: Jesus began his answer with a warning: "See that no one leads you astray" (Matthew 24:4). On this reading, one modern form of being led astray is confident date-setting. A journalist once recalled reading, as a boy, an old book that said the world would end around 1934. He felt only relief that it was all past. Edgar Whisenant's book 88 Reasons said the rapture would come in September 1988. When it did not, he moved the date, then moved it to 1989. Each failure teaches outsiders that Christians cannot be trusted on the future. It also teaches believers to stop reading prophecy carefully. Scripture gives a test: a word that does not come to pass was not spoken by the Lord (Deuteronomy 18:21-22).
examples: Edgar Whisenant's 88 Reasons Why the Rapture Will Be in 1988 sold millions of copies. The dates of September 11-13, 1988 passed without event.
In 1844 the Millerite movement expected Christ on October 22. The "Great Disappointment" left thousands disillusioned.
questions.other: Most Christians of every view reject date-setting. Responsible futurists say no one can know the day (Matthew 24:36), but believers can still watch for signs that show the season is near (Matthew 24:33). They argue that false dates do not prove the signs are false, only that people misused them.

questions.q: Is the world "stage set" for the end, as some modern writers have claimed?
questions.short: This reading says such claims have been made in every age and keep failing. The signs Jesus gave belonged to his own generation, not to ours.
questions.answer: In 1988 John Walvoord wrote that the closing years of the twentieth century were pointing to end-time events. In his book on oil and the Middle East he said the world was like a stage set for a drama, with all actors ready. Television ministries announced that "the end of the world is coming soon". On the fulfilled reading, the problem is not watchfulness but misplaced signs. Jesus said the signs would come before his own generation passed (Matthew 24:34). Claims that "our generation" is the last have been made for centuries. Jack Van Impe once said the Soviet flag would fly over Independence Hall by 1976. Such sayings fade from memory, but they shape how people see the faith. Paul warned believers not to be quickly shaken by reports that the day had come (2 Thessalonians 2:2).
examples: Medieval writers saw the year 1000, the Mongol invasions and the Black Death (1347-1351) as final signs.
Martin Luther believed the end was very near in the 1500s and that the Turks were Gog.
questions.other: Futurists respond that Israel's return to the land in 1948, the growth of global systems and Middle East tensions are unique in history. They argue these fit Ezekiel 38 and Revelation 13 in a way earlier ages did not. Amillennial readers say the signs are present in every age between the comings.

questions.q: Why does fulfilled prophecy strengthen faith?
questions.short: Because it shows God knows and controls the future. Predictions made centuries before, and then fulfilled in detail, support the Bible's claim to be God's word.
questions.answer: God himself appeals to fulfilled prophecy: "I declare the end from the beginning" (Isaiah 46:9-10). Psalm 22 describes pierced hands and feet and the casting of lots for clothing. The Gospels show these happening at the cross (John 19:23-24). Isaiah 53 describes a servant who is wounded for others, silent before his accusers and buried with the rich. Isaiah wrote centuries before Jesus. Older writers counted hundreds of Old Testament predictions fulfilled in Christ. On the fulfilled reading, the New Testament's own prophecies should be expected to show the same accuracy. Jesus' words about the temple, the siege and the generation can be checked against history. When they are, the result strengthens faith. Speculation about tomorrow's headlines cannot do this, because it has not happened yet.
examples: Micah 5:2 named Bethlehem as the Messiah's birthplace about seven centuries before Jesus was born there (Matthew 2:5-6).
Isaiah 44:28-45:1 names Cyrus as the one who would rebuild; Cyrus allowed the return in 538 BC (Ezra 1:1-4).
questions.other: All Christian views value fulfilled prophecy. Futurists agree that many prophecies were fulfilled at the first coming. They say others, given in the same passages, wait for the second coming, as Isaiah 61:1-2 was split by Jesus in Luke 4:18-21. They see this as a model for a gap.

questions.q: Was Jesus' prediction that no stone would be left on another fulfilled?
questions.short: Yes. In AD 70 the Romans burned the temple and then pulled down its buildings. Josephus said visitors could hardly believe the place had been inhabited.
questions.answer: In August of AD 70 Roman soldiers set fire to the temple during the siege of Jerusalem. Josephus, a Jewish priest and historian who watched from the Roman camp, records that Titus then ordered the city and temple to be demolished. Only three towers and part of the western wall were left to show how strong the city had been (Jewish War 7.1.1). He wrote that nothing was left to make visitors believe the place had ever been lived in. Later Jewish tradition says a Roman officer ploughed the temple site, fulfilling Micah 3:12, "Zion shall be ploughed like a field" (Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 29a). Eusebius said he saw the site in ruins. On this reading, Jesus' word came true within about forty years, just as he said.
examples: Josephus dates the burning to the tenth of the month Lous (Av), the same day Babylon had burned the first temple (Jewish War 6.4.5-8).
The Western Wall seen today belonged to the retaining wall of Herod's platform, not to the temple building Jesus pointed to.
questions.other: Almost all interpreters accept this fulfillment. Some futurists point to the Western Wall and argue that a final, complete fulfillment awaits. Most scholars of all views answer that Jesus spoke of the temple buildings, which were completely destroyed, not the platform's outer support walls.

questions.q: What did the disciples actually ask in Matthew 24:3?
questions.short: They asked when the temple would fall, what sign would show Jesus' coming, and what would mark the end of the age. On this reading, all three concern one event.
questions.answer: The disciples asked: "When will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?" The question came right after Jesus said the temple would be torn down. On the fulfilled reading, the parts are linked: (1) the time of the temple's ruin; (2) the sign of Jesus' coming in judgment connected with that ruin; (3) the end of the age that the temple's fall would bring. For a first-century Jew, the fall of the temple would mean the end of an era. Alfred Plummer noted that men who heard of the temple's overthrow would naturally think of it as the end of the age. Mark and Luke record the question only as "when will these things be, and what will be the sign?" (Mark 13:4; Luke 21:7). That suggests one event, not several far apart.
examples: Mark 13:4: "Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?"
Luke 21:7 has the same simple form. Only Matthew adds "your coming" and "end of the age", for Jewish readers.
questions.other: Many interpreters believe the disciples assumed the temple's fall and the end of the world would be one event. On this view, Jesus separated them in his answer: AD 70 first, then the final return after an unknown time. Dispensationalists often see the whole answer as future, with Luke 21:20-24 alone describing AD 70.

questions.q: Did the disciples ask about the end of the "world" or the end of the "age"?
questions.short: The Greek word is aion, "age", not kosmos, "world". This reading takes it as the end of the Old Covenant era, not the end of the planet.
questions.answer: The King James Version translates Matthew 24:3 as "the end of the world". But the Greek word is aion, which means an age or era. The word for the physical world is kosmos, which Matthew uses elsewhere (Matthew 24:21; 26:13). Most modern translations now read "end of the age". On this reading, the disciples were asking when time would run out for the temple, the city and the Mosaic system of sacrifices, washings and priests. Their focus was the building in front of them. Nothing in their training or in what Jesus had said would make them ask about the end of the physical universe. N. T. Wright makes this point: first-century Jews thought of the end of an era, not the end of space and time.
examples: Matthew 13:39-40 uses the same phrase, "end of the age", in the parable of the weeds.
Hebrews 9:26 says Christ appeared "at the end of the ages" to put away sin, meaning his first coming.
questions.other: All scholars agree the word means "age". Many say the age that ends is the present evil age before the age to come, which begins at the final return (Matthew 13:39-43; 28:20). On that view, "end of the age" still points to the last judgment, even if it is not the end of the physical world.

questions.q: What were the "two ages" in Jewish thought, and how does that help here?
questions.short: Jews spoke of "this age" and "the age to come", the age of the Messiah. This reading says the Messiah's arrival and the temple's fall marked the change between them.
questions.answer: Jewish teachers divided history into "this age" and "the age to come". The age to come was the time of the Messiah and of God's kingdom. Jesus used the same language (Matthew 12:32). The disciples asked before the ascension, "Will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" (Acts 1:6). They expected a change of age. On the fulfilled reading, the New Testament shows the change already underway. Paul says the ends of the ages had come upon his readers (1 Corinthians 10:11). Hebrews says believers have tasted "the powers of the age to come" (Hebrews 6:5). The old age, tied to the temple and the law, ended visibly when the temple fell. The Messiah's age had begun with his death, resurrection and enthronement.
examples: George Hill, an 18th-century Scottish theologian, wrote that Jews divided time into the age of the law and the age of the Messiah.
Hebrews 8:13 (written before AD 70) says the old covenant is "becoming obsolete and growing old" and is "ready to vanish away".
questions.other: Many scholars accept the two-age frame but say the ages overlap. The age to come has begun with Christ ("already") but will be complete only at his return ("not yet"). On this view, AD 70 was a key moment but not the full change. Dispensationalists see a future millennial age as well.

questions.q: What exactly ended at "the end of the age" on this reading?
questions.short: The Old Covenant system of temple, priests and animal sacrifice. Christ had replaced each part, and the temple's fall removed the last visible shadow.
questions.answer: On the covenantal reading, "end of the age" means the end of the Mosaic way of worship. Each part of it pointed to Christ. Jesus is the Lamb of God who takes away sin (John 1:29). He is the true temple where God dwells (John 2:19-21). He serves in the true tabernacle (Hebrews 8:2). He is the perfect high priest who offered himself once for all (Hebrews 7:26-27). The law was a guardian to lead us to Christ, and now that faith has come we are no longer under it (Galatians 3:24-25). The end of the age also meant the opening of the covenant to the Gentiles (Matthew 21:43; 22:9-10). When the temple fell, there was no place left to carry out the old system. The shadows had given way to the reality.
examples: Romans 10:4 calls Christ "the end (telos) of the law" for righteousness to all who believe.
After AD 70 the daily sacrifice ceased. Jewish worship reshaped itself around prayer and study, led by the rabbis at Yavneh.
questions.other: Most Christians agree Christ fulfilled the Old Covenant at the cross. Many date the end of the old order to the cross and resurrection rather than AD 70. Dispensationalists say the church age is a parenthesis and that God's program for national Israel, including a temple, resumes later.

questions.q: What do Paul, Hebrews and Peter say about when the "end" was?
questions.short: They speak of it as present or near: the ends of the ages "have come", Christ appeared "at the end of the ages", and "the end of all things is at hand".
questions.answer: Paul says the Old Testament stories were written "for our instruction, on whom the ends of the ages have come" (1 Corinthians 10:11). Hebrews says Christ "has appeared once for all at the end of the ages" (Hebrews 9:26). Peter says Christ was revealed "in these last times for your sake" (1 Peter 1:20). He also says "the end of all things is at hand" (1 Peter 4:7). James says "the coming of the Lord is at hand" (James 5:8). On the fulfilled reading, these writers understood that they were living in the final years of the old age. The end they expected was near to them. Milton Terry described it as the end of the pre-Messianic age, which Hebrews 12:26-27 pictures as a shaking of earth and heaven.
examples: Hebrews 12:26-28: what can be shaken is removed so that the kingdom that cannot be shaken may remain.
2 Corinthians 3:13: Moses veiled his face so Israel would not see the end of what was "passing away".
questions.other: Other readers say "last days" names the whole time between Christ's first and second comings. On this view, the nearness language expresses certainty and readiness, since a thousand years are like a day with the Lord (2 Peter 3:8). They argue the end has been "near" for the church in every age.

questions.q: How can Jesus be said to have "come" in AD 70?
questions.short: In the Old Testament God often "came" in judgment on nations without being seen. This reading says Jesus came in the same way, through the Roman armies.
questions.answer: The Old Testament often speaks of God "coming down" or "riding on a cloud" to judge. "The LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt" (Isaiah 19:1). That judgment came through the Assyrians. God "came down" to see Babel (Genesis 11:5). He came out of his place to tread on the high places of Samaria (Micah 1:3-6). In Psalm 18:9-14 David describes God coming on clouds with thunder to save him from Saul. No one saw God's body in these events. On the fulfilled reading, Jesus' coming in judgment on Jerusalem follows this pattern. Jesus said his generation would see these things (Matthew 24:34). So the "coming" of Matthew 24:27-30 must have a meaning that could be fulfilled then. It was a visible judgment showing that Jesus was enthroned.
examples: Isaiah 19:1: "The LORD rides on a swift cloud" to Egypt. Assyria conquered Egypt in the 7th century BC.
Matthew 26:64: Jesus told the high priest, "You will see the Son of Man... coming on the clouds."
questions.other: Futurists and most traditional readers hold that Matthew 24:30 describes the visible, bodily second coming (Acts 1:11). They accept God's "cloud comings" in the Old Testament but say the New Testament promises a personal return that every eye will see (Revelation 1:7). Partial preterists also expect that final return.

questions.q: Do the warnings to the churches in Revelation 2-3 show that Jesus can "come" in a limited way?
questions.short: Yes, on this reading. Jesus warned Ephesus, Pergamum and Sardis that he would "come" to them in judgment if they did not repent. That was not his final return.
questions.answer: Jesus told Ephesus, "I will come to you and remove your lampstand, unless you repent" (Revelation 2:5). He told Pergamum, "I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth" (Revelation 2:16). He told Sardis, "I will come like a thief" (Revelation 3:3). These comings depend on whether a single church repents. They were threatened against a particular church at a particular time. So they cannot all be the one final return of Christ to the whole world. On the fulfilled reading, this shows the New Testament uses "coming" for acts of judgment in history. Jesus' coming against Jerusalem in AD 70 is the largest example. Robert Thomas has argued these are all forms of the second coming, but the conditional wording makes that hard.
examples: Revelation 3:10-11: to Philadelphia Jesus says "I am coming soon", in a letter to a real first-century city.
John 14:23: Jesus and the Father will "come" and make their home with the one who loves him.
questions.other: Many scholars of all views agree the church warnings are historical visits in judgment. Some, like Robert Thomas, argue they are threats tied to the final coming, which would affect those churches if it came in their time. Others see both: near judgments that preview the final one.

questions.q: What did Jesus mean when he said some standing there would not taste death before seeing him come in his kingdom (Matthew 16:28)?
questions.short: On this reading, he meant a coming within their lifetime: the judgment on Jerusalem and the full showing of his kingdom. Some disciples, such as John, lived to see it.
questions.answer: Jesus said the Son of Man would come with his angels in his Father's glory and repay each person. Then he added: "Some standing here will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom" (Matthew 16:27-28). "Not taste death" implies that most would die but some would still be alive. That fits a span of about forty years, not a week. Henry Alford tied this to the destruction of Jerusalem and the clear display of Christ's kingdom. Peter later asked about John, and Jesus said, "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?" (John 21:22). On this reading, the question about "the end of the age" was asked with this promise in mind.
examples: Matthew 10:23: "You will not finish going through the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes."
Early tradition says John lived into the reign of Trajan, around AD 98 (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5; 3.3.4).
questions.other: Many interpreters link Matthew 16:28 to the transfiguration six days later (Matthew 17:1-8), as 2 Peter 1:16-18 seems to do. Others point to the resurrection or Pentecost. Some see AD 70. Futurists usually choose the transfiguration as a preview of the second coming.

questions.q: To whom did Jesus say, "See that no one leads you astray" (Matthew 24:4)?
questions.short: To the disciples sitting with him on the Mount of Olives. This reading says the warning was first for them and the events they would face.
questions.answer: The discourse was given in private to Peter, James, John and Andrew (Mark 13:3). Jesus said to them: "See that no one leads you astray. For many will come in my name, saying, 'I am the Christ,' and they will lead many astray" (Matthew 24:4-5). He told them they would hear of wars and must not be alarmed. He said, "They will deliver you up... and kill you, and you will be hated" (Matthew 24:9). On the fulfilled reading, the conclusion is direct. The warnings were for the generation that asked about the temple. Comparing the New Testament with historians of the time shows the predicted signs happening before the Roman attack on Jerusalem. That does not make the passage useless for us. It teaches us how faithful Jesus' words are and how to stand firm under deception.
examples: Mark 13:3 names the four listeners: Peter, James, John and Andrew.
Acts 20:29-30: Paul warned the Ephesian elders that fierce wolves would come in and men would rise to draw disciples away.
