questions.other: Futurists say the disciples represent believers, or the Jewish remnant, at the end of history. Many amillennial and historic premillennial readers see the warnings as for all believers in every age, with AD 70 as the first case. Christians of all views use the passage as a call to discernment today.

questions.q: Did false messiahs and false prophets appear before AD 70?
questions.short: Yes. Acts and Josephus name several leaders who drew crowds with promises of deliverance, especially in the 40s and 50s AD.
questions.answer: Gamaliel mentioned Theudas, who claimed to be somebody, and Judas the Galilean, who led a revolt at the census (Acts 5:36-37). Josephus describes a Theudas under the governor Fadus (about AD 45) who said he was a prophet and would part the Jordan. Roman cavalry killed many and beheaded him (Antiquities 20.5.1). Under Felix (AD 52-59) an Egyptian false prophet led thousands to the Mount of Olives, promising Jerusalem's walls would fall (Antiquities 20.8.6; Acts 21:38). Josephus says impostors and deceivers persuaded crowds into the desert with promised signs, and many were killed (Jewish War 2.13.4). On the fulfilled reading, this is exactly what Jesus foretold. Strictly, Jesus warned of both false christs and false prophets (Matthew 24:24), and these men fit one or both labels.
examples: Acts 21:38: the Roman officer asked Paul, "Are you not the Egyptian who led four thousand men into the wilderness?"
Josephus (Jewish War 6.5.2) says a false prophet led people to the temple during the fire of AD 70, promising signs of deliverance; about six thousand died.
questions.other: Many scholars note that Gamaliel's Theudas (spoken of about AD 35) seems earlier than Josephus' Theudas (about AD 45); there may have been two men of that name. Futurists agree false leaders arose then but expect a final wave of deception led by the Antichrist (2 Thessalonians 2:9-10).

questions.q: What do early sources say about Simon the magician of Acts 8?
questions.short: Acts says he claimed to be "someone great" and was called "the Great Power of God". Second-century writers say he claimed divine status and gained followers in Rome.
questions.answer: Luke records that Simon practised magic in Samaria and amazed the people. They said, "This man is the power of God that is called Great" (Acts 8:9-10). Justin Martyr, himself from Samaria, wrote around AD 155 that Simon came to Rome under Claudius and was honored as a god (First Apology 26). Irenaeus said Simon presented himself as a high divine power (Against Heresies 1.23). On the fulfilled reading, Simon is an early example of someone "saying, I am he". One correction is needed. Justin said a statue in Rome was inscribed "To Simon the holy god". In 1574 a base was found on the Tiber island reading "Semoni Sanco Deo Fidio". It honored Semo Sancus, a Sabine god. Justin probably misread it. Simon's claims are still well attested.
examples: Acts 8:18-24: Simon tried to buy the power to give the Spirit; from his name comes the word "simony".
Eusebius (Church History 2.13) repeats Justin's account and calls Simon the first author of heresy.
questions.other: Scholars of all views treat the later Simon stories with caution, since they grew over time. Most agree he was a real figure who made great claims. Some see him less as a messiah figure and more as an early Gnostic teacher, which fits Jesus' warning about false prophets rather than false christs.

questions.q: Are false messiahs in our day a fulfillment of Matthew 24:5?
questions.short: Not on this reading. False christs still appear, and believers must reject them. But the prophecy was fulfilled in the generation before AD 70.
questions.answer: Since the first century many people have claimed to be Christ or a messiah. Examples include Simon bar Kokhba (AD 132), Sabbatai Zevi (1665) and many modern cult leaders. Christians must test every spirit, because many false prophets have gone out into the world (1 John 4:1). On the fulfilled reading, however, the presence of false christs today does not fulfill Matthew 24:5. Jesus set the time limit of "this generation" (Matthew 24:34). The deceivers he predicted came in that period. Later deceivers repeat the pattern but are not the sign Jesus gave. This distinction matters. It keeps believers from reading each new cult leader as a countdown signal, and it keeps the focus on the clear warning: do not follow anyone but the true Christ.
examples: Simon bar Kokhba led the revolt of AD 132-135; Rabbi Akiva hailed him as messiah. It ended in disaster for Judea.
1 John 2:18 says "many antichrists have come; therefore we know that it is the last hour": John saw them in his own day.
questions.other: Futurists teach that false christs will increase toward the end and climax in the Antichrist. Many amillennial readers see Matthew 24:5 as a pattern for the whole church age, fulfilled again and again. Both agree that false messiahs today must be resisted with Scripture.

questions.q: Is our generation seeing signs that no earlier generation has seen?
questions.short: This reading says no. War, famine, plague and earthquake fill all of history. Jesus tied his signs to the generation of his hearers.
questions.answer: Many modern books claim that no previous generation has seen so many signs so close together. But the history of the world is full of war, famine and disease. The fourteenth century lost perhaps a third of Europe to the Black Death. The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) devastated central Europe. Every age has had reasons to think the end was near. On the fulfilled reading, Jesus gave a clear time frame for his signs: "This generation will not pass away until all these things take place" (Matthew 24:34). The signs were meant to warn the disciples to flee before Jerusalem fell (Luke 21:20-21). History shows those signs did appear between about AD 30 and 70. Reading them into our news overlooks both the time text and the record of history.
examples: The Antonine Plague (AD 165-180) killed millions across the Roman Empire, long after AD 70.
The influenza pandemic of 1918 killed tens of millions; many at the time saw it as an end-time sign.
questions.other: Futurists answer that the signs are like birth pains: they grow in frequency and strength toward the end (Matthew 24:8). They point to world wars, nuclear weapons and global reach as new. Amillennial readers say the signs mark the whole age and call every generation to be ready.

questions.q: How could there be "wars and rumors of wars" during the Roman Peace?
questions.short: The Roman Peace was fragile. Revolts, border wars and riots broke out across the empire, and Jesus' warning stood out because people expected peace.
questions.answer: Augustus began the Pax Romana after the civil wars ended (about 27 BC). Rome boasted of peace. But peace was never complete. In AD 40 the emperor Caligula ordered his statue set up in the Jerusalem temple. Jews refused, and war seemed certain until his death in AD 41 (Josephus, Antiquities 18.8.2-9). Tacitus in his Annals reports troubles in Germany, Africa, Thrace, Gaul, Britain and Armenia. Boudica's revolt in Britain (AD 60-61) killed tens of thousands. On the fulfilled reading, "wars and rumors of wars" make a fitting sign in a time that boasted of peace. Jesus told his disciples not to be alarmed: "the end is not yet" (Matthew 24:6). These events were the first birth pains, not the final blow.
examples: The near-war over Caligula's statue (AD 40-41) was a "rumor of war" that came to the very temple.
Tacitus, Histories 1.2, describes the period AD 69 as "rich in disasters, terrible with battles, torn by civil strife".
questions.other: Futurists note that wars have always existed and so cannot alone be a final sign. They argue that Jesus' point was that wars are not the end, and the real signs are those later in the discourse. Many readers of all views see the verse as a warning against panic in any age.

questions.q: What conflicts in the first century fit "nation will rise against nation"?
questions.short: Riots and massacres between Jews and Greeks or Syrians in many cities, the Jewish revolt, and Rome's own civil wars all happened before AD 70.
questions.answer: Josephus records that when the war began in AD 66, the Greeks of Caesarea killed about twenty thousand Jews in one hour (Jewish War 2.18.1). Fighting then spread through the cities of Syria, where Jews and Gentiles divided into armed camps. In Alexandria about fifty thousand Jews died (Jewish War 2.18.8). In Damascus about ten thousand were killed (Jewish War 2.20.2). Earlier, around AD 40, more than fifty thousand Jews were killed at Seleucia in Mesopotamia (Antiquities 18.9.9). On the fulfilled reading, these clashes between peoples ("nation against nation") and between realms ("kingdom against kingdom") fit Jesus' words in time and place. They show that the birth pains were real and intense for the generation he addressed. The suffering fell heavily on Jewish communities, and that should be remembered with sorrow.
examples: Jewish War 2.18.2: after Caesarea, Josephus says every city in Syria was divided into two armies.
Josephus says he gave only a brief account of Rome's civil wars because so many other writers had described them (Jewish War 4.9.2).
questions.other: Futurists read "nation against nation" as a global pattern of wars at the end, often linking it to the world wars of the twentieth century. Some scholars note the phrase echoes Isaiah 19:2 and 2 Chronicles 15:6, where it describes local chaos in judgment, which suits either a first-century or a later setting.

questions.q: What was the "year of the four emperors", and why does it matter here?
questions.short: In AD 68-69 four men held power in Rome in quick succession: Nero, Galba, Otho and Vitellius. All died violently, showing how unstable the empire was before Jerusalem fell.
questions.answer: Nero killed himself in June AD 68. Galba was murdered in January 69. Otho took his own life in April 69. Vitellius was killed in December 69 as Vespasian's forces took Rome. Vespasian had been leading the war in Judea. He left his son Titus to finish the siege of Jerusalem, which fell in AD 70. On the fulfilled reading, this crisis fits Jesus' picture of kingdoms in turmoil. It also shows how closely the Jewish war was tied to the empire's fate. Some even see a link with Revelation 17:10, which speaks of seven kings, "five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come". On a Neronic dating, the sixth king would be Nero, and the brief seventh would be Galba.
examples: Tacitus (Histories 1.4) says the death of Nero revealed a secret of empire: an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome.
Suetonius (Vespasian 4-5) reports a widespread belief that men from Judea would rule the world; Vespasian was proclaimed emperor in the east in July 69.
questions.other: Historians accept these facts. The debate is about their prophetic meaning. Futurists see Revelation 17 as describing future kingdoms or empires. Scholars who date Revelation to about AD 95 read the seven kings differently. Many simply treat the year of four emperors as background, not fulfillment.

questions.q: Was there a famine in the first century that fits Jesus' words?
questions.short: Yes. The prophet Agabus foretold a great famine over the world, and Luke says it happened under Claudius (AD 41-54). Roman writers also record food shortages then.
questions.answer: Acts records that Agabus, speaking by the Spirit, predicted "a great famine over all the world" (oikoumene). Luke adds, "This took place in the days of Claudius" (Acts 11:28). The believers in Antioch sent relief to Judea. Later Paul collected gifts from churches in Galatia, Macedonia and Achaia for the poor in Jerusalem (1 Corinthians 16:1-3; Romans 15:25-26). Josephus describes severe famine in Judea about AD 46-48, when Queen Helena of Adiabene bought grain from Egypt for the city (Antiquities 20.2.5). Tacitus says that in AD 51 Rome had only fifteen days of grain left (Annals 12.43). On the fulfilled reading, the disciples hearing these reports would have remembered Jesus' words on the Mount of Olives.
examples: Suetonius (Claudius 18) says Claudius was pelted with crusts in the Forum during a grain shortage.
Acts 11:29-30: each disciple gave as able, and Barnabas and Saul carried the gift to the elders in Judea.
questions.other: Futurists agree famines occurred then but argue they were local and limited. They expect worldwide famine in the future tribulation (Revelation 6:5-8). Many scholars note that famines happen in every age, so Jesus listed them as "the beginning of birth pains" rather than as a precise end-time clock.

questions.q: How severe was the famine during the siege of Jerusalem?
questions.short: Extremely severe. Josephus describes houses full of the dying and streets full of the dead as Titus' siege cut off all food.
questions.answer: In AD 70 Titus surrounded Jerusalem with a wall to stop people leaving and food entering (Jewish War 5.12.1-2). This fulfilled Jesus' words that enemies would "set up a barricade around you and surround you" (Luke 19:43). Josephus writes that famine then swallowed whole houses and families. Upper rooms were full of dying women and children, and lanes were full of the old who had died. Young men wandered the markets like shadows, swollen from hunger, and fell where they stood (Jewish War 5.12.3). He even records the terrible case of a mother named Mary who ate her child (Jewish War 6.3.4). On the fulfilled reading, war and famine go together, and Jesus lists famines right after wars. His tears over the city (Luke 19:41) show this was a grief to him, not a triumph.
examples: Deuteronomy 28:53-57 warned that in a siege parents would eat their children. Lamentations 4:10 records this in 586 BC.
Luke 23:28-29: Jesus told the women of Jerusalem to weep for themselves and their children.
questions.other: Most Christian readers accept that the siege fulfilled Luke 19:43-44 and Luke 21:20-24. Futurists separate these Luke texts, which they agree describe AD 70, from Matthew 24:15-22, which they see as a future great tribulation. Some scholars caution that Josephus may have heightened some details for effect.

questions.q: Did Jesus say earthquakes would increase in number and strength before the end?
questions.short: No. He said there would be earthquakes "in various places" and Luke says "great earthquakes". He said nothing about a rising count.
questions.answer: Some modern writers claim the Lord meant earthquakes of record-breaking size and number. But Jesus simply said, "There will be famines and earthquakes in various places" (Matthew 24:7). Luke adds "great earthquakes" (Luke 21:11). He does not say they will grow in frequency. Geologists also report that the number of strong earthquakes has stayed fairly steady. The apparent rise is because there are far more seismic stations to record small quakes. Christian geologist Steven Austin and New Testament scholar Mark Strauss made this point in 1999. On the fulfilled reading, the claim of an "increase" is read into the text. It also sets believers up for disappointment, since the data do not show it. The sign was met in the generation Jesus addressed.
examples: The United States Geological Survey reports that large quakes (magnitude 7 or more) average about 15 a year, with no long-term rise.
In 1931 there were about 350 seismic stations worldwide; today there are thousands, so many more small quakes are recorded.
questions.other: Some futurists still argue that the birth-pain image implies increasing intensity. Others agree there is no statistical increase and say earthquakes are simply among the signs that mark the age. Many scholars see earthquakes in prophecy as symbols of God shaking the nations (Haggai 2:6).

questions.q: Were there significant earthquakes before AD 70?
questions.short: Yes. The Bible records earthquakes at the cross, the resurrection and in Philippi. Roman writers record quakes at Laodicea, Pompeii and many other places.
questions.answer: Matthew records an earthquake when Jesus died (Matthew 27:51-54) and a great earthquake at the resurrection (Matthew 28:2). Acts tells of a great earthquake that shook the prison in Philippi (Acts 16:26). Outside the Bible, Tacitus says Laodicea was ruined by an earthquake in AD 60 and rebuilt without Roman help (Annals 14.27). A strong quake damaged Pompeii in February AD 62 (Tacitus, Annals 15.22; Seneca, Natural Questions 6.1). Some writers date it to 63. Crete, Smyrna, Chios, Samos, Hierapolis, Colossae and Rome are also listed in this period. Josephus records a violent storm and earthquake in Judea in AD 68, which he said showed God's anger (Jewish War 4.4.5). On the fulfilled reading, the sign was met in full in that generation.
examples: Revelation 3:17 has the church at Laodicea saying "I am rich", and Tacitus confirms the city rebuilt itself from its own wealth.
Edward Plumptre wrote that perhaps no period was so marked by such shocks as the years between the cross and the fall of Jerusalem.
questions.other: Few dispute these events. Futurists respond that first-century quakes were a foretaste, and that the final period will include a greater quake than any before (Revelation 16:18). Some readers see Jesus' list as general marks of the whole age, so quakes in any era are reminders, not timers.

questions.q: Were there "terrors and great signs from heaven" (Luke 21:11) before AD 70?
questions.short: Yes. Roman and Jewish writers record comets and strange sights in the sky in those years, including a comet that stood over Jerusalem.
questions.answer: Luke alone records "terrors and great signs from heaven" in his list of wars, quakes, famines and plagues. In the ancient world comets were often seen as signs of political change. Tacitus says a comet appeared in AD 60, and people began to ask who would succeed Nero (Annals 14.22). Suetonius says that after a comet Nero put to death leading men and their families (Nero 36). Halley's Comet passed in AD 66, the year the Jewish war began. Josephus writes of "a star resembling a sword" over the city and a comet that lasted a whole year (Jewish War 6.5.3). He also describes a bright light around the altar at night and a heavy temple gate opening by itself. On the fulfilled reading, Luke 21:11 was met within the generation.
examples: Tacitus (Histories 5.13) records that armies were seen clashing in the sky and the temple doors opened, with a voice saying the gods were leaving.
Matthew 2:1-3: a star brought joy to the wise men but alarm to Herod, who feared a rival.
questions.other: Futurists say these sights were minor compared with the cosmic signs still to come (Revelation 6:12-14). Skeptical historians treat the portents as legends that grew after the event. Some interpreters read "signs from heaven" symbolically, as God's judgments on rulers, rather than as astronomy.

questions.q: Must the heavenly signs of Luke 21:11 have a modern, sensational fulfillment?
questions.short: This reading says no. When a first-century fulfillment is on record, stretching the text to fit UFOs or modern technology misreads it.
questions.answer: Some popular writers, such as Chuck Missler, have suggested that Luke 21:11 points to UFOs or alien and demonic activity in our time. The fulfilled reading answers that this stretches Jesus' words beyond their plain meaning. Jesus gave these signs to his disciples so they would know when to flee Jerusalem (Luke 21:20-21). A sign is useful only to the people who are meant to see it. The first-century record shows comets, portents and fear in exactly that period. To skip over that record and search for a modern match puts speculation in place of history. It also makes the Bible's message depend on the latest trend. The safer method is to ask what the first hearers would have understood.
examples: Luke 21:28: "When these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads." The signs were for those who would live through them.
Deuteronomy 29:29: secret things belong to the Lord, but revealed things belong to us and our children.
questions.other: Most scholars of all views reject UFO readings. Futurists who do not hold such ideas still expect literal cosmic disturbances in the future. Amillennial readers often see the heavenly signs as symbols that recur whenever God judges proud powers.

questions.q: Were the disciples delivered up to tribulation and killed, as Matthew 24:9 says?
questions.short: Yes. Acts records arrests, floggings and the deaths of Stephen and James. Peter and Paul were killed under Nero, before AD 70.
questions.answer: Persecution began soon after Pentecost. Peter and John were jailed and warned (Acts 4:3, 17). They were later flogged (Acts 5:40). Stephen was stoned (Acts 7:54-60). A great persecution scattered the church from Jerusalem (Acts 8:1). Herod Agrippa I killed James the brother of John with the sword and arrested Peter (Acts 12:1-3). Paul was stoned at Lystra and left for dead (Acts 14:19). He lists beatings, lashes and dangers from both Jews and Gentiles (2 Corinthians 11:24-26). He stood before Gallio, Felix, Festus and Agrippa (Acts 18:12; 24-26). Tacitus says Nero blamed Christians for the fire of AD 64 and had them killed in cruel ways (Annals 15.44). Early tradition says Peter and Paul died in that persecution (1 Clement 5). On the fulfilled reading, Matthew 24:9 came true in detail.
examples: Tacitus, Annals 15.44: Christians were covered with animal skins and torn by dogs, or set on fire as torches at night.
Revelation 1:9: John calls himself a "partner in the tribulation" with the churches.
questions.other: Futurists agree persecution happened then but see Matthew 24:9 as also describing a future tribulation for believers, especially Jewish believers, under the Antichrist. Many amillennial readers see the verse as true of the whole church age. No view denies the first-century persecutions.

questions.q: Were Christians "hated by all nations" before AD 70?
questions.short: In a real sense, yes. They faced hostility from Jewish authorities in Judea and from pagan crowds and rulers across the empire, climaxing in Nero's persecution.
questions.answer: Jesus said, "You will be hated by all nations for my name's sake" (Matthew 24:9). In Acts, believers are opposed in Jerusalem, Damascus, Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth and Ephesus. They are called men who "have turned the world upside down" (Acts 17:6). Jews in Rome told Paul that this sect was "spoken against everywhere" (Acts 28:22). Tacitus calls Christians a group hated for their "crimes" and charged with "hatred of the human race" (Annals 15.44). Tertullian later wrote that the very name of Christian was under attack (Apology 2). On the fulfilled reading, this widespread hatred within Jesus' generation fits his words. Peter's first letter, written to scattered believers, assumes they are being insulted for the name of Christ (1 Peter 4:14-16).
examples: Acts 28:22: "With regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against."
Suetonius (Nero 16) lists punishments on Christians, "a class of men given to a new and harmful superstition".
questions.other: Futurists expect a worldwide hatred of believers in the final tribulation, beyond the first-century scale. Amillennial readers say "all nations" describes how the church is treated in every age. All agree the early church suffered widely and that Jesus' words gave it courage.

questions.q: If Matthew 24:9 was fulfilled before AD 70, does that mean Christians today will not face tribulation?
questions.short: No. Jesus said, "In the world you will have tribulation". The specific prophecy was fulfilled then, but suffering for Christ is part of every age.
questions.answer: The fulfilled reading does not promise an easy life. Jesus said, "In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world" (John 16:33). Paul said that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). He also said all who desire to live a godly life in Christ will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12). The point is narrower. The specific sufferings in Matthew 24:9 were linked to the time before Jerusalem's fall. Believers today still suffer, and in some lands very severely. But they should not read their troubles as a countdown clock. They can take comfort from how God kept his word to the first church. The same God will strengthen the church now (Romans 8:35-37).
examples: Paul wrote that the folly of false teachers "will be plain to all" (2 Timothy 3:9); God vindicated his church then and can do so now.
Romans 5:3: "We rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance."
questions.other: All Christian views agree that believers suffer in this age. Pretribulationists add that the church will be removed before a future seven-year tribulation of God's wrath. Posttribulationists say the church will go through a final tribulation. Amillennialists see tribulation as the normal mark of the whole age.

questions.q: Was there a falling away and betrayal among believers before AD 70?
questions.short: Yes. Paul names people who deserted him, and the letters warn often of false teachers. Jesus said many would fall away and betray one another.
questions.answer: Jesus said many would fall away, betray one another and hate one another (Matthew 24:10). Paul wrote that "all who are in Asia turned away from me", naming Phygelus and Hermogenes (2 Timothy 1:15). Demas left him, "in love with this present world" (2 Timothy 4:10). At his first defense "all deserted me" (2 Timothy 4:16). Alexander the coppersmith did him great harm (2 Timothy 4:14). Hymenaeus and Philetus swerved from the truth, saying the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:17-18). Hebrews warns readers not to drift back from Christ under pressure (Hebrews 6:4-6; 10:26-29). Tacitus says some arrested Christians under Nero gave the names of others (Annals 15.44). On the fulfilled reading, these betrayals fit Jesus' words in the same generation.
examples: Tacitus, Annals 15.44: first those who confessed were seized; then, on their information, a vast number more.
Galatians 1:6: Paul was astonished that the Galatians were "so quickly deserting" the gospel.
questions.other: Futurists expect a great end-time apostasy, often linked with 2 Thessalonians 2:3. Others note that partial preterists also read 2 Thessalonians 2:3 as first-century. Amillennial readers see falling away as a recurring danger for the church in every generation.

questions.q: Did false prophets and growing lawlessness mark the church's first generation?
questions.short: Yes. The later New Testament letters are full of warnings about false teachers already present, and John says "many antichrists have come".
questions.answer: Jesus said many false prophets would arise and lead many astray, and because lawlessness would increase, the love of many would grow cold (Matthew 24:11-12). Peter warned that false teachers would arise among believers, just as false prophets arose in Israel (2 Peter 2:1). Jude says such people "have crept in unnoticed" already (Jude 4). John writes that "many false prophets have gone out into the world" (1 John 4:1). He adds, "Many antichrists have come. Therefore we know that it is the last hour" (1 John 2:18). Jesus' letter to Ephesus says they had "abandoned the love you had at first" (Revelation 2:4). On the fulfilled reading, the apostles saw Jesus' words being fulfilled around them, and they read it as a sign that the end of the age was near.
examples: 1 John 2:18: John reasons from the presence of many antichrists to "it is the last hour".
Revelation 2:2: Ephesus tested those who called themselves apostles and found them false.
questions.other: Many readers agree the apostles saw these warnings fulfilled in their day. Futurists add that a greater climax of deception and lawlessness will come before Christ returns. Amillennial readers say "the last hour" covers the whole time from Christ's first coming to his return.

questions.q: What "end" did Jesus mean in "the one who endures to the end will be saved" (Matthew 24:13)?
questions.short: On this reading, the end of the age that the disciples asked about: the fall of the temple. Those who held firm and obeyed Jesus' warning were kept safe.
questions.answer: The disciples asked about the end of the age in connection with the temple (Matthew 24:3). Jesus had just said the house would be left desolate and that "all these things will come upon this generation" (Matthew 23:36-38). So the "end" here is that end. On the fulfilled reading, "saved" includes being kept alive through the war, though it does not exclude final salvation. Jesus told them to flee to the mountains when they saw the sign (Matthew 24:16). Eusebius records that the Jerusalem church, warned by a revelation, left the city before the war and settled in Pella beyond the Jordan (Church History 3.5.3). Henry Alford wrote that no Christian is known to have died in the siege. The word "end" always needs its context. Here the context is the temple.
examples: Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3: believers in Jerusalem moved to Pella, a city of the Decapolis, before the siege.
Luke 21:18-19: "Not a hair of your head will perish. By your endurance you will gain your lives."
questions.other: Many interpreters take "the end" as the end of a believer's life or the end of history, and "saved" as eternal salvation. Some scholars question how much of the Pella tradition is historical. Futurists see the verse as speaking to believers who live through the final tribulation.

questions.q: If "the end" in Matthew 24 is still future, why do futurist timelines have so much happening after it?
questions.short: Because "end" always means the end of something named in the context. This reading says the context of Matthew 24 is the end of the temple age.
questions.answer: Futurist timelines place many events after the "end": a great tribulation, Christ's return, a thousand-year kingdom, a final rebellion, and the new heavens and earth. So even on their view, the "end" of Matthew 24:14 is not the end of everything. On the fulfilled reading, this shows that "end" must be defined by its setting. In Matthew 24 the setting is the disciples' question about the temple and the end of the age (Matthew 24:2-3). The kingdom would be taken from the leaders of that time and given to a fruitful people (Matthew 21:43-45). For them it was "the end". Revelation likewise says its events are "near" (Revelation 1:3). Pushing these texts two thousand years away makes time words almost meaningless.
examples: 1 Peter 4:7: "The end of all things is at hand" was written to believers in the AD 60s.
1 Corinthians 15:24 speaks of a different "end": when Christ hands over the kingdom after defeating death.
questions.other: Futurists answer that "the end" in Matthew 24 means the end of the present age before the kingdom, which fits their timeline. Amillennial readers see one final end at Christ's return. Many agree that the word needs context, but they read the context as wider than the temple.

questions.q: Was the gospel preached "in the whole world" before AD 70, as Matthew 24:14 requires?
questions.short: Yes, according to Paul. He wrote that the gospel had been proclaimed "in all creation under heaven" and was bearing fruit "in the whole world".
questions.answer: Jesus said, "This gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come" (Matthew 24:14). Some futurist writers stress that the end can come only after the gospel reaches all nations. On the fulfilled reading, Paul says this had happened in his own day. The gospel "has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven" (Colossians 1:23). It was "bearing fruit and growing in the whole world" (Colossians 1:6). The faith of the Romans was "proclaimed in all the world" (Romans 1:8). Paul applied Psalm 19:4 to the preaching: "Their voice has gone out to all the earth" (Romans 10:18). Henry Alford noted that every nation of the Roman world had heard before Jerusalem fell. That gave scattered Jewish communities a chance to receive Christ.
examples: Acts 19:10: "All the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks", within two years.
Romans 15:24, 28: Paul planned to go to Spain, the western edge of the known world.
questions.other: Futurists and many others say Paul used representative or hopeful language, and that Matthew 24:14 still drives world missions today. They connect it with Revelation 7:9, where people from every nation stand before the throne. Many amillennial readers see a first fulfillment then and a fuller one before the return.

questions.q: What does "whole world" (oikoumene) mean in Matthew 24:14?
questions.short: It means the inhabited world known to the writer, often the Roman Empire. Luke uses the same word for Caesar's census of "all the world".
questions.answer: The Greek word in Matthew 24:14 is oikoumene, "the inhabited earth". Luke 2:1 uses the same word: Caesar Augustus ordered that "all the world" should be registered. That clearly means the Roman Empire. Agabus foretold a famine over "all the world" (oikoumene), which happened under Claudius (Acts 11:28). Paul's enemies said he stirred up Jews "throughout the world" (Acts 24:5). Some critics, such as Thomas Ice, ask whether preterists think the gospel reached the Western Hemisphere before AD 70. The fulfilled reading answers with the same question about Luke 2:1. No one thinks Augustus took a census of the Americas. Words must be read as their first readers used them. Even where kosmos is used, Paul says the gospel had gone into the whole world (Colossians 1:6).
examples: Luke 2:1: "a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world (oikoumene) should be registered."
Acts 17:6: the missionaries were accused of turning "the world" (oikoumene) upside down.
questions.other: Futurists accept that oikoumene can mean the Roman world. They argue that Matthew's "all nations" (also in Matthew 28:19) widens the scope to the whole globe. Some scholars note that oikoumene can also mean the whole inhabited earth in other texts (Acts 17:31).

questions.q: Does "to all nations" in Matthew 24:14 mean every people group on earth today?
questions.short: This reading says no. Paul wrote that the gospel "has been made known to all nations" in his day, using the same phrase.
questions.answer: Some commentators argue that "all nations" sets the scope of Matthew 24:14. Since not every nation had heard before AD 70, they say, the verse is still future. But Paul ends Romans by praising God for the gospel that "has now been disclosed and made known to all nations" (Romans 16:25-26). If "all nations" sets the scope, Paul says it was met. The parallel in Mark says the gospel must "first be proclaimed to all nations" (Mark 13:10), again in the context of the disciples' own trials. Philip Doddridge, an 18th-century writer, gathered early traditions that apostles preached in Syria, Egypt, Ethiopia, Parthia, Persia, India and the west within thirty years of the cross. Many of these traditions are late and uncertain. But Paul's own statement is clear.
examples: Acts 2:5-11: at Pentecost there were Jews "from every nation under heaven", from Parthia to Rome, who heard the gospel and carried it home.
Acts 8:27-39: an Ethiopian court official believed and returned to Africa.
questions.other: Many missions-minded Christians read Matthew 24:14 as an unfinished task that must be completed before Christ returns. They see Paul's words as a statement of the gospel's reach in principle, not a completed census. Others hold both: a first-century fulfillment and a continuing pattern for mission.

questions.q: Do modern plans for a third temple in Jerusalem relate to Bible prophecy?
questions.short: This reading says no. Some groups prepare vessels and priestly garments, but no New Testament verse links a future temple to God's plan.
questions.answer: Since the 1980s some Jewish groups have studied how to rebuild the temple and restore its priesthood. The Temple Institute in Jerusalem has made vessels and garments. Stories spread among Christians about stones cut abroad or a prefabricated temple. Some Christian writers see these plans as signs that the end is near. On the fulfilled reading, such plans have no role in the fulfillment of prophecy. The New Testament nowhere says a temple must be rebuilt. The temple Jesus spoke of was the one standing in his day, which fell in AD 70. Christians should treat their Jewish neighbours' hopes with respect. But they should not build their own theology on news reports. Many Jewish leaders themselves are divided, and some teach that the Messiah alone may rebuild.
examples: A 1989 news report described a small group of Israelis and Jews abroad quietly preparing for a third temple.
Maimonides (12th century) taught that the Messiah would rebuild the temple (Mishneh Torah, Kings 11.1); many rabbis therefore oppose human efforts now.
questions.other: Dispensational writers believe a third temple will be built, either before or during a future seven-year tribulation. They see current preparations as preparing the stage. Most amillennial, postmillennial and historic premillennial Christians agree with this reading that no rebuilt temple is required by Scripture.

questions.q: What happened to predictions that the temple would be rebuilt by a certain date?
questions.short: They failed. For example, a Jerusalem rabbi said in 1991 that the temple would be rebuilt in 1992. Dates like this show the danger of reading headlines as prophecy.
questions.answer: During the Gulf War of 1991 a Jerusalem-based rabbi linked the war with Iraq to old texts about Babylon. He said preparation for the Messiah began with the Balfour Declaration of 1917, continued with Jerusalem's reunification in 1967, and would end with the temple's rebuilding in 1992. That year passed with no temple. Christian writers have made similar forecasts. On the fulfilled reading, these failures repeat a pattern. Current events are tied to prophecy, dates are set, and then the dates pass. Jesus warned against being led astray by people who say "the time is at hand" (Luke 21:8). The safest path is to read prophecy in its own time setting and to test claims by Scripture rather than by the news.
examples: Luke 21:8: Jesus warned of those who say "The time is at hand! Do not go after them."
Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970) suggested the generation after 1948 would see the end within about forty years.
questions.other: Futurist teachers today usually avoid dates and say only that a temple will be built at some point. They agree that failed predictions are harmful. They argue that failed dates show human error, not that the temple prophecies are false.

questions.q: Does the New Testament predict that the temple will be rebuilt?
questions.short: No verse says so. Even leading futurist writers admit there is no verse that says "there will be a third temple". They infer it from other texts.
questions.answer: Read the New Testament for a promise of a rebuilt temple, and none is found. Futurist authors Thomas Ice and Timothy Demy wrote that there are no Bible verses that say there will be a third temple. They infer it from texts that mention a temple in the end-time events: Matthew 24:15, 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Revelation 11:1-2. On the fulfilled reading, there is a simple reason for the silence. The real temple of God in the New Testament is the church, built on Christ as the cornerstone (1 Peter 2:4-7). The stone temple was about to pass away (Hebrews 8:13). The three texts that mention a temple were all written while Herod's temple still stood. Their first readers would have thought of that building.
examples: Ephesians 2:20-22: believers are "being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit".
1 Corinthians 3:16: "Do you not know that you are God's temple?" Paul wrote this while the Jerusalem temple stood.
questions.other: Futurists say a rebuilt temple is a valid inference, as the Trinity is a valid inference without the word. They argue that 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Revelation 11 describe events that did not happen in AD 70, so a later temple is needed. Others read these texts as symbols of the church.

questions.q: Why do futurist systems need a rebuilt temple?
questions.short: Because they place the "abomination of desolation" and the man of lawlessness in the future. Those events need a temple standing in Jerusalem.
questions.answer: In the futurist scheme, a future Antichrist makes a covenant with Israel for seven years. In the middle he breaks it, stops the sacrifices and sets himself up in a rebuilt temple as God. This is the "abomination of desolation" (Matthew 24:15; Daniel 9:27) and the man of lawlessness sitting in God's temple (2 Thessalonians 2:4). So a temple must exist for this to happen. On the fulfilled reading, the need for a rebuilt temple comes from the system, not from the texts. When Jesus spoke of "the holy place", the temple was still standing in "the holy city" (Matthew 4:5; 27:53). He walked away from that temple (Matthew 24:1). His disciples would have thought of it, not of a building to be raised two thousand years later.
examples: Luke 21:20 explains the "abomination" for Gentile readers: "When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near."
Matthew 4:5 and 27:53 call first-century Jerusalem "the holy city".
questions.other: Dispensationalists answer that the rebuilt temple is required by a literal reading of Daniel 9:27, 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Revelation 11:1-2, which they say were not fulfilled in AD 70. Some non-dispensational futurists share this view. Others read the "temple" in 2 Thessalonians as the church.

questions.q: Which temple did Jesus mean when he spoke of the abomination "standing in the holy place" (Matthew 24:15)?
questions.short: On this reading, the temple standing at that time, the one the disciples had just pointed out. Nothing in the text points to a different building.
questions.answer: The setting of Matthew 24 is one temple. Jesus leaves it (24:1). The disciples point to its buildings. He says its stones will be thrown down (24:2). He then tells them what sign to watch for: "When you see the abomination of desolation... standing in the holy place, then let those in Judea flee to the mountains" (24:15-16). The command to flee from Judea only makes sense for people living there when the sign appears. Luke records the same moment as Jerusalem being surrounded by armies (Luke 21:20). On the fulfilled reading, Jesus would not leave out a crucial detail such as a temple being rebuilt if one were needed. If a future building were meant, his hearers would have had no way to know it.
examples: Josephus (Jewish War 6.6.1) records that Roman soldiers set up their standards in the temple court and sacrificed to them after it burned.
Daniel 11:31 and 1 Maccabees 1:54 describe an earlier "abomination" under Antiochus IV in 167 BC, in the second temple.
questions.other: Futurists answer that the abomination includes a person who claims to be God (2 Thessalonians 2:4), which did not happen in AD 70. They see a future temple. Some amillennial and historic premillennial readers see AD 70 as a first fulfillment and expect a final, greater one.

questions.q: What temple would the first readers of 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Revelation 11:1-2 have thought of?
questions.short: The one still standing in Jerusalem. This reading says all New Testament texts that mention the temple in prophecy were written before AD 70.
questions.answer: Futurist writers rely on three main New Testament texts for a future temple: Matthew 24:15, 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Revelation 11:1-2. Paul wrote 2 Thessalonians about AD 50-51, while the temple stood. On the fulfilled reading, Revelation was also written before AD 70, likely in the reign of Nero. In Revelation 11:1-2 John is told to measure the temple and altar but to leave out the outer court. It will be trampled by the nations for forty-two months. The Roman war against Judea lasted about that long, from spring AD 67 to August AD 70. Any reader in the 50s or 60s would have taken these words as referring to the existing temple. To look for another building, the reader would need a clear signal in the text.
examples: Luke 21:24: "Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles", the same image as Revelation 11:2.
Vespasian began the campaign in Galilee in spring AD 67; the temple fell in August AD 70, about 42 months later.
questions.other: Most scholars date Revelation to about AD 95, under Domitian, citing Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.3). On that dating the temple in Revelation 11 must be symbolic (often the church) or future. Many amillennial scholars read 2 Thessalonians 2:4 as the church or as a general picture of blasphemy.

questions.q: Is there a gap of two thousand years between the 69th and 70th weeks of Daniel 9?
questions.short: This reading says no. Daniel presents seventy weeks as one unbroken period. Nothing in the text signals a pause after the 69th week.
questions.answer: Daniel 9:24 says "seventy weeks are decreed" to finish transgression, make atonement and bring everlasting righteousness. Verses 25-27 count seven weeks, then sixty-two weeks, then one week. Dispensationalists place the first 69 weeks before the Messiah's death. They then insert a gap of the church age before the last week, which they place in the future. On the fulfilled reading, this breaks the plain sense of a counted number. If someone said "seventy years" and stopped the clock after sixty-nine, the count would lose meaning. Jeremiah's seventy years ran without a break (Daniel 9:2). The text says the Messiah would "make a strong covenant with many for one week" and "put an end to sacrifice" in the middle (Daniel 9:27). This reading sees that in Christ's ministry and death, with the city's destruction following.
examples: Jeremiah 25:11-12 and 29:10: Daniel read Jeremiah's seventy years as a continuous span (Daniel 9:2).
Hebrews 10:9-10, 18: Christ's offering did away with the old sacrifices; "there is no longer any offering for sin."
questions.other: Dispensationalists defend the gap by pointing to other prophecies with gaps, such as Isaiah 61:1-2 in Luke 4:18-19. They read "he" in Daniel 9:27 as "the prince who is to come", the Antichrist, not the Messiah. Many scholars also hold that the seventieth week ends with the events of AD 70 or with the gospel going to the Gentiles.

questions.q: Is the gap in Daniel's seventy weeks a new idea in church history?
questions.short: Its modern form, with a secret rapture and a church-age parenthesis, came in the 1800s. But some early writers also placed the last week at the end of history.
questions.answer: The fulfilled reading stresses that the dispensational "great parenthesis" became popular through J. N. Darby and the Scofield Reference Bible (1909). Most commentators before them, from Eusebius to the Reformers, saw the seventy weeks fulfilled in Christ's first coming. A correction is needed, however. Some early church writers did separate the last week. Irenaeus (about AD 180) placed half of the last week under the Antichrist (Against Heresies 5.25.4). Hippolytus (about AD 204) explicitly put the seventieth week at the end of the world (Commentary on Daniel 4.35; On Christ and Antichrist 43). So a gap is not entirely new. What is new is the full system built on it. The strongest case for this reading rests on the text of Daniel, not on history alone.
examples: Eusebius (Demonstration of the Gospel 8.2) tied the seventy weeks to Christ's coming and the following events in Judea.
The Scofield Reference Bible's note on Daniel 9:24 spread the parenthesis view widely in the 20th century.
questions.other: Dispensationalists cite Irenaeus and Hippolytus to show that a future seventieth week has early roots. Others note that many church fathers held a variety of views on Daniel 9. Historians agree that the full pretribulational system with a church-age parenthesis was formed in the 1830s.

questions.q: What is God's temple in the New Testament?
questions.short: Christ himself, and the people joined to him. Believers are "living stones" built into a spiritual house where God's Spirit lives.
questions.answer: Peter writes, "You yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ" (1 Peter 2:5). Paul says believers "are the temple of the living God" (2 Corinthians 6:16). He describes Jews and Gentiles joined on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone. In him the whole structure grows into "a holy temple in the Lord" (Ephesians 2:20-22). Each believer's body is also a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19). On the covenantal reading, this is the temple that the prophets' hopes pointed to. It is made of people from every nation. It is not torn down by armies. Calling for a new stone temple, on this view, turns attention back from the reality to the shadow.
examples: 1 Corinthians 3:16-17: "God's temple is holy, and you are that temple."
Revelation 21:22: in the new Jerusalem John saw no temple, "for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb".
questions.other: All Christian traditions agree that the church is now God's temple. Dispensationalists hold this too but add that God will also restore a physical temple for Israel's role in the tribulation and millennium. They see the church and a future temple as serving different purposes in God's plan.

questions.q: Were the Old Testament promises of a rebuilt temple fulfilled?
questions.short: Yes, on this reading. They were fulfilled when the exiles rebuilt the temple after Babylon and, more fully, in Christ and his church.
questions.answer: Prophets such as Haggai and Zechariah urged the returned exiles to rebuild the temple. It was finished in 516 BC (Ezra 6:15). Haggai promised that the glory of the latter house would be greater than the former (Haggai 2:9). This reading says that greater glory came when the Lord himself entered that temple in the person of Jesus (Malachi 3:1). Zechariah said a man named "the Branch" would build the temple of the LORD and be a priest on his throne (Zechariah 6:12-13). The New Testament presents Jesus as that priest-king building a house of living stones (Hebrews 3:3-6). Amos foretold the rebuilding of "the booth of David". James said this was being fulfilled as Gentiles turned to God (Acts 15:15-17).
examples: Ezra 6:15: the second temple was completed in the sixth year of Darius, 516 BC.
Acts 15:16-17: James quotes Amos 9:11-12 about rebuilding David's fallen tent and applies it to the Gentile mission.
questions.other: Dispensationalists agree some promises were fulfilled after the exile. They argue that others, such as Ezekiel 40-48 and Zechariah 14, describe a future millennial temple, because their details did not fit the second temple. Some progressive dispensationalists accept the Acts 15 reading as an initial fulfillment.

questions.q: How should Ezekiel's temple vision (Ezekiel 40-48) be read?
questions.short: This reading sees it as a vision for the exiles about restored worship, written in the symbols of their day, and fulfilled at last in Christ and his church.
questions.answer: Ezekiel received the vision in 573 BC, during the exile (Ezekiel 40:1). E. W. Hengstenberg argued that its first readers would have expected it to apply to the return from Babylon. Jeremiah had promised the city and temple would be restored after seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10). Ezekiel himself said restoration would follow soon after destruction (Ezekiel 11:16-17). On this reading, the vision gave the exiles a picture of a purified people, with God dwelling among them. The river flowing from the temple to heal the Dead Sea (Ezekiel 47:1-12) is clearly symbolic, and Jesus used the image for the Spirit (John 7:37-39). Revelation 21-22 then takes up Ezekiel's images for the new Jerusalem. The vision points beyond any building to God's presence with his people.
examples: Ezekiel 48:35: the city's name will be "The LORD is there". Revelation 21:3 says God's dwelling is with people.
Ezekiel 47:12 and Revelation 22:2 both describe trees by the river whose leaves bring healing.
questions.other: Dispensationalists read Ezekiel 40-48 as a literal temple in a future millennium, because of its detailed measurements. Many amillennial scholars read it as symbolic of the church or the new creation. Some see it as an ideal plan that the post-exilic community never fully carried out.

questions.q: Do some futurist writers teach that two more temples are coming?
questions.short: Yes. Some teach a third temple to be defiled by the Antichrist and a fourth, millennial temple described by Ezekiel. This reading finds neither in the New Testament.
questions.answer: Some popular writers describe four temples in all. The first was Solomon's. The second was rebuilt after the exile and expanded by Herod. A third will be built on Mount Moriah and desecrated by the Antichrist. A fourth will be built in the millennium by the Messiah, following Ezekiel 40-48. On the fulfilled reading, this multiplies buildings that the New Testament never mentions. Hebrews, which explains the temple more than any other book, says nothing of a future rebuilding or of a millennial temple. It says instead that the first covenant is obsolete and ready to vanish (Hebrews 8:13). It says believers have come to the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22). The only future temple the New Testament describes is God and the Lamb (Revelation 21:22).
examples: Hebrews 9:8-9: the first tent was "a symbol for the present age" while it was still standing.
Hebrews 12:22: "You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem."
questions.other: Dispensationalists hold that the third and fourth temples follow from a literal reading of Daniel 9:27, 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Ezekiel 40-48. They see no conflict with Hebrews, since Hebrews addresses the church, not Israel in the millennium. Many other Christians find this distinction unconvincing.

questions.q: Would animal sacrifices in a future millennial temple conflict with the book of Hebrews?
questions.short: This reading says yes. Ezekiel's sacrifices are "to make atonement", while Hebrews says Christ's one offering ended all offerings for sin.
questions.answer: Ezekiel 45:15, 17 and 20 describe offerings "to make atonement" for the people and the house. The same word is used in the law of Moses for sacrifices that cover sin (Leviticus 16:30-34). Hebrews teaches that the blood of bulls and goats cannot take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). Christ "offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins" (Hebrews 10:12). Where there is forgiveness, "there is no longer any offering for sin" (Hebrews 10:18). On the fulfilled reading, a future temple with atoning sacrifices would have Jesus overseeing the very offerings his blood replaced. That seems to go against the whole message of Hebrews. This reading therefore takes Ezekiel's vision as describing worship for the restored community after the exile, in the forms they knew.
examples: Hebrews 10:1: the law has only "a shadow of the good things to come", not the true form.
Ezekiel 43:18-27 describes a seven-day sin offering to cleanse the altar, using the language of atonement.
questions.other: Dispensational scholars such as Jerry Hullinger argue that Ezekiel's sacrifices remove ritual uncleanness so God can dwell among a still-mortal people. They say this does not deal with eternal guilt, which Christ alone removes. Others see the sacrifices as memorials, like the Lord's Supper.

questions.q: Can the sacrifices in Ezekiel's temple be explained as memorials?
questions.short: This reading finds that hard. The text calls them offerings "to make atonement", not memorials. Calling them memorials departs from the literal reading the system requires.
questions.answer: The Scofield Reference Bible (1909) offered two options for Ezekiel's sacrifices. Either they will be memorials looking back to the cross, or the reference to sacrifices is not literal. On the fulfilled reading, both options create a problem. Nothing in Ezekiel says the sacrifices are memorials. They are offerings for atonement (Ezekiel 45:15, 17). The second option gives up literal reading, which dispensationalism names as its key rule. Charles Ryrie defined literal interpretation as giving each word its normal meaning. By that rule, atonement means atonement. This reading concludes that it is simpler to read Ezekiel as speaking to the restored exiles in their own terms. The vision should not be moved 2,500 years ahead into a kingdom where atoning blood is offered in the presence of the crucified Christ.
examples: The Lord's Supper is a true memorial: "Do this in remembrance of me" (1 Corinthians 11:24-25), but it uses bread and cup, not blood sacrifice.
Ezekiel 45:17: the prince provides offerings "to make atonement for the house of Israel".
questions.other: Many dispensationalists now prefer the view that the sacrifices bring ritual cleansing, not memorials. They note that Old Testament sacrifices also never removed sin in an ultimate sense (Hebrews 10:4), yet God commanded them. On that view, millennial offerings could serve a similar temporary purpose without denying the cross.

questions.q: Was the earthly temple designed to become obsolete?
questions.short: On this reading, yes. God said heaven is his throne and earth his footstool, so no house can contain him. The temple was a copy that would give way to Christ.
questions.answer: Isaiah 66:1 says, "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me?" Solomon said the same at the temple's dedication: heaven itself cannot contain God, "how much less this house" (1 Kings 8:27). The tabernacle was made after a pattern shown to Moses (Exodus 25:9, 40). Hebrews explains that it was a copy of the heavenly sanctuary (Hebrews 8:5; 9:24). On the covenantal reading, the temple was built with an end in view. Jesus' body was the lasting temple (John 2:19-21). He said worship would no longer be bound to Jerusalem (John 4:21-24). Paul says the present Jerusalem is in slavery with her children, while the Jerusalem above is free (Galatians 4:25-26).
examples: Acts 7:48-50: Stephen quoted Isaiah 66:1-2 before the council, shortly before he was stoned.
Hebrews 9:24: Christ entered "not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself".
questions.other: Most Christians agree the temple pointed to Christ. Dispensationalists argue that a temple's role as a type does not prevent God from using a literal temple again in the future. They note that God told David's son to build it and promised blessing for the house (2 Samuel 7:13).

questions.q: Why does Isaiah 66:3 compare offering an ox to killing a man?
questions.short: Because worship without a humble heart is worthless to God. This reading applies the verse especially to sacrifice offered after Christ's one true sacrifice.
questions.answer: Isaiah 66:3 says that whoever slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man, and whoever offers grain is like one who offers pig's blood. God says this of those who have "chosen their own ways". In verse 2 he says he looks to the one who is humble and contrite and trembles at his word. The prophets often said God rejects ritual without obedience (Isaiah 1:11-15; Amos 5:21-24). Edward J. Young applied Isaiah 66:3 first to those who built the second temple in their own spirit, and more fully to those who kept offering sacrifices after Christ's one sacrifice. On this reading, once the true Lamb had come, the old sacrifices could no longer be offered as before. This reading stresses that this is a theological claim about sacrifices, not a judgment on the hearts of Jewish people in general.
examples: Isaiah 1:11: "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the LORD."
Hosea 6:6, quoted by Jesus in Matthew 9:13: "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice."
questions.other: Many scholars read Isaiah 66:3 as a word to Isaiah's own time against worship mixed with idolatry or hypocrisy, not as a prophecy about the first century. Others translate the verse differently, as listing both proper offerings and pagan practices done by the same people.

questions.q: If a temple were rebuilt in Jerusalem today, what would it mean on this reading?
questions.short: It would have no place in fulfilling New Testament prophecy. For Christians, sacrifice for sin was finished at the cross, and God's temple is his people.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, a temple built now would not be the temple of Matthew 24, 2 Thessalonians 2 or Revelation 11. Those texts spoke of the building standing in the first century. Hebrews teaches that Christ "has appeared once for all" to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself (Hebrews 9:26). So Christians believe no new animal sacrifice can add to his work (Hebrews 10:18). A new temple would show only that its builders do not yet see Jesus as the Messiah, which is the same disagreement that existed in the first century. This should lead Christians to prayer and gentle witness, not to excitement about a countdown. Paul longed for his own people to be saved (Romans 10:1). He also warned Gentile believers against pride (Romans 11:18-20).
examples: Romans 10:1: "My heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved."
In AD 363 Emperor Julian tried to rebuild the temple to disprove Christianity; the work stopped after fires broke out (Ammianus Marcellinus, History 23.1.2-3).
questions.other: Dispensationalists would see a rebuilt temple as an important prophetic event, since it would make possible the events of Daniel 9:27 and 2 Thessalonians 2:4. They also stress love for the Jewish people. Many other Christians, with this reading, see no prophetic weight in such a building.

questions.q: What is the "abomination of desolation" that Jesus mentions in Matthew 24:15?
questions.short: It is Daniel's phrase for a sacrilege in God's house that leads to its ruin. Jesus said his own hearers would see it.
questions.answer: The phrase comes from Daniel 9:27, 11:31 and 12:11. In the Old Testament an "abomination" is false worship or the defiling of true worship (Deuteronomy 7:25; Deuteronomy 17:1). "Desolation" means the place is left empty and ruined. So the phrase means a defiling act that brings the sanctuary to ruin. Jesus told his disciples, "when you see" it, and then he said that "this generation" would not pass before all these things happened (Matthew 24:15, 34). On the fulfilled reading, the event belongs to the years before AD 70, when the temple in Jerusalem was still standing. Daniel 9:26 had already joined the phrase to the destruction of "the city and the sanctuary" after the Messiah is "cut off". Jesus is pointing his hearers to that ruin.
examples: Daniel 9:26-27 places the desolation after the Messiah is "cut off" and links it to the ruin of the city and the sanctuary.
1 Maccabees 1:54 uses the same phrase for the pagan altar set up by Antiochus IV in December 167 BC, so first-century Jews knew the words well.
questions.other: Dispensational futurists see a double reference: Antiochus was a preview, and the full fulfilment comes when a future Antichrist defiles a rebuilt temple in the middle of a seven-year tribulation. Many amillennial and historic premillennial scholars accept AD 70 as the main fulfilment but also see a pattern that may recur at the end.

questions.q: Does Matthew 24:15 require a rebuilt temple in our future?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, no. The "holy place" Jesus meant was the temple his disciples were looking at, which stood until AD 70.
questions.answer: The whole discourse begins with the temple in front of the disciples. Jesus said of those buildings, "not one stone here will be left on another" (Matthew 24:1-2). The disciples then asked when "these things" would happen (Matthew 24:3). Read in that setting, the "holy place" of verse 15 is the same temple. Nothing in the chapter speaks of a second building or a gap of many centuries. Jesus also tied every item to "this generation" (Matthew 24:34). So this reading says a future temple must be brought into the text from elsewhere. It is not found in the text itself. The fulfilled reading adds that Hebrews calls the earthly sanctuary a "copy and shadow" which was ready to vanish (Hebrews 8:5, 13).
examples: Matthew 24:1-3 moves straight from the standing temple to the question "when will these things be?"
The Herodian temple was burned in August AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-7). No later temple has been built on the site.
questions.other: Futurists point to 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Revelation 11:1-2, which they read as a future temple. They argue that Jesus' words were only partly fulfilled in AD 70 and await a final completion. Some premillennial scholars expect a temple without holding a strict seven-year timetable.

questions.q: What did Antiochus IV Epiphanes do, and why does it matter for Matthew 24?
questions.short: In 167 BC he set up a pagan altar on God's altar and forced Jews to break the law. Jews of Jesus' day saw this as the classic "abomination".
questions.answer: Antiochus IV ruled the Seleucid empire. In December 167 BC (15 Kislev), his officials set up an "abomination of desolation" on the altar of burnt offering. Ten days later pagan sacrifice was offered there (1 Maccabees 1:54, 59). He banned circumcision and Sabbath keeping. Many who refused were killed (1 Maccabees 1:60-63). Judas Maccabeus cleansed the temple in December 164 BC, which Hanukkah remembers (1 Maccabees 4:52-59; John 10:22). Daniel 11:31 is widely read as foretelling this. When Jesus used the same phrase, his hearers would think of a pagan power defiling the sanctuary. The fulfilled reading says Jesus was warning that a similar event would come in their own lifetime, but this time it would end in the temple's total ruin.
examples: Some summaries date the altar to 168 BC. 1 Maccabees 1:54 gives the year 145 of the Seleucid era, which is December 167 BC.
Josephus says Antiochus forced the Jews to leave their infants uncircumcised and to offer swine on the altar (Jewish War 1.1.2).
questions.other: Most scholars of every view agree that Daniel 11:31 points to Antiochus. Futurists add that Daniel 11:36-45 shifts to a later king. They also note that Jesus spoke of the abomination as still to come, so Antiochus cannot be its only fulfilment. Critical scholars date Daniel to the time of Antiochus.

questions.q: How does Luke 21:20 help us understand Matthew 24:15?
questions.short: Where Matthew says "abomination of desolation", Luke says "Jerusalem surrounded by armies". Both give the same signal to flee from Judea.
questions.answer: Matthew 24:15-16, Mark 13:14 and Luke 21:20-21 sit at the same point in the same discourse. Each is followed by the same command: "let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains". Luke, writing for Gentile readers, explains the Hebrew phrase in plain terms. The desolation is near when armies surround Jerusalem. On the fulfilled reading, this ties the sign to the Roman war of AD 66-70. The armies arrive, the desolation follows, and the disciples must leave at once. Luke also adds that Jerusalem would be "trodden down by the Gentiles" and its people led away captive (Luke 21:24). That happened in AD 70. Comparing the three Gospels side by side lets Scripture explain Scripture.
examples: Matthew 24:16, Mark 13:14 and Luke 21:21 all give the identical command to flee to the mountains.
Cestius Gallus surrounded Jerusalem in November AD 66. Titus set up a full siege in spring AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 2.19; 5.1-2).
questions.other: Many futurists accept that Luke 21:20-24 describes AD 70 but argue that Matthew 24:15 describes a later event. Others say Luke keeps both levels in view, moving to the end of the age at Luke 21:25. Some evangelical scholars hold that Luke shows the AD 70 meaning, while Matthew's wording leaves room for a later echo.

questions.q: Do Matthew and Luke describe two different events, one past and one future?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says no. The setting, the question, the warning and the time limit are the same in all three Gospels.
questions.answer: Some dispensational writers, such as Arno Gaebelein, taught that Luke records the fall of Jerusalem under Titus while Matthew 24 skips it and describes a future tribulation. The fulfilled reading answers that the three accounts share the same setting on the Mount of Olives, the same question from the disciples, and the same command to flee from Judea. They also share the same time limit: "this generation will not pass away" (Matthew 24:34; Mark 13:30; Luke 21:32). If the time limit is the same, the events cannot be separated by thousands of years. Matthew wrote for Jewish readers and kept Daniel's words. Luke wrote for Gentiles and explained them. The difference is in the wording, not in the event.
examples: The time statement is almost identical in Matthew 24:34, Mark 13:30 and Luke 21:32.
Matthew 24:20 adds "nor on a Sabbath", a detail that suits Jewish readers in first-century Judea.
questions.other: Futurists answer that Matthew and Mark do not mention armies, and that Matthew 24:21 speaks of unequalled distress, which they think fits the end. Some say Luke 21:24 shows a long gap ("the times of the Gentiles") between AD 70 and the final signs. Historic premillennial writers often see a near and a far fulfilment woven together.

questions.q: Did first-century Jews expect Daniel's abomination to happen in their own day?
questions.short: Yes. When Emperor Gaius (Caligula) ordered his statue placed in the temple about AD 40, many Jews feared Daniel's words were being fulfilled.
questions.answer: Around AD 39-40 the Emperor Gaius, called Caligula, ordered the governor Petronius to set up a statue of himself in the Jerusalem temple. Thousands of Jews pleaded with Petronius and said they would die first. Petronius delayed. Caligula was murdered in January AD 41, and the plan died with him (Philo, Embassy to Gaius 188-337; Josephus, Antiquities 18.8.2-9; Tacitus, Histories 5.9). This crisis shows that Jews of that time thought Daniel's warning could come true in their generation. Mark 13:14 was written soon after. The fulfilled reading says the danger was only delayed. What Caligula failed to do in AD 40, the Roman legions did in AD 70, when they brought their standards into the temple court.
examples: Tacitus records that the Jews took up arms rather than let Caligula's statue be set up (Histories 5.9).
Philo led a delegation to Caligula in Rome about AD 40 and wrote an account of it.
questions.other: Most scholars of all views accept these historical details. Some futurists see the Caligula crisis as one more "preview" that shows how a future ruler might act. Some critical scholars think Mark 13 was shaped by the Caligula crisis.

questions.q: Did Josephus think Daniel's prophecy was fulfilled in the Roman war?
questions.short: Yes. Josephus wrote that Daniel foresaw Roman rule and that Jerusalem would be taken and the temple laid waste.
questions.answer: Josephus was a Jewish priest and general who later lived under Roman patronage. In Antiquities 10.11.7 (10.276) he says Daniel wrote about the Roman government and that Jerusalem would be taken and the temple made desolate. He also tells of an old saying that the city would fall when Jews themselves defiled the temple. He saw this fulfilled in the crimes of the Zealots inside the temple courts in 67-68 (Jewish War 4.6.3; 6.2.1). So a Jewish writer who was not a Christian linked Daniel to the events of AD 66-70. On the fulfilled reading, this shows that the AD 70 interpretation is not a later Christian invention. It fits how Jews read Daniel at the time.
examples: Antiquities 10.11.7: Daniel "also wrote concerning the Roman government" and its taking of Jerusalem.
Jewish War 6.2.1: Josephus urges the rebels to see that ancient prophecies about the city's fall were being fulfilled.
questions.other: Futurists reply that Josephus was not inspired and that his reading of Daniel does not settle what Jesus meant. They note that Josephus also hailed Vespasian as the ruler foretold in Jewish oracles (Jewish War 6.5.4), which shows his views served his Roman patrons.

questions.q: Could the Zealots' actions in the temple be the abomination?
questions.short: Many think so. In 67-68 the Zealots turned the temple into a fortress, shed blood in its courts and made a mock high priest.
questions.answer: The Zealots were Jewish nationalists who fought Roman rule. One of Jesus' apostles had been called "Simon the Zealot" (Luke 6:15). During the revolt, Zealot groups seized the temple. Josephus says they made the holy place a stronghold, let men with blood on their hands walk inside, and killed people in the courts (Jewish War 4.3.7). In the winter of 67-68 they chose a new high priest by lot. He was Phannias (Phanni), a country man who did not even understand the office (Jewish War 4.3.8). The former high priest Ananus wept and said he wished he had died before seeing God's house so defiled (Jewish War 4.3.10). This reading fits the idea of defilement "by Jewish hands", which Josephus saw in an old prophecy.
examples: Jewish War 4.3.8: Phannias is chosen by lot and dressed in the high priest's robes.
Jewish War 4.3.10: Ananus mourns that the holy places are "crowded with the feet of murderers".
questions.other: Some scholars think the Zealot occupation came too late to serve as a signal to flee, since by then escape was hard. Others prefer the Roman armies, following Luke 21:20. Futurists say none of these acts fully matches an abomination set up "in the holy place" by one ruler who claims to be God.

questions.q: What happened when the Idumeans entered Jerusalem, and why did Josephus see it as a turning point?
questions.short: The Idumeans, let in by the Zealots in a storm, killed thousands in the temple courts and murdered the former high priest Ananus. Josephus dates the city's ruin from that day.
questions.answer: The Idumeans lived south of Judea in old Edom. In 68 the Zealots called them to Jerusalem, and about 20,000 came (Jewish War 4.4.2). The gates were shut against them, but during a violent storm at night the Zealots sawed through the bars and let them in (Jewish War 4.4.6-7). Josephus says the outer temple court flowed with blood, and about 8,500 died there (Jewish War 4.5.1). They killed Ananus and other priests and left their bodies unburied. Josephus writes that the death of Ananus was the beginning of the city's destruction (Jewish War 4.5.2). The fulfilled reading adds a contrast. If a Jewish writer could see the city's fall flowing from the murder of a high priest, the Gospels see it flowing from the rejection of Jesus, the great High Priest (Luke 21:22; Acts 3:14-15).
examples: Jewish War 4.5.2: "the death of Ananus was the beginning of the destruction of the city".
Some writers suggest the Christians left for Pella around this time. Eusebius only says they left before the war (Church History 3.5.3).
questions.other: Scholars of all views accept these events as history. Some question whether they are the specific "abomination" Jesus meant. Futurists see them as part of a local judgment that does not exhaust the prophecy. Critics note that Josephus wrote with his own bias against the rebel groups.

questions.q: Were the Roman legions and their standards the abomination?
questions.short: This is the most common fulfilled view. The legions surrounded the city, and once the temple burned the soldiers sacrificed to their standards in the temple court.
questions.answer: Roman legions carried standards topped with eagles and images of the emperor. Soldiers gave them religious honour. Jews saw them as idols, so governors normally kept them out of Jerusalem. When Pilate brought images into the city by night, Jews protested so strongly that he removed them (Josephus, Antiquities 18.3.1). In August AD 70, while the temple was still burning, soldiers set up their standards near the eastern gate. They offered sacrifices to them there and hailed Titus as imperator (Jewish War 6.6.1). An idol set up and honoured where God's altar stood fits "abomination". An army that destroys fits "desolation". This view also matches Luke 21:20, where the sign is Jerusalem surrounded by armies.
examples: Jewish War 6.6.1: the Romans brought their standards into the temple and offered sacrifices to them.
Antiquities 18.5.3: the Roman official Vitellius led his army around Judea so that its images would not pass through Jewish land.
questions.other: Some object that the sacrifice to the standards came after the temple burned, too late to warn anyone to flee. Fulfilled interpreters answer that the armies' approach was the warning, and the sacrifice completed the act. Futurists say the act was not done by one man claiming deity, as 2 Thessalonians 2:4 describes.

questions.q: Could the temple's own priesthood be the deepest form of the abomination?
questions.short: Some fulfilled interpreters think so. After Christ's sacrifice, ongoing animal sacrifices by priests who rejected him were, on this view, false worship in God's sight.
questions.answer: This view starts with Ezekiel. In Ezekiel 5:11 God says he will withdraw because his own people defiled his sanctuary. In Ezekiel 8-11 the prophet sees idolatry inside the temple, and then God's glory leaves (Ezekiel 10:18; 11:23). Only after that did Babylon destroy it. In the Gospels Jesus calls the temple a "house of trade" and a "den of robbers" (John 2:16; Matthew 21:13). The chief priests led the call for his death (Matthew 27:20). On this reading, once the true Lamb had died, sacrifices offered by priests who rejected him became an empty and offensive rite. God then left the house "desolate" (Matthew 23:38). John Calvin wrote along similar lines that the temple lost its holiness once the covenant was broken. Outside armies only finished what the inner defilement began.
examples: Ezekiel 10:18 and 11:23: God's glory leaves the temple, and only then does Babylon burn it in 586 BC.
Hebrews 10:11-14: after Christ's one offering, the daily repeated sacrifices can no longer take away sins.
questions.other: Many scholars, including some who hold the fulfilled view, think this stretches the word "abomination", which in Daniel points to a pagan idol. Futurists hold that the term requires an idol set up by a ruler. Some note that the apostles still worshipped in the temple (Acts 3:1; 21:26), so it was not yet simply false worship.

questions.q: What does the law of the leprous house (Leviticus 14) have to do with Jesus leaving the temple?
questions.short: On this reading, Jesus acts like the priest who inspects a diseased house. He goes out, declares it desolate, and foretells that its stones will be torn down.
questions.answer: Leviticus 14:33-47 gives a law for a house with spreading mould. The priest inspects it, goes out of the house, and shuts it up (Leviticus 14:38). If the disease returns, the house is unclean. It must be torn down, and its stones taken outside the city (Leviticus 14:44-45). The fulfilled reading sees a pattern in Jesus' actions.
