questions.short: Yes. When God heals his people, the prophets say the moon will shine like the sun and the sun seven times brighter. This is clearly figurative.
questions.answer: Isaiah 30:26 says that on the day the Lord binds up his people's wounds, the moon will shine like the sun and the sun will be seven times brighter. Taken literally, this would scorch the earth. The verse itself gives the meaning: God "binds up the brokenness of his people". Isaiah 60:19-20 says the sun will no longer set and the moon will not wane, because the Lord will be an everlasting light. Revelation 21:23 uses the same picture for the new Jerusalem. The fulfilled reading sees a pair. Bright lights picture a nation raised up and blessed. Darkened lights picture a nation brought down in judgment. Both are figures for what God does to peoples in history.
examples: Isaiah 30:26: the sun shines seven times brighter "in the day when the Lord binds up" his people.
Isaiah 60:20: "your sun shall no more go down" — followed by "the days of your mourning shall end".
questions.other: Most scholars agree these blessing texts are figurative. Futurists often place them in a future millennium or the new creation, and some expect real changes in the natural world then. Amillennial scholars usually read them as pictures of the church or the new creation.

questions.q: If Israel's "lights" went out in AD 70, who now carries God's light to the nations?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, the new covenant people of God—Jews and Gentiles in Christ—carry the light that Israel was called to show the nations.
questions.answer: Israel was called to be a light to the nations (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6). On the fulfilled reading, the old covenant order with its temple and priesthood ended in AD 70. Hebrews says God was shaking what can be shaken so that what cannot be shaken may remain (Hebrews 12:26-28). It calls the old covenant "ready to vanish" (Hebrews 8:13). Daniel foretold a kingdom that would never be destroyed (Daniel 2:44). Jesus called his disciples "the light of the world" (Matthew 5:14). Peter applied Israel's titles to the church: a chosen people and a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9). The first church was made up of Jews, and it then welcomed Gentiles. This reading does not say God has cast off the Jewish people (Romans 11:1-2). It says the light now shines through Messiah's people.
examples: Acts 13:47: Paul and Barnabas apply Isaiah 49:6, "a light for the Gentiles", to their own mission.
Philippians 2:15: believers "shine as lights in the world".
questions.other: Dispensationalists hold that God's promises to national Israel remain in force and will be fulfilled in a future kingdom. They reject any idea that the church has replaced Israel. Many other scholars hold that Romans 11:25-26 promises a future large-scale turning of Jewish people to Christ.

questions.q: Can Christians today point to signs that show Jesus will return in our lifetime?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, no. The Olivet signs led up to AD 70. Scripture gives no puzzle of modern signs that dates the final coming.
questions.answer: Read in its setting, the sign list of Matthew 24, Mark 13 and Luke 21 answers the disciples' question about the temple (Matthew 24:1-3). Those signs were wars, famines, false messiahs, persecution and armies around Jerusalem. They came before and during the Roman war of AD 66-70. So this reading holds that the discourse gives no countdown for our day. Jesus said plainly that no one knows the day of the final coming (Acts 1:7). Every generation that has tried to fit current news into a sign puzzle has been wrong. Statements such as "the Antichrist is alive now" or "I will see the rapture in my lifetime" go beyond what the text says. Christians should be ready at all times, not because the news looks dark, but because Christ is Lord and judge at every moment.
examples: A Special Notice in an Oklahoma newspaper on 25 July 1986 said Christ was coming soon and added side predictions about the U.S. President in Jerusalem on 15 May 1988. None of it happened.
In 1991 John Walvoord told Newsweek he expected the rapture in his own lifetime. He died in 2002.
questions.other: Futurists answer that the signs of Matthew 24 will be repeated or completed in a final tribulation, so the "birth pains" can grow stronger before Christ comes. Historicists see signs spread across church history. Many teachers in all camps agree that no date can be set.

questions.q: Can the Bible words "soon" and "near" mean an open-ended span of time?
questions.short: This reading says no. If prophecy is read plainly, "near" must mean near for the people first addressed, not near for some later age.
questions.answer: The New Testament repeatedly told first readers that the Lord's coming was close. James wrote that the coming of the Lord "is at hand" (James 5:8). Peter wrote that the end of all things was near (1 Peter 4:7). Revelation says its events "must shortly come to pass" (Revelation 1:1). On the fulfilled reading, these words had a real meaning for the churches that read them first. A teacher who claims to read prophecy literally cannot turn "near" into "possible at any moment, even after two thousand years." That move, this reading argues, empties the words of their meaning. Instead, the near coming refers to Christ's judgment on Jerusalem within that generation. The final coming at the resurrection is real, but the Bible does not attach these nearness words to a far-future date.
examples: Compare Matthew 26:18: "My time is at hand" meant Jesus' death within days.
Compare Mark 1:15: "The kingdom of God is at hand" meant the kingdom was arriving in Jesus' ministry, not millennia later.
questions.other: Futurists say "near" means "next on God's calendar" or "imminent," so it could happen at any time. Others appeal to 2 Peter 3:8, that a day is like a thousand years with the Lord, and say God measures nearness differently from people.

questions.q: If the Olivet signs are past, what does Scripture say must happen before the final return of Christ?
questions.short: Christ reigns now from heaven until every enemy is put under his feet. When that reign has done its work, he returns to raise the dead and judge.
questions.answer: Paul says Christ must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet; the last enemy is death (1 Corinthians 15:24-26). Psalm 110:1 gives the pattern. The Messiah sits at God's right hand until his enemies become his footstool. Peter quotes this psalm at Pentecost and applies it to the risen Jesus (Acts 2:34-35). Heaven is God's throne and earth his footstool (Isaiah 66:1). So, on this reading, the one "sign" before the end is the completed spread of Christ's rule. This is not a calendar sign. It is a process. When the reign has finished its work, the dead are raised and the living and dead are judged. The text sets no date, and it calls for faithful work, not anxious watching of headlines.
examples: Psalm 110:1 is the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New Testament, applied to Jesus' present reign in Acts 2, Hebrews 1 and 10.
Hebrews 10:12-13 pictures Christ seated, "waiting" until his enemies are made a footstool.
questions.other: Premillennialists agree Christ reigns now in heaven, but hold that the defeat of enemies will be finished in a future earthly kingdom after his return. Amillennialists agree with a present reign but expect evil to grow until the end. Postmillennialists expect wide gospel success before he comes.

questions.q: Does 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 teach a secret rapture followed later by an earthly millennium?
questions.short: This reading says no. The text speaks of resurrection, meeting the Lord, and being with him for ever. It says nothing of a later seven years or an earthly kingdom.
questions.answer: Paul comforts grieving believers. The Lord comes with a shout and a trumpet; the dead in Christ rise first; the living are caught up with them; and so they are with the Lord always (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17). On this reading, the passage describes one public event: the resurrection at the last day. Nothing in it mentions a tribulation before or after, a return seven years later, a rebuilt temple, or a restored sacrificial system. The verse ends with "for ever with the Lord." No further stage is named. The two-stage scheme must therefore be brought to the text from other passages. This reading holds that this is reading in, not reading out. The plain point is hope at death and resurrection.
examples: The shout, the archangel's voice and the trumpet are loud and public, not secret (compare 1 Corinthians 15:52).
Jesus links resurrection to "the last day" in John 6:39-40, not to a day seven years before the end.
questions.other: Pretribulationists say the passage describes the Lord coming for his church, while other texts describe his coming with his saints later. They argue the church is not appointed to wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9). Posttribulationists agree the event is single and public but place it after a future tribulation.

questions.q: Which event does Matthew 24:30, the Son of Man coming on the clouds, describe?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, it describes Christ's vindication and his judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, because Jesus put it within "this generation."
questions.answer: Jesus said that all these things would happen before that generation passed away (Matthew 24:34). The coming on the clouds stands inside "all these things." It also follows "immediately after" the tribulation of those days (Matthew 24:29). So this reading concludes that verse 30 cannot be a rapture or the final bodily return far in the future. It is the moment when Jesus is shown to be the enthroned Son of Man, and his rule is displayed in judgment on the city that rejected him. The wording comes from Daniel 7:13, where the Son of Man receives a kingdom. The destruction of the temple was public proof that the old order had ended and that Jesus had been given authority.
examples: Matthew 16:27-28 also ties the Son of Man coming "in his kingdom" to some who were standing there.
The temple burned in August of AD 70 (the month of Av), within about forty years of the prophecy (Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-6.4.8).
questions.other: Futurists read verse 30 as the visible Second Coming after a future tribulation. Some preterists and many evangelical scholars split the discourse, applying the near signs to AD 70 and the cloud-coming to the end. Others see a double fulfillment: AD 70 as a preview of the final coming.

questions.q: Why does Matthew 24 give so much detail about the tribulation but say nothing of a rapture, rebuilt temple or earthly millennium after Jesus comes?
questions.short: This reading says the silence is because those events are not in the prophecy. The discourse is about the fall of the old temple, not a later kingdom program.
questions.answer: Jesus gave careful detail about the time before the city fell: when to flee, not to go back for a coat, to pray it would not be winter (Matthew 24:16-20). If a rapture and a thousand-year kingdom followed straight after his coming, one would expect at least a word about them. Yet verse 30 is followed by the gathering of the elect and the parable of the fig tree. There is no rebuilt temple, no new Israeli state and no earthly reign from Jerusalem. On the fulfilled reading, the silence is meaningful. The subject is the end of the old covenant age and the passing of its temple. Any later program must be supplied from outside the passage.
examples: Compare the precise instruction in Luke 21:20-21: when you see armies around Jerusalem, flee to the mountains.
Church tradition records that Jerusalem Christians left for Pella before the siege (Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3).
questions.other: Dispensationalists answer that Matthew 24 focuses on Israel's tribulation, while the rapture is revealed later to the church in Paul's letters, and the kingdom details come from Revelation 20 and the Old Testament prophets. Silence, they say, is not denial.

questions.q: When the prophets say God "comes down" in judgment, as in Micah 1:3-4, is that a visible, bodily coming?
questions.short: No. In Micah God "came" against Samaria and Jerusalem through the Assyrian and Babylonian armies. Nobody saw God himself, and the mountains did not literally melt.
questions.answer: Micah says the Lord comes out of his place, treads on the heights, and the mountains melt like wax (Micah 1:3-4). The target is named: Samaria and Jerusalem (Micah 1:5). Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC. Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 586 BC. In neither case did people see God walking on the hills. The language is poetic. It means God acted in history to judge. On this reading, the New Testament uses the same kind of language for Christ's coming against Jerusalem in AD 70. The words are no less true for being figurative. They tell us who stands behind the armies of history: God himself.
examples: Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6).
Isaiah 19:1 says the Lord rides a swift cloud into Egypt; the judgment came through human rulers (Isaiah 19:2-4).
questions.other: Many futurists agree that Old Testament "comings" were figurative, but argue that Jesus' coming is unique because he has a human body and ascended visibly (Acts 1:11). So, they say, his return must also be visible and bodily.

questions.q: What do clouds stand for when the Bible links them with God?
questions.short: Clouds mark God's presence, glory, rule and judgment. They are a sign of the divine King at work, not a weather report.
questions.answer: God led Israel in a pillar of cloud (Exodus 13:21). He came to Sinai in a thick cloud (Exodus 19:9). Cloud filled the tabernacle and the temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:10-12). Clouds and darkness surround his throne (Psalms 97:2). He makes the clouds his chariot (Psalms 104:3). The day of the Lord is a day of clouds (Ezekiel 30:3; Joel 2:2). Clouds are the dust of his feet (Nahum 1:3). Across these texts the cloud is a symbol of divine presence, often in judgment. So when the Son of Man "comes with clouds," a Jewish listener would hear a claim to divine authority, the right to act as God acts. On the fulfilled reading, that is the point of Matthew 24:30.
examples: The cloud at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:5) marks God's presence and voice.
Nahum 1:3 used cloud language for God's judgment on Nineveh, which fell in 612 BC.
questions.other: Interpreters of all schools accept that clouds signal divine glory. Futurists add that Acts 1:9-11 shows Jesus left in a literal cloud and will return "in the same way," so the cloud imagery at the final coming is also literal.

questions.q: Is God riding a swift cloud into Egypt (Isaiah 19:1) meant literally?
questions.short: No. The picture shows God ruling over nations. Egypt's judgment came through civil war and a harsh ruler, not a visible God on a cloud.
questions.answer: Isaiah pictures the Lord riding a fast cloud into Egypt. The idols tremble and Egyptians fight one another (Isaiah 19:1-2). God then gives them over to a cruel master (Isaiah 19:4). The events are political and military. No Egyptian saw God sitting on a cloud. In the same way, Psalm 104 says God walks on the wings of the wind and makes the winds his messengers (Psalms 104:3-4). No one takes this as physical description. The question this reading asks is simple: if this language is figurative in the Old Testament, why should the same language suddenly be read with wooden literalism when Jesus uses it about Jerusalem? Consistency asks that Scripture be read by its own patterns of speech.
examples: Egypt was conquered by Assyria under Esarhaddon in 671 BC; many see this as the fulfillment of Isaiah 19:4.
Psalm 18:9-11 describes God bending the heavens and coming down in darkness to rescue David from Saul.
questions.other: Futurists agree Isaiah 19:1 is figurative, but they argue that the New Testament adds literal details to Jesus' return, such as a visible body, a shout, and the gathering of believers. Those details, they say, mark it off from Old Testament imagery.

questions.q: In Daniel 7:13, which way does the Son of Man travel: down to earth or up to God?
questions.short: Up. He comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and is presented before him to receive a kingdom.
questions.answer: Daniel sees one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven. He comes to the Ancient of Days, is brought near before him, and is given dominion, glory and a kingdom (Daniel 7:13-14). The movement is toward God's throne, not toward the earth. The aim is not to collect saints but to receive royal power. On this reading, when Jesus quotes this verse (Matthew 24:30; 26:64), he is speaking of his enthronement, which took place at his resurrection and ascension. AD 70 then publicly showed that this enthronement was real. Scholars such as R. T. France and N. T. Wright argue that the Daniel text speaks of vindication and exaltation, not descent.
examples: Acts 1:9 and Mark 16:19: Jesus is taken up in a cloud and sits at God's right hand, matching Daniel's direction of travel.
Ephesians 1:20-22: God seated Christ far above all rule and put all things under his feet.
questions.other: Many futurist and traditional scholars accept that Daniel 7:13 shows an ascent, but argue that the New Testament reuses the phrase for Christ's return (Acts 1:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:16), so its direction can be reversed in later fulfillment.

questions.q: What did Jesus mean when he told the high priest, "From now on you will see the Son of Man... coming on the clouds" (Matthew 26:64)?
questions.short: On this reading, Caiaphas would witness the evidence that Jesus had been raised and enthroned: the rise of the church and the judgment that fell on the temple leaders.
questions.answer: Jesus spoke to Caiaphas and the council, using "you." He said that from now on they would see him seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds (Matthew 26:64). "From now on" points to the near future, not to a time thousands of years later. Caiaphas did not need to see a figure flying in the sky. He would see events that proved Jesus right: the empty tomb reports, the growth of the apostles' movement, and finally the collapse of the temple system that had condemned him. On this reading, these events vindicated Jesus as a true prophet and as the Messiah who reigns from heaven.
examples: Luke 22:69 reads "from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God."
Acts 4:5-13: the same rulers face the apostles and cannot deny that a healing miracle has happened in Jesus' name.
questions.other: Futurists say "you will see" means the judges will see Jesus when they stand before him at the final judgment after their resurrection. Others say "from now on" refers to the enthronement only, while the cloud-coming is still future.

questions.q: Why did the high priest tear his robes and call Jesus' words blasphemy?
questions.short: Because Jesus claimed to be Daniel's Son of Man who shares God's throne. The high priest understood it as a claim to divine rule.
questions.answer: When Jesus joined Psalm 110:1 (seated at God's right hand) with Daniel 7:13 (coming with the clouds), he claimed the highest place beside God. Caiaphas tore his robes and said Jesus had blasphemed (Matthew 26:65). This shows that the high priest heard a claim about authority and throne, not a claim about a far-off trip through the sky. On this reading, Jesus was saying that he would occupy David's throne in heaven (Acts 2:30-36). God raised him and seated him over every power (Ephesians 1:20-23). So the temple and its priesthood had become obsolete. In a sense, the high priest grasped the meaning of Daniel 7 better than many modern date-setters.
examples: Matthew 22:41-46: Jesus earlier used Psalm 110:1 to ask how David's son can also be David's Lord.
Leviticus 21:10 forbade the high priest to tear his clothes in mourning; his act showed extreme outrage.
questions.other: All Christian views agree that Jesus claimed divine authority here. Futurists add that his claim will be finally displayed at his visible return, when every eye sees him. Some also see the cloud-coming in Jesus' reply as still future for Caiaphas, to be seen at the last judgment.

questions.q: What did Stephen see in Acts 7:56, and why does it matter for the meaning of the Son of Man's "coming"?
questions.short: Stephen saw Jesus standing at God's right hand. On this reading, he saw the enthroned Son of Man and announced judgment on those who rejected him.
questions.answer: Just before his death Stephen said he saw heaven opened and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand (Acts 7:56). This is the only time outside the Gospels that the title "Son of Man" is used by a human speaker. It matches Daniel 7: the Son of Man before God's throne. Stephen had just charged his hearers with resisting the Holy Spirit and killing the prophets (Acts 7:51-52). On this reading, the vision confirmed that the kingdom had passed to Jesus and his people (Matthew 21:43). The sentence on the temple leaders would be carried out within a generation. Stephen, like his Lord, prayed for the forgiveness of his killers (Acts 7:60).
examples: Matthew 21:43: the kingdom will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruit.
1 Peter 2:9 calls the church, made of believing Jews and later Gentiles, a "holy nation."
questions.other: Many interpreters see Stephen's vision as Jesus rising to welcome his martyr or to act as his advocate. They do not tie it to AD 70, and futurists still expect a later bodily coming of the Son of Man.

questions.q: Is "the sign of the Son of Man in heaven" a visible object in the sky?
questions.short: On this reading, no. The sign is that the Son of Man is in heaven, enthroned. The fall of the temple was the proof of it.
questions.answer: The Greek of Matthew 24:30 can be read word for word: "then will appear the sign of the Son of Man in heaven." The word ouranos means heaven as well as sky. The phrase "in heaven" belongs most naturally with "the Son of Man," not with "the sign." So the sign shows that the Son of Man is in heaven, ruling. On this reading, the visible event was on earth: the end of the temple and city. That event proved that Jesus sat at the Father's right hand (Acts 2:33; Hebrews 9:24). Some early writers expected a visible sign, such as a cross in the sky, but even they did not think the sign was Jesus himself.
examples: Matthew 12:39-40: the only sign given to that generation was the sign of Jonah, that is, Jesus' resurrection.
Josephus reports strange portents before the war, but these are reports, not the meaning of Jesus' sign (Jewish War 6.5.3).
questions.other: Futurists expect a visible sign in the sky at the Second Coming. Early writers such as the Didache (16:6) spoke of a sign spread out in heaven, and some have suggested the Shekinah glory or a great cross. Others take the sign to be Christ himself appearing.

questions.q: Does "all the tribes of the earth will mourn" in Matthew 24:30 mean every people on the planet?
questions.short: On this reading, it means "all the tribes of the land," that is, Israel in Judea. The Greek word ge often means land.
questions.answer: The Greek word ge can mean soil, ground, the land of Israel, or the whole earth. Context decides. In Matthew 2:20-21 it clearly means the land of Israel. In the Olivet Discourse Jesus is speaking to Jews about Judea (Matthew 24:16). "Tribes" is a natural word for Israel's twelve tribes. Zechariah 12:10-14, which lies behind this verse, describes the families of the land of Israel mourning, clan by clan. Some translators, such as Ronald Knox, render it "the tribes of the land." The Hebrew word eretz behaves the same way: it often means the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18). On this reading, the mourning belongs to first-century Judea, not to all nations.
examples: Luke 21:23 speaks of "great distress in the land and wrath upon this people," using the same word.
Zechariah 12:12-14 lists the mourning by family: David, Nathan, Levi, Shimei.
questions.other: Most translations and futurist interpreters read "all the tribes of the earth," linking it with Revelation 1:7 and the worldwide reach of the final return. Some see a first fulfillment in Israel and a fuller one among all nations.

questions.q: Who are "those who pierced him" in Zechariah 12:10 and Revelation 1:7, and when did they see him?
questions.short: On this reading, they are first-century Judeans connected with the crucifixion, who "saw" him in the judgment of AD 70 within their generation.
questions.answer: Zechariah 12:10 says people of Jerusalem will look on the one they pierced and mourn. The order of Zechariah's Messiah prophecies is telling. The king on a donkey (9:9) was fulfilled at the triumphal entry (Matthew 21:5). The thirty pieces of silver and the potter (11:12-13) were fulfilled with Judas (Matthew 27:3-10). The struck shepherd and scattered sheep (13:7) were fulfilled at Jesus' arrest (Matthew 26:31). The piercing and mourning stand between these first-century events. John 19:37 applies the piercing to the crucifixion. So Revelation 1:7, written to people expecting things "soon," fits the generation that crucified him. It is important to add that the New Testament blames the leaders and the crowd of that day. It never blames Jewish people as a whole for all time. Many Jews mourned and believed (Acts 2:37-41).
examples: Acts 2:36-37: listeners were "cut to the heart" when told they had crucified the Lord.
Matthew 27:3-10 fulfills the thirty-pieces-of-silver prophecy of Zechariah 11:12-13.
questions.other: Futurists see Zechariah 12:10 fulfilled when Israel as a nation turns to Jesus at his return, linking it with Romans 11:26. Revelation 1:7 is then read as worldwide sight of the returning Christ. Some see both an AD 70 and a final fulfillment.

questions.q: How could people "see" the Son of Man coming if he did not appear bodily in the sky?
questions.short: In Scripture, "seeing" often means understanding. The crucifiers would grasp, through the judgment, who Jesus really was.
questions.answer: Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:10: God blinded their eyes so they would not see, understand and turn (John 12:40). This blindness is spiritual, not physical. In Luke 24:31 the disciples' eyes were opened and they recognized Jesus. Paul was sent to open eyes and turn people from darkness to light (Acts 26:18). Romans 15:21 says those who were not told will "see," that is, understand. On this reading, "every eye will see him" means people would perceive his power at work as he judged the city and prospered his church. They did not see his body after the ascension, but they saw his rule in their history. The Greek verb horao (future opsontai) can mean perceive as well as look.
examples: John 3:36: whoever does not obey the Son "will not see life," meaning will not experience it.
Luke 17:22: the disciples will long "to see" one of the days of the Son of Man.
questions.other: Futurists answer that "every eye" in Revelation 1:7 is universal and physical, as Acts 1:11 promises Jesus will come back "in the same way" he left. They grant that "see" can mean understand, but say this context requires literal sight.

questions.q: After AD 70, where is the centre of God's worship and the throne of David?
questions.short: In heaven. Christ sits on David's throne in the heavenly Jerusalem, and worship is no longer tied to one mountain or city.
questions.answer: Jesus told the Samaritan woman that an hour was coming when people would worship the Father neither on her mountain nor in Jerusalem (John 4:21-24). He called his own body the temple (John 2:19-21). Peter preached that God swore to seat David's descendant on his throne, and that this happened when Jesus was raised and exalted to God's right hand (Acts 2:30-33). Paul calls believers children of "the Jerusalem above" (Galatians 4:26). Hebrews says Christians have come to the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22). On this reading, the fall of the earthly temple confirmed this change. The promises of a son of David on the throne for ever are fulfilled in Jesus now.
examples: Matthew 1:1 and Luke 3:31 trace Jesus as the son of David.
After AD 70 the temple was never rebuilt; an attempt under Emperor Julian in AD 363 failed (Ammianus Marcellinus, History 23.1.2-3).
questions.other: Dispensationalists agree Christ sits on his Father's throne now (Revelation 3:21), but hold that David's throne will be set up on earth in Jerusalem during the millennium, with a restored temple described in Ezekiel 40-48.

questions.q: What did God remove when he shook "not only the earth but also heaven" (Hebrews 12:26-27)?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, he removed the shakable old-covenant order: temple, priesthood and animal sacrifice. The unshakable kingdom remained.
questions.answer: Hebrews quotes Haggai 2:6: God will once more shake earth and heaven. The writer explains that this means removing things that can be shaken, "as of things that are made," so that what cannot be shaken remains (Hebrews 12:26-27). He then says believers are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:28). The letter has already said the old covenant is "ready to vanish away" (Hebrews 8:13). On this reading, the shaking came in AD 70. The temple fell, the priesthood stopped, and the sacrifices ended. Those things were "made with hands" and temporary. What stayed was Christ's kingdom and his spiritual temple.
examples: Hebrews 8:13, written before AD 70, says the old covenant is "growing old" and near to disappearing.
Daily sacrifice in the temple stopped in July/August AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 6.2.1).
questions.other: Many interpreters read the shaking as the final judgment at the end of history, when the physical creation is renewed. Others see a partial fulfillment at Christ's first coming and a final one at his return.

questions.q: If the stone temple was thrown down, what temple did God build in its place?
questions.short: A temple of people. Jews and Gentiles joined in Christ are built into a spiritual house with Christ as the cornerstone.
questions.answer: Peter calls believers "living stones" being built into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood that offers spiritual sacrifices through Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:5). Paul says Gentiles who were far off have been brought near by Christ's blood (Ephesians 2:13). Jews and Gentiles together are no longer strangers but fellow citizens and members of God's household. They are built on the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone, growing into a holy temple in the Lord (Ephesians 2:19-21). On this reading, the gathering of the elect in Matthew 24:31 is the building of this new temple out of all nations. The message is no longer only for "the lost sheep of Israel" (Matthew 15:24) but for the scattered children of God (John 11:52).
examples: 1 Corinthians 3:16: "you are God's temple."
Acts 15:14-17: James applies Amos's rebuilt "tent of David" to Gentiles coming in.
questions.other: All Christian views see the church as God's temple now. Dispensationalists add that a literal temple will also be built in Jerusalem in the future, either for the Antichrist's period or for the millennium.

questions.q: Does Matthew 24:31 mean angels will carry Jewish people from around the world back to Jerusalem?
questions.short: This reading says no. Old Testament "gathering" texts never use angels, and the gathering is the gospel bringing people into Christ.
questions.answer: Some dispensational writers teach that angels will supernaturally bring scattered Israelites back to the land at Christ's return. One writer joked that it will be angels "rather than El Al airline." God can do anything (Mark 10:27). Yet the question is what Jesus meant. When Moses and Isaiah speak of God gathering his people from the ends of the earth, no angels appear (Deuteronomy 30:1-4; Isaiah 11:12). God gathers through repentance, return and his own hand. On this reading, Matthew 24:31 describes the worldwide mission that followed the fall of the old order: messengers sent out with the gospel to gather the chosen from every nation.
examples: Deuteronomy 30:3-4: God himself gathers his people "from the farthest parts under heaven."
Isaiah 11:12: God raises a banner for the nations to gather the dispersed.
questions.other: Dispensationalists, such as J. Dwight Pentecost, see a literal final regathering of Israel by angels after the tribulation. Other futurists see the gathering of all believers at the resurrection (compare Matthew 13:41, 49, where angels gather at the end).

questions.q: Can the "angels" of Matthew 24:31 be human messengers?
questions.short: Yes. The Greek word angelos means messenger, and Scripture uses it for prophets, priests, John the Baptist and others.
questions.answer: Angelos is the ordinary Greek word for a messenger. Context tells whether a heavenly or a human messenger is meant. Haggai is called "the Lord's messenger" (Haggai 1:13). The priest is the messenger of the Lord of hosts (Malachi 2:7). John the Baptist is the messenger sent ahead (Matthew 11:10). Jesus sent messengers ahead of him into a Samaritan village (Luke 9:52). Rahab received the "messengers" Joshua sent (James 2:25). Even a dispensational writer such as Ed Hindson notes that the "angels" of the seven churches may be their leaders (Revelation 2:1). On this reading, the angels of Matthew 24:31 are gospel preachers sent out to gather God's people.
examples: 2 Chronicles 36:15-16: God sent his messengers again and again, but the people mocked them until there was no remedy. This pattern led to Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC.
Mark 1:2 quotes Malachi 3:1 about John: "I send my messenger before your face."
questions.other: Most commentators take "angels" in Matthew 24:31 as heavenly beings, because elsewhere the Son of Man comes "with his angels" (Matthew 16:27; 25:31) and angels reap at the end of the age (Matthew 13:39).

questions.q: What do "the four winds" and "from one end of heaven to the other" mean?
questions.short: They mean everywhere. The gathering reaches the whole world, not only the land of Israel.
questions.answer: "Four winds" is a common Bible picture for the four directions (Zechariah 2:6; Daniel 7:2; Revelation 7:1). "From one end of heaven to the other" means the whole horizon (Deuteronomy 4:32). Mark's parallel adds "from the end of the earth to the end of heaven" (Mark 13:27). On this reading, Jesus is saying that his people will be gathered from all over the world. The mission that began among "the lost sheep of Israel" (Matthew 15:24) now reaches the nations, as he promised: many will come from east and west to eat with Abraham (Matthew 8:11). The same language was used of judgment on Elam, scattered to the four winds (Jeremiah 49:36).
examples: Acts begins in Jerusalem and ends in Rome. To a Jew in Jerusalem, Rome was "the end of the earth" (Acts 1:8).
Revelation 7:9: a great crowd from every nation, tribe, people and language.
questions.other: Futurists read the same phrases as the worldwide gathering at Christ's visible return. Both sides agree the words mean "everywhere"; they differ on whether the gathering is the gospel mission or a single final event.

questions.q: Does Bible language like "four corners of the earth" teach a flat or square earth?
questions.short: No. It is a figure of speech for the whole world, just as "the four winds" means every direction.
questions.answer: Scripture speaks of the four corners of the earth (Isaiah 11:12; Revelation 7:1). It also pictures the earth as a house with foundations and pillars, and heaven as a house with many rooms (John 14:2). These are images, not science. Isaiah also speaks of God sitting above "the circle of the earth" (Isaiah 40:22). The point of such language is God's rule over the whole world. This matters for prophecy too. If we do not read "four corners" with wooden literalism, we should not demand wooden literalism for clouds, falling stars and angel trumpets. Each image must be read the way Scripture uses it.
examples: People still say "the sun rises" without teaching that the sun moves round the earth.
Ezekiel 7:2 announces an end on "the four corners of the land" of Israel.
questions.other: All major Christian views accept that "four corners" is figurative. The debate is over which details in prophecy are figurative and which are literal; futurists hold that historical narrative and plain prediction should be taken literally unless the text signals otherwise.

questions.q: What is the "great trumpet" in Matthew 24:31?
questions.short: On this reading, it is the gospel call. It echoes the silver trumpets that gathered Israel and the Jubilee trumpet that proclaimed release.
questions.answer: In Numbers 10:1-10 God told Moses to make two silver trumpets to call the assembly and to start the camp marching. The Jubilee year was announced by trumpet on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 25:9-10). It meant release of slaves and return of land. Jesus began his ministry by reading Isaiah 61, the "acceptable year of the Lord," and said it was fulfilled that day (Luke 4:16-21). Isaiah 27:13 says a great trumpet will sound and the scattered will come to worship. Prophets were told to lift their voice like a trumpet (Isaiah 58:1). On this reading, the great trumpet is the proclamation of the gospel calling people from every nation into God's assembly.
examples: Isaiah 27:13: "the great trumpet shall be blown," and the lost in Assyria and Egypt come to worship.
2 Corinthians 6:2: "now is the acceptable time; now is the day of salvation."
questions.other: Futurists link this trumpet to the "last trumpet" of 1 Corinthians 15:52 and the trumpet of 1 Thessalonians 4:16, and so to a single final event. Pretribulationists usually separate the Matthew 24 trumpet (for Israel) from the rapture trumpet (for the church).

questions.q: What does the word "gather together" in Matthew 24:31 suggest?
questions.short: The verb is episynago, related to synagoge. God is gathering a new assembly in Christ, made of believing Jews and Gentiles.
questions.answer: Matthew 24:31 uses the verb episynago, "gather together." It is related to synagoge, a gathering or synagogue. Jesus used the same verb when he wept over Jerusalem: he longed to gather her children as a hen gathers her chicks, but they were not willing (Matthew 23:37). On this reading, after the judgment on the city he gathers his elect from all over the world into a new assembly. John says Jesus died to gather into one the scattered children of God (John 11:52). Peter tells such people that once they were not a people, but now they are God's people (1 Peter 2:9-10). Note that the gathered church began with Jewish believers. Many thousands of Jews believed in Jerusalem itself (Acts 21:20).
examples: Matthew 23:37 and 24:31 use the same verb, linking the lament and the gathering.
Hebrews 10:25 uses the related noun for believers meeting together.
questions.other: Many futurists note that Paul uses the noun form for "our gathering together to him" at Christ's coming (2 Thessalonians 2:1), and take Matthew 24:31 as the same future event.

questions.q: Why does this reading link the worldwide gathering of the elect with the time after AD 70?
questions.short: The gospel went to the Jew first. After the old order fell, the mission to all nations went forward without the temple at its centre.
questions.answer: The gospel began at Pentecost, but it went first to Jews (Romans 1:16). Paul usually began in the synagogue (Acts 17:1-2). The Jerusalem church kept close ties to the temple (Acts 21:26). When the temple fell, the old centre was gone. On this reading, the mission to the nations went forward in new fullness, as Christ had commanded: make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:18-20). The commentator R. V. G. Tasker argued that only after the old order ended could the church, now clearly distinct from the temple system, sound the gospel trumpet across the world. History shows the elect still being gathered from every tribe and language.
examples: The early Christian movement spread widely across the Roman world in the second and third centuries, even under persecution.
Romans 15:19-24 shows Paul planning a mission as far as Spain.
questions.other: Other views point out that the Gentile mission was already strong well before AD 70 (Acts 13-28; Colossians 1:6). Futurists see Matthew 24:31 as the end of the mission, not its continuation.

questions.q: Does the fig tree budding in Matthew 24:32-33 point to Israel becoming a state in 1948?
questions.short: This reading says no. The fig tree is a simple picture from nature: when leaves appear, summer is near. The "things" were the signs before AD 70.
questions.answer: Hal Lindsey called Israel's rebirth on 14 May 1948 the most important sign, and he read the fig tree as Israel. If a generation is about forty years, he suggested, all these things could happen within about forty years of 1948. Chuck Smith said the generation alive in 1948 would not pass away before Christ came. On this reading, the whole scheme rests on one assumption: that the fig tree means the modern state. But Jesus explains his own picture. When the branch is tender and leaves come out, you know summer is near; so when you see "all these things," know that he is near (Matthew 24:32-33). "All these things" are the signs he has just listed. Those signs were for his hearers, and they came before AD 70.
examples: Lindsey, The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), linked 1948 + about 40 years with the end.
In 1988 and the years after, many readers who had expected Christ by then had to rethink.
questions.other: Many dispensationalists still see 1948 as a key sign of the last days, even if they no longer use a forty-year count. Others in the same tradition, like John Walvoord, did not read the fig tree as Israel but still expected a future tribulation.

questions.q: Is the fig tree ever used in Scripture as a symbol of national Israel?
questions.short: Figs and fig trees do picture Israel's condition in some texts, but not its future restoration. In the Gospels the barren fig tree pictures judgment.
questions.answer: John Walvoord argued that the fig tree is not clearly used as a symbol of Israel. Good and bad figs picture exiles and those left behind (Jeremiah 24:1-8). Hosea compares Israel's fathers to early figs (Hosea 9:10). In Judges 9:10-11 the fig tree in Jotham's story is not Israel. In the Gospels, Jesus curses a fig tree with leaves but no fruit, and it withers (Matthew 21:18-20; Mark 11:12-14, 20-21). This happened in the week he judged the temple. On this reading, if the fig tree links with Israel at all, it stands for a fruitless system facing judgment, not a nation about to bloom again. Even so, Matthew 24:32 does not draw on that link; it uses the tree as a seasonal clock.
examples: Luke 13:6-9: a fig tree with no fruit for three years is given one more year before being cut down.
Mark 11 sandwiches the cursing of the fig tree around the cleansing of the temple.
questions.other: Some futurists say the cursed fig tree pictures Israel set aside, and the budding fig tree pictures Israel restored. Others accept Walvoord's view that the tree is only a natural illustration and does not stand for Israel.

questions.q: What does Luke's wording, "the fig tree and all the trees," add to the parable?
questions.short: It shows the point is ordinary seasons, not one nation. Any tree in leaf tells you summer is near.
questions.answer: Luke records Jesus saying: look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they put out leaves, you know summer is near. So when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near (Luke 21:29-31). If the fig tree were a code for Israel, what would "all the trees" stand for? On this reading, the added words show that Jesus was using a common sight from nature. Leaves on trees signal a coming season. In the same way, the signs he listed would signal that the judgment and the kingdom's coming in power were at the door. Near to what? Near to fulfilling his promise about the temple within that generation.
examples: In Israel, fig leaves appear in late spring, shortly before summer fruit.
Song of Songs 2:11-13 uses the fig tree's early fruit as a simple sign that spring has come.
questions.other: Some futurists answer that "all the trees" may represent other nations reviving in the end times alongside Israel. Most commentators of all schools agree the illustration is mainly seasonal, though they differ on whether "these things" point to AD 70, to a future tribulation, or to both.

questions.q: Does the fig tree picture allow a forty-year "generation of the fig tree"?
questions.short: This reading says no. Leaves in spring point to one coming summer. A single season is in view, not decades of waiting.
questions.answer: Some teachers speak of "the generation of the fig tree," meaning the generation born after 1948. On this reading, that misuses the picture. Leaves are a short-term sign. When you see them, summer is weeks away, not forty or fifty summers. In the same way, when Jesus' hearers saw the listed signs, the judgment was close. The leaves in the parable correspond to the signs of the 60s AD: false messiahs, war, armies around Jerusalem. They have nothing to do with 1948, the Six-Day War of 1967, or the peace accords of 1993. Each of those events has been offered as "the" sign, and each forecast built on them has failed.
examples: Jerusalem was surrounded by Roman armies first under Cestius Gallus in AD 66 and then under Titus in AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 2.19.4-7; 5.2.1-3).
The Oslo Accords were signed in 1993; some prophecy writers presented them as the start of the seven-year tribulation.
questions.other: Futurists who use the "fig tree generation" idea answer that the signs begin with Israel's rebirth and then build over a lifetime. Many futurist scholars now reject fixed-length generation counts, while still seeing modern Israel as prophetically significant.

questions.q: If Israel's rebirth were the chief sign, why would Jesus hide it in an unexplained picture?
questions.short: This reading argues he would not. Jesus spoke clearly about non-signs and gave a clear sign: the abomination and armies around Jerusalem.
questions.answer: In Matthew 24:4-14 Jesus spent many words warning what should not be taken as signs of the end: wars, rumours of wars, famines and earthquakes are only the beginning. Then he gave a definite sign: when you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, flee (Matthew 24:15). Luke explains it as Jerusalem surrounded by armies (Luke 21:20). On this reading, it would be strange for Jesus, after such clarity, to make the most important sign of all a symbol he never defined. The fig tree comes after the main teaching, as a summary picture of timing. It does not introduce a new, hidden sign.
examples: Matthew 24:6: "see that you are not troubled... the end is not yet."
Luke 21:20 names the sign plainly: armies surrounding Jerusalem.
questions.other: Futurists respond that prophecy is often understood fully only when fulfilled (Daniel 12:4, 9), so the fig tree's meaning could become clear later, as they believe it did in 1948.

questions.q: What pictures does the New Testament use for God's people, if not the fig tree?
questions.short: The vine, the olive tree, the lump of dough and the flock. These describe one people of God joined to Christ.
questions.answer: Jesus calls himself the true vine and his disciples the branches (John 15:1-8). Paul pictures one olive tree, with natural branches broken off by unbelief and wild branches grafted in by faith. Natural branches can be grafted back in if they believe (Romans 11:16-24). He speaks of the first part of the dough making the whole lump holy (Romans 11:16). Jesus calls his people a little flock (Luke 12:32) and says he has other sheep to bring in, so there will be one flock and one shepherd (John 10:16). On this reading, these pictures stress one people in Christ, not a separate future program for a political state.
examples: Isaiah 5:1-7 already pictured Israel as God's vineyard; Jesus applies the vine picture to himself.
John 10:16: other sheep, one flock, one shepherd.
questions.other: Dispensationalists and many others note that Romans 11 itself speaks of a future turning of Israel ("all Israel will be saved," Romans 11:26). They say the olive tree shows a distinct future for ethnic Israel within God's plan.

questions.q: Why is Matthew 24:34 called the key to the whole chapter?
questions.short: Because it sets the time limit. Jesus said all the things he had just described would happen before his hearers' generation passed away.
questions.answer: Jesus said: truly, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place (Matthew 24:34). The verse looks back over everything from verse 4 to verse 33. J. Marcellus Kik called it the key to Matthew 24. On the fulfilled reading, once this time marker is taken at face value, the rest of the chapter falls into place. The temple's fall, the tribulation, the cosmic language and the Son of Man's coming all belong to the first century. Without this key, every generation can find its own news in the chapter, and wild speculation follows. With it, the chapter becomes a fulfilled prophecy that confirms Jesus as a true prophet.
examples: Matthew 23:36 uses the same phrase: "all these things will come upon this generation." Few doubt that meant his hearers.
Mark 13:30 and Luke 21:32 repeat the time limit in nearly the same words.
questions.other: Futurists answer that "this generation" means the generation alive when the signs begin, or that "all these things" refers only to verses 4-28. Some scholars think Jesus expected the end in his generation and was mistaken, a view all the views in this study reject.

questions.q: How does Luke 21:36 help decide who "this generation" is?
questions.short: Jesus told the same listeners to pray that they might escape the things "about to" happen. "You" and "this generation" are the same people.
questions.answer: In Luke's account Jesus says: stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are about to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man (Luke 21:36). The "you" are the disciples he was speaking to. They were to watch and pray. The events were "about to" take place. On this reading, the meaning of "you" settles the meaning of "this generation." Jesus was not addressing unknown people two thousand years later while speaking to Peter, James, John and Andrew (Mark 13:3). The warnings were personal and urgent: flee, pray, watch. They make sense only if the hearers would live through the events.
examples: Mark 13:3 names the four disciples who asked the question privately.
Luke 21:20: "when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation is near."
questions.other: Futurists reply that "you" can mean the disciples as representatives of all believers, including those living at the end. Jesus often addresses the church through the apostles (Matthew 28:20). So, they say, the warnings to watch and pray apply to every later generation of believers too.

questions.q: Can the Greek word genea in Matthew 24:34 mean "race" rather than "generation"?
questions.short: Standard lexicons place Matthew 24:34 under "generation," that is, people living at the same time. "Race" is a rare meaning that does not fit here.
questions.answer: Some writers, including Arno Gaebelein and the Scofield Reference Bible, said genea here means "race": the Jewish people will not die out before the end. But the main Greek lexicons do not support this for Matthew 24:34. Thayer defines genea as the whole multitude of people living at the same time and lists Matthew 24:34 and Mark 13:30 under that sense. The Bauer-Arndt-Gingrich lexicon notes the "nation" view but places Matthew 24:34 under "contemporaries." Kittel's Theological Dictionary says this generation is to be understood in a time sense. On this reading, the natural, unforced meaning is the generation then alive.
examples: Thayer, Greek-English Lexicon (1889): genea = "the whole multitude of men living at the same time," citing Matthew 24:34.
Matthew 1:17 uses genea for the fourteen generations from Abraham to David.
questions.other: Some scholars, including William Hendriksen, argued genea can mean a kind of people or a race marked by unbelief, so Jesus meant the Jewish people, or unbelieving humanity, would last until the end. Others read "this kind of generation."

questions.q: What is the difference between genea and genos?
questions.short: Genos is the usual word for race or nation. Genea is the usual word for generation. The Gospel writers used genea in this verse.
questions.answer: When the New Testament wants to say "race," "nation" or "stock," it normally uses genos. Paul calls himself "of the stock (genos) of Israel" (Philippians 3:5). Peter calls the church "a chosen race (genos)" (1 Peter 2:9). Barnabas is a Levite "of Cyprus by birth (genos)" (Acts 4:36). Gaebelein cited 1 Peter 2:9 for his "race" view, but that verse uses genos, not genea. On this reading, if Matthew, Mark and Luke had meant "this race," they had a clear word for it. All three chose genea instead. That choice supports the ordinary meaning: the people living in that period.
examples: Mark 7:26: the woman was a Syrophoenician "by race" (genos).
Acts 7:19: Pharaoh dealt craftily with "our race" (genos).
questions.other: Those who favour "race" say the two words overlap in some Greek writers and that genea can carry the idea of a family line. They argue the theological sense, an unbelieving kind of people, fits Jesus' usage.

questions.q: How does Matthew use "this generation" elsewhere in his Gospel?
questions.short: Every time, it refers to Jesus' own contemporaries, often to warn them of judgment.
questions.answer: Matthew uses "this generation" in several places. Jesus compares this generation to children in the market who will not dance or mourn (Matthew 11:16). He calls them an evil and adulterous generation seeking a sign (Matthew 12:39; 16:4). The men of Nineveh will rise in judgment with this generation (Matthew 12:41-42). He says, "O faithless generation, how long shall I be with you?" (Matthew 17:17). He warns that the blood of the prophets will come on this generation (Matthew 23:36). In every case the people are those Jesus faced. On this reading, a sound method compares Matthew with Matthew. A writer such as William Hendriksen, who argued for another meaning, did not let these uses decide the case.
examples: Matthew 23:36 comes just a few verses before 24:34 and uses the same phrase for the same people.
Matthew 12:45: "so shall it be also unto this wicked generation."
questions.other: Some answer that these texts use "generation" in a moral sense ("evil generation"), so it describes a kind of people, not a time period. The moral sense, they say, could extend to later unbelievers.

questions.q: Does "save yourselves from this crooked generation" (Acts 2:40) show that genea means the Jewish race?
questions.short: No. Peter, himself a Jew, was not calling his own race crooked. He meant the generation of that time, which faced judgment.
questions.answer: Some point to Acts 2:40 to support "race." Peter urges his listeners: be saved from this crooked generation. But Peter was Jewish. He stayed Jewish after he followed Christ. The three thousand who believed that day were Jews and converts to Judaism (Acts 2:5, 41). On this reading, Peter was not condemning the Jewish people as a race; there was nothing crooked about being Jewish. He was warning about his own generation, which had rejected the Messiah and was heading toward the judgment Jesus had foretold. Those who believed were rescued, as Jesus promised the elect would be (Matthew 24:22). This is also a needed guard against antisemitism: the text blames a generation's response, not a people's birth.
examples: Deuteronomy 32:5 uses similar words, "a perverse and crooked generation," of the wilderness generation.
Philippians 2:15 uses the same phrase for the world around the church in Philippi.
questions.other: Those who read genea as "race" respond that the phrase describes unbelieving Israel as a group, not just one age. Most other interpreters, futurist or not, agree Acts 2:40 means Peter's contemporaries.

questions.q: Does Hebrews 3:10, "I was angry with that generation," support the "race" meaning?
questions.short: No. It speaks of one generation, the Israelites who wandered forty years in the wilderness.
questions.answer: Hebrews quotes Psalm 95: your fathers tested me and saw my works for forty years; therefore I was angry with that generation (Hebrews 3:9-10). The generation in view is the one that left Egypt and died in the wilderness (Numbers 14:29-35; 32:13). Their children entered the land. So the verse is about one span of people, not the whole race. On this reading, it also gives a helpful link. The wilderness generation lasted forty years. The time from Jesus' prophecy (about AD 30-33) to the fall of Jerusalem (AD 70) was roughly the same. The writer of Hebrews warns his readers not to repeat that generation's unbelief, because "today" was still open (Hebrews 3:13).
examples: Numbers 32:13: God made them wander forty years until all that generation had died.
About forty years separate the crucifixion (AD 30 or 33) and the burning of the temple (AD 70).
questions.other: Few interpreters use Hebrews 3:10 for the "race" view today. Futurists who reject AD 70 point out that "forty years" is a rough biblical figure and should not be pressed into a fixed rule for prophecy.

questions.q: How do Bible translations render genea in Matthew 24:34?
questions.short: Almost all major translations say "generation." Some list "race" only in a footnote as an alternative.
questions.answer: The King James Version, the American Standard Version (1901), the Revised Standard, the New English Bible, the New King James, the Jerusalem Bible, the New International Version and the New American Standard all read "generation" in Matthew 24:34. Some, such as the NIV and NASB, have a footnote offering "race" as an alternative. On this reading, the agreement of translators from many traditions is telling. If "race" were the plain meaning, one would expect at least some major translations to put it in the text. The translators judged that the context is about time, not ethnic survival.
examples: KJV (1611): "This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled."
Young's Literal Translation (1862) also reads "this generation."
questions.other: Supporters of "race" reply that translation choices do not settle the theology, since translators may follow tradition. They note the footnotes show the alternative was taken seriously by scholars, and that context and theology, not majority choice, must decide the meaning.

questions.q: Did leading futurists accept the "race" reading of genea?
questions.short: Not all. Hal Lindsey said the context is about time, not race, and called "race" a remote meaning of the word.
questions.answer: In a 1977 interview with Eternity magazine, Hal Lindsey was asked whether "this generation" might mean the race of people. He said no, because the context speaks of time, not race. He called "race" a very remote meaning of the word. Lindsey did not apply the generation to Jesus' hearers, though. He applied it to the generation that saw Israel reborn in 1948. On this reading, Lindsey's rejection of "race" is an important admission. Once genea means people living at one time, the question is only which time. The context of Matthew 24, addressed to the disciples, points to the first century.
examples: Lindsey, Eternity, January 1977: he said he had debated the point with Earl Radmacher.
J. Dwight Pentecost, by contrast, called the "race" view the best explanation in Things to Come (1958).
questions.other: Futurists who agree with Lindsey on "generation" hold that it is the generation that sees the signs begin. Those who disagree with him prefer "race" or "kind of people." Both reject the first-century reading.

questions.q: Does the English word "generation" mean "race," as the Scofield note claimed?
questions.short: Only as a rare, late-listed sense. Common English use means people living at the same time, as in "generation gap."
questions.answer: The Scofield note claimed that genea, "as does the English word," means primarily race, family or stock. Noah Webster's 1828 dictionary defines generation first as a single step in natural descent, and then as the people living at the same period. It lists "race" only far down the list. The Shorter Oxford English Dictionary also lists "race" last. Everyday speech confirms this. A "generation gap" is a gap between people raised in different times, not between races. On this reading, both the English and the Greek point the same way. The natural sense of "this generation" is the people of that time, and Jesus' prophecy has already become history.
examples: Webster (1828) quotes Luke 9:41, "O faithless and perverse generation," as an example of people living at the same time.
"The World War II generation" means people of a certain era, not a race.
questions.other: Defenders of the Scofield note say dictionary order does not limit meaning in a theological text. They argue that the phrase "this generation" in the Gospels often carries a moral sense of a kind of people.

questions.q: If Adam Clarke translated genea as "race," why did he still apply Matthew 24 to AD 70?
questions.short: Clarke offered no evidence for "race," yet he still held that everything Jesus foretold about the temple and city came true in AD 70.
questions.answer: Adam Clarke, the Methodist commentator, first published his Matthew commentary in 1810. He suggested genea could mean "race" but gave no cross-references for it. Yet he called Matthew 24 a prediction of the utter ruin of the city and temple and the end of the Jewish political state. He said everything Jesus foretold had been fulfilled exactly. On this reading, Clarke's case shows two things. First, the "race" rendering was not created to protect a future fulfillment; even an AD 70 reader used it. Second, modern writers who use "race" to push the chapter into the future cannot claim Clarke's support for their timing. Clarke saw Matthew 24 as strong evidence for the truth of Christianity.
examples: Clarke said the prophecy's fulfillment was among the strongest proofs of the truth of Christianity.
Thomas Newton's Dissertations on the Prophecies (1754) also applied Matthew 24 to AD 70.
questions.other: Futurists note that Clarke, like many Protestant commentators of his time, did not share modern dispensational assumptions. They grant his AD 70 reading but disagree with it on other grounds.

questions.q: Was everything in Luke 21:10-24 actually fulfilled by the end of AD 70?
questions.short: On this reading, yes. The temple was destroyed, the city lay in ruins, many thousands died, and many were taken captive.
questions.answer: Luke records Jesus foretelling wars, earthquakes, famines, persecution of the disciples, armies around Jerusalem, the fall of the city by the sword, captivity among the nations, and Jerusalem trampled by Gentiles (Luke 21:10-24). The South African scholar Norval Geldenhuys noted that by the end of AD 70, about forty years later, these things had happened. Josephus records the siege, the famine, the burning of the temple and the many prisoners sold or sent away (Jewish War 6.9.2-3). On this reading, this is exactly what "before this generation passes away" requires. The historical record matches the prophecy point by point.
examples: Josephus records that 97,000 were taken captive and gives the number of the dead as 1,100,000, many of them pilgrims trapped by the siege (Jewish War 6.9.3). Modern historians think these figures are likely exaggerated, but the loss was immense.
Acts records famine under Claudius (Acts 11:28) and persecution of apostles (Acts 12:1-3), all before AD 70.
questions.other: Most interpreters agree Luke 21:20-24 describes AD 70. Futurists add that "the times of the Gentiles" (Luke 21:24) leaves room for a later section about the end, beginning at verse 25.

questions.q: Could "this generation" mean a future generation, the one that will see the signs?
questions.short: This reading says no. Jesus said "this" generation, not "that" one, and spoke to people he told to watch and flee.
questions.answer: One futurist answer is that "this generation" means the generation alive when the signs appear, whenever that is. On this reading, the wording does not allow it. "This" points to something near the speaker. If Jesus meant a far generation, he could have said "that generation," as he said "that day" in verse 36. Every other time Jesus says "this generation" in the Gospels, he means the people around him. And the instructions, to flee Judea and pray the flight is not in winter or on a Sabbath (Matthew 24:16-20), fit first-century Judea. Several interpretive models have been offered to avoid the plain meaning, but this reading holds that none fits the grammar as well.
examples: Matthew 24:36 uses "that day" for something future to the speaker, showing Jesus could mark distance when he wished.
Matthew 16:28 makes a similar time promise: "some standing here will not taste death."
questions.other: Futurists such as John Walvoord and Darrell Bock argued that "this generation" can mean the generation that sees "these things" begin, since the signs themselves define the generation. Bock notes the phrase can point to a kind of people as well as to a time.

questions.q: What did the disciples ask in Matthew 24:3, and how did they link Jesus' coming with "the end of the age"?
questions.short: They asked when the temple would fall and what would signal his coming and the end of the age. They saw these as one connected event.
questions.answer: Jesus had just said the house would be left desolate and that all these things would come on this generation (Matthew 23:36-38). He then said not one stone of the temple would be left on another (Matthew 24:2). The disciples asked: when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age? (Matthew 24:3). On the fulfilled reading, they joined the temple's fall, Jesus' coming and the end of the age as one complex event. Jesus did not correct them. The "coming" here is his coming in judgment on Jerusalem. James could therefore tell first-century readers that the Lord's coming was at hand (James 5:8).
examples: Mark 13:4 records the question as "when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be fulfilled?"
Luke 21:7 records it simply about the temple: "when will these things be?"
questions.other: Many scholars say the disciples mistakenly merged the temple's fall with the end of the world, and Jesus' answer separates the two. Futurists hold that the "coming" in verse 3 is the visible Second Coming.

questions.q: Does "the end of the age" mean the end of the world?
questions.short: On this reading, no. The word is aion (age), not kosmos (world). It means the end of the old covenant era, which closed in AD 70.
questions.answer: The disciples asked about the end of the aion, the age. They did not ask about the end of the kosmos, the physical world. The King James Version's "end of the world" has misled many readers. R. T. France explains it as the end of the Jewish age, the move from a national to an international people of God. Milton Terry called it the close of the pre-Messianic age, the crisis that came when the temple fell. On this reading, the only nearby event that fits "end of the age" is the destruction of Jerusalem. Its fall ended the temple, the priesthood and the sacrifices, and opened the new covenant age in full.
examples: Matthew 28:20: "I am with you always, to the end of the age," uses the same phrase.
Hebrews 9:26: Christ appeared "at the end of the ages" to put away sin, meaning in the first century.
questions.other: Futurists and many traditional readers note that Matthew 13:39-40 links the end of the age with the final harvest and judgment, and Matthew 28:20 promises Christ's presence until history's close. So they take the "end of the age" as the end of the present era at Christ's return.

questions.q: Did New Testament writers say the end of the ages had already come upon them?
questions.short: Yes. Paul, Hebrews and Peter all speak of the "last times" or "end of the ages" as their own time.
questions.answer: Paul wrote that the Old Testament examples were written for "us, on whom the ends of the ages have come" (1 Corinthians 10:11). Hebrews says Christ appeared once "at the end of the ages" to put away sin (Hebrews 9:26). Peter says Christ was revealed "in these last times" for your sake (1 Peter 1:20). He also wrote that the end of all things was at hand (1 Peter 4:7). John said it was "the last hour" (1 John 2:18). On the fulfilled reading, these writers lived in the closing period of the old covenant age, roughly AD 30 to 70. Their "last days" were the last days of that age, not the last days of the planet.
examples: Hebrews 1:1-2: God has spoken "in these last days" by his Son.
Acts 2:16-17: Peter says Joel's "last days" prophecy is happening at Pentecost.
questions.other: Most evangelical scholars agree the "last days" began at Christ's first coming, but say they stretch from then until his return. On this view the whole church age is the last days.

questions.q: What is "the age to come" in Jesus' teaching?
questions.short: On this reading, it is the Messiah's age, the new covenant era that followed the old order. It is not only life after the final judgment.
questions.answer: Jesus said blasphemy against the Spirit would not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come (Matthew 12:32). Jewish teachers spoke of "this age" and "the age to come," the age the Messiah would bring. The commentator Charles H. H. Wright explained that the Synagogue called the Messiah's period "the world to come." On this reading, "this age" was the age of the law, and "the age to come" is the Christian era the prophets foresaw. Abraham rejoiced to see Christ's day (John 8:56). Hebrews says its readers had tasted the powers of the age to come (Hebrews 6:5). The old covenant, with animal sacrifice and earthly priests, passed away when the Lamb of God took away sin.
examples: Hebrews 6:5: believers have "tasted... the powers of the age to come."
Ephesians 1:21 speaks of Christ's rule "not only in this age but also in the one to come."
questions.other: Most interpreters hold that "the age to come" is the eternal state after the return of Christ, partly tasted now through the Spirit. They see an "already and not yet" pattern, with the age to come begun but not completed.

questions.q: Does Jesus change the subject at Matthew 24:35-36 from AD 70 to his final coming?
questions.short: Many preterists say yes. This reading says no: verse 35 confirms the preceding prophecy, and verse 36 still speaks of the coming judgment on Jerusalem.
questions.answer: Respected writers such as J. Marcellus Kik and Kenneth Gentry, and earlier Charles Spurgeon, held that verse 36 begins a new subject: the final coming. This reading respects them but differs. Verse 35, heaven and earth will pass away but my words will not, affirms the certainty of what Jesus just said. Verse 36, no one knows that day and hour, follows straight on. The central topic of the discourse is the desolation of Israel's house (Matthew 23:38). Nothing in the text announces a new topic or a gap of thousands of years. On this reading, "that day" is the day of the judgment Jesus had just described, which would fall within the generation, though its exact day was unknown.
examples: Henry Alford took verse 35 as a solemn confirmation of what came before.
Luke 21:33-36 has the same saying about heaven and earth, followed by a warning to watch so as to escape "these things."
questions.other: Partial preterists such as Kik and Gentry see a clear transition at verse 36, from near signs to a far, signless coming. Futurists also see a shift, or none at all because they place the entire chapter in the future.

questions.q: What did Jesus mean by "heaven and earth will pass away" in Matthew 24:35?
questions.short: On this reading, it means the passing of the old covenant world, the temple-centred order of Israel, which ended in AD 70.
questions.answer: On the covenantal reading, "heaven and earth" in prophecy often stands for a whole ordered world of worship and rule. The temple was built as a small picture of the cosmos. When God judged his people in the Old Testament, an old order fell and a new one rose: new rulers, a new sanctuary. In the same way, the new covenant brought a new priesthood, new sacrifice, new tabernacle (John 1:14) and new temple (John 2:19; Ephesians 2:21). In effect, a new heaven and earth. The falling stars and darkened sun of verse 29 say the same thing in picture form. So verse 35 means that the old world would pass away, but Jesus' words would stand.
examples: Isaiah 51:15-16: God planted the heavens and laid the earth's foundations when he said to Zion, "You are my people."
Jeremiah 4:23-28 describes the land of Judah's ruin as earth "without form and void" and dark heavens.
questions.other: Most interpreters take Matthew 24:35 as a contrast: the physical universe will one day pass away, but Jesus' words are more lasting still. They link it with 2 Peter 3:10 and Revelation 21:1 as a future renewal of creation.

questions.q: How do falling stars and a darkened sun relate to heaven and earth passing away?
questions.short: They are the same idea in picture form. In prophecy, falling stars mean rulers and powers falling under God's judgment.
questions.answer: Matthew 24:29 says the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, the stars will fall and the powers of heaven will be shaken. On this reading, this is a vivid way of saying "heaven and earth will pass away." In other texts, falling stars stand for fallen powers. Isaiah calls the king of Babylon a fallen day star (Isaiah 14:12). Daniel sees a horn cast down some of the host and stars (Daniel 8:10). Revelation pictures stars falling to the earth (Revelation 6:13; 12:4). Such pictures signal judgment in history. The passing of heaven and earth, then, was the end of the old order led by those who "crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Corinthians 2:8).
examples: Isaiah 13:10 uses darkened sun, moon and stars for the fall of Babylon in 539 BC.
Ezekiel 32:7-8 uses the same images for the judgment of Pharaoh and Egypt.
questions.other: Futurists accept that Old Testament sun-moon-star language is often figurative, but expect real cosmic disturbances at Christ's return, citing Luke 21:25-26 and Revelation 6:12-14. Some hold both: a symbolic fulfillment in AD 70 and a literal one at the end.

questions.q: Did respected earlier scholars read "heaven and earth passing away" as the end of the Jewish order?
questions.short: Yes. John Owen, John Lightfoot and John Brown all read some heaven-and-earth texts as the end of the Mosaic order in AD 70.
questions.answer: The Puritan John Owen (1616-1683) taught that the heaven and earth of 2 Peter 3:5-7 referred not to the final judgment but to the ruin of the Jewish church and state. John Lightfoot (1602-1675), a Hebrew scholar, applied the passing of heaven and earth to the destruction of Jerusalem, as if the whole frame of the world were dissolved. The Scottish expositor John Brown (1784-1858), commenting on Matthew 5:18, said those who know Old Testament language know that the ending of the Mosaic economy is often described as the removal of the old heavens and earth. On this reading, this is not a modern invention. It has a long line of careful Protestant scholars behind it.
examples: Owen preached on 2 Peter 3 in a sermon later printed in his Works, volume 9.
Lightfoot drew on Jewish writings to show how "heaven and earth" language was used for Israel's order.
questions.other: Many Reformed scholars, including most of Owen's and Lightfoot's contemporaries, applied these texts to the end of history. Others accept the covenantal sense for some passages (like Matthew 24:29) but not for 2 Peter 3 or Revelation 21.

questions.q: Does the contrast between "this generation" (verse 34) and "that day" (verse 36) show two different events?
questions.short: This reading says no. "This" fits something present and "that" fits something future to the speaker, whether it is forty years away or far longer.
questions.answer: Kenneth Gentry argued that "this generation" points to what is near and "that day" to what is far. If Jesus meant the same time, he would have said "this day." On this reading, the argument does not hold. "This generation" was the present generation Jesus addressed, so "this" was the right word. The day of judgment was still future to his hearers, so "that" was the right word. The Bauer-Arndt-Gingrich lexicon notes that houtos (this) refers to what is relatively near, and ekeinos (that) to what is relatively farther. A day forty years away is "that day." John Gill read "that day and hour" as the day of vengeance on Jerusalem.
examples: Luke 17:31 speaks of "that day" for the day of the Son of Man, inside the same AD 70-type warnings about fleeing from housetops.
Matthew 7:22: "many will say to me in that day," for a future day.
questions.other: Gentry and other partial preterists hold the contrast is deliberate and marks a shift to the final coming. Many futurists see the shift too, or read both phrases as future.

questions.q: If Jesus put the event within his generation, how could he say no one knows "that day and hour"?
questions.short: Knowing the generation is not knowing the day. Jesus gave a time limit but not the exact date.
questions.answer: Jesus said the events would come before his generation passed, yet the exact day and hour was known only to the Father (Matthew 24:36). These do not conflict. A person can know a harvest will come this year without knowing the date. On this reading, the disciples knew the window but not the day. That is why Jesus told them to pray the flight would not be in winter or on a Sabbath (Matthew 24:20). Adam Clarke noted that hora can mean "season," and that the disciples did not know the season either. John Lightfoot said it was a wonder anyone applied these words to the last judgment, since the whole discourse concerns Jerusalem.
examples: A pregnant woman knows her child will come within a few weeks, but not the hour (compare 1 Thessalonians 5:3).
The Roman siege began near Passover AD 70, and the temple burned in late summer. Believers who had fled earlier were spared (Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3).
questions.other: Partial preterists and futurists answer that "that day and hour" refers to the final coming, for which no time limit is given. They see verse 36 as a deliberate contrast with the dated events of verse 34.

questions.q: Why are there fewer signs after Matthew 24:35, if the subject has not changed?
questions.short: The signs had already been given. After verse 35 the focus moves from signs to watchfulness while waiting.
questions.answer: Some argue that the specific signs of verses 4-34 give way to general warnings after verse 35, so a new event must be in view.
