But dispensationalists themselves run the seven and the sixty-two together without a break. They have no reason in the text to treat the last division differently. Moses' 120 years fall into three forties (Acts 7:23, 30; Deuteronomy 34:7), yet no one adds gaps. E. W. Hengstenberg asked how anyone could imagine an interval between the sixty-nine and the one when together they make up the seventy. Milton Terry noted that in Hebrew the plural "seventy weeks" takes a singular verb, "is decreed" (Daniel 9:24). The seventy are treated as one unit.
examples: Daniel 9:24, Hebrew: shavu'im shiv'im nechtak. A plural noun with a singular verb ("is decreed").
7 + 62 + 1 = 70: the parts add up to the stated whole, leaving nothing over for a gap.
questions.other: Dispensationalists reply that the text places the Messiah's cutting off and the city's destruction "after" the sixty-two weeks (9:26), not "in" the seventieth. This, they say, signals a break. Some amillennialists, such as Meredith Kline, also see the seventieth week as symbolic and stretching across the church age.

questions.q: Does "prophetic postponement" in other Old Testament texts justify a gap in Daniel 9?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, no. Even if some prophecies are fulfilled in stages, none of the examples involves a stated, counted number of years being stopped and restarted.
questions.answer: Some dispensational scholars, such as Randall Price, argue for "prophetic postponement". In their view many Old Testament prophecies have a partial fulfilment in history and a complete one in the end times, with a gap between. They cite passages such as Isaiah 9:6-7, Isaiah 61:1-2 and Zechariah 9:9-10. On the fulfilled reading, these examples are open to debate. More importantly, none of them contains a numbered time span like "seventy weeks". A prophecy that does not give a timetable may unfold in stages. A prophecy that says exactly how many years will pass cannot be paused without changing its meaning. Daniel 9 is precisely the kind of text where a gap would undo the prophecy's own claim.
examples: Luke 4:18-21: Jesus stops reading before "the day of vengeance". But Isaiah 61 has no number of years.
Daniel 9:24 by contrast states a count: "seventy weeks are decreed".
questions.other: Dispensationalists answer that if the prophets could leave unmarked gaps between two comings of Christ, Daniel could too. They see verse 26's events, placed "after" the sixty-two weeks but not in the seventieth, as exactly such a gap. Many amillennial and historic premillennial scholars also accept staged fulfilments of prophecy in general.

questions.q: Does Daniel 9:26 describe a "period between" the sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks?
questions.short: The text says certain events happen "after" the sixty-two weeks. It does not say "but not in the seventieth". The fulfilled reading says no period of time can sit between two weeks unless the text states one.
questions.answer: Some writers, such as Robert Culver, call it the "one natural interpretation" that verse 26's events belong to a period between the two weeks. In that period God sets Israel aside until a future restoration. But the text never mentions such a period. As Hans LaRondelle noted, it says "after the sixty-two weeks". It does not say "after the sixty-two weeks, but not in the seventieth". The next week naturally follows the sixty-two, as January 1 follows December 31. On the fulfilled reading, the Messiah was cut off early in the seventieth week, which is after the sixty-ninth. That fits the text exactly. To assume a "period between" first and then find it in the text is to argue in a circle.
examples: Daniel 9:26: "after the sixty-two weeks Messiah will be cut off". This is in the seventieth week, which comes right after the sixty-second.
A modern parallel: a 70-week contract has no week between week 69 and week 70 unless the contract says so.
questions.other: Dispensationalists hold that if the Messiah's death came "in" the seventieth week, the text would say so. They take the destruction of the city, also "after" the sixty-two, as clearly outside the seventieth week, so a gap is already present. Historicists and amillennialists usually agree with the continuous reading.

questions.q: Does Daniel 9 promise a future restoration of Israel to the land at the end of the seventy weeks?
questions.short: The text does not mention a later return to the land. Israel was in the land through all seventy weeks and when the temple fell in AD 70. Joshua 21:43-45 also says God fulfilled his land promise.
questions.answer: Daniel prayed about the return from Babylon, and that return happened under Cyrus (Ezra 1:1-4). The seventy weeks that follow are about what God would do for "your people and your holy city". He would finish transgression, atone for sin, bring everlasting righteousness and anoint a most holy place (Daniel 9:24). Then the city and sanctuary would be destroyed (9:26). Nothing in the passage foretells a second return after a long gap. Israel was in the land when the sixty-ninth week ended, when the seventieth began, and when Jerusalem fell. Joshua 21:43-45 says that not one of God's good promises about the land failed. On the fulfilled reading, the seventy weeks end with atonement in Christ, not with a modern political event.
examples: Joshua 21:45: "Not one word failed of all the good things which the LORD had spoken".
Nehemiah 9:7-8: the returned exiles praise God for keeping his land promise to Abraham.
questions.other: Dispensationalists and many other premillennialists answer that later prophets still promised a future regathering (Ezekiel 36-37; Amos 9:14-15). They say the Abrahamic land promise is eternal (Genesis 17:8). Many also see the modern return of Jews to the land as part of God's purpose, though views differ on how.

questions.q: Would a future seven-year judgment on Israel mean God punishes the nation twice for the same sin?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading argues that the judgment for rejecting the Messiah fell in AD 70. Nahum's "distress will not rise up twice" suggests God does not repeat a completed judgment.
questions.answer: Jesus said that the blood of the prophets would be required of "this generation" (Matthew 23:35-36; Luke 11:50-51). He described Jerusalem's fall as "days of vengeance, that all things which are written may be fulfilled" (Luke 21:22). On the fulfilled reading, that judgment was complete in AD 70. Nahum 1:9 says of God's judgment on Nineveh that "distress will not rise up a second time". The same principle applies here: a completed sentence is not carried out again. To expect a future tribulation in which most of Israel suffers again for the same rejection would mean repeating a judgment Scripture describes as finished. The good news for every generation, Jewish or Gentile, is the open door of Christ (Romans 10:12-13; 11:23).
examples: Luke 21:22: "all things which are written" are fulfilled in those days of vengeance.
Romans 11:23: if they do not continue in unbelief, they will be grafted in. The door stays open.
questions.other: Futurists reply that the future tribulation is not a second punishment for the cross. They say it is a time of refining that brings Israel to faith (Jeremiah 30:7; Zechariah 13:8-9) and also judges a rebellious world. Nahum 1:9 refers to Assyria. It is not a rule for all future history.

questions.q: If Jerusalem fell in AD 70, about forty years after the seventieth week, doesn't Daniel 9 need some gap anyway?
questions.short: No. On the fulfilled reading, the city's destruction was "determined" within the seventy weeks but carried out later, as a sentence is given on one day and carried out on another.
questions.answer: Daniel 9:26 says "desolations are determined". On the fulfilled reading, the decisive cause, the rejection and killing of the Messiah (Acts 3:14-15), happened within the seventy weeks. Its outworking came a generation later. Jesus pronounced the temple "desolate" when he left it (Matthew 23:38), forty years before it fell. He told the women of Jerusalem to weep for their children (Luke 23:27-31). Adam was told he would die "in the day" he ate. He died spiritually that day, and physically later (Genesis 2:17; 5:5). A judge passes sentence on one day and it is carried out later. In addition, if a gap were needed, a forty-year gap within that generation would be more natural than one of two thousand years.
examples: Matthew 23:38: "your house is left to you desolate". This was declared in about AD 30 and carried out in AD 70.
Genesis 2:17 and 5:5: death sentenced "in the day". Adam lived 930 years.
questions.other: Dispensationalists take this as proof that the prophecy spans more than 490 continuous years, which supports some kind of interval. Critical scholars refer the destruction language to Antiochus's profaning of the temple in 167 BC, so they need no gap.

questions.q: Was the continuous reading of the seventy weeks the historic view before the 1800s?
questions.short: Largely, yes. Many Protestant interpreters before the 1800s saw the seventieth week fulfilled in Christ. The future-week view spread through J. N. Darby and the Scofield Reference Bible.
questions.answer: From the Reformation onward, most Protestant commentators held that the seventy weeks ran in sequence to Christ. They taught that Christ confirmed the covenant and ended the sacrifices by his death, and that Jerusalem's ruin followed as a result. This was the main view among the Reformers and the Puritans, and among later writers such as Matthew Henry, E. W. Hengstenberg and Philip Mauro. Details differed, especially the starting decree. John Lightfoot, in the 1600s, summed it up this way: Daniel traces Jerusalem from Cyrus's rebuilding to its destruction by Titus, and John's Revelation begins where Daniel ends. On the fulfilled reading, the future seventieth week is a nineteenth-century innovation tied to Darby's sharp separation of Israel and the church.
examples: John Calvin, Commentary on Daniel 9:27 (1561): Christ confirmed the covenant and abolished the sacrifices.
J. N. Darby (1800-1882) developed the "church parenthesis". The Scofield Reference Bible (1909, 1917) made it widely known.
questions.other: Futurists point out that some early church writers held a future final week. Irenaeus (about 180) and Hippolytus (about 204) set the last week at the end of the age with the Antichrist. So the view is not purely modern. Historicists also held continuous fulfilment but differed on many details.

questions.q: If one vision shows events far apart in time, isn't that a kind of gap?
questions.short: Nebuchadnezzar saw one statue with four kingdoms that followed each other over centuries. That shows sequence, not a pause. Each kingdom followed the last without an empty stretch of time.
questions.answer: Daniel 2 shows four kingdoms in one image, and the stone strikes them all together (Daniel 2:34-35). Yet history spread them over centuries. Babylon fell in 539 BC, Persia in 331 BC, and Greek rule gave way to Rome in the 60s BC. Some argue this shows that prophecy can compress time, so a gap in Daniel 9 is possible. On the fulfilled reading, this confuses compression with interruption. Each kingdom in Daniel 2 follows the one before it in an unbroken line. No time passes with no kingdom in place. Daniel 9 also lists its parts in unbroken sequence (7, 62, 1). The judgment on the statue was announced when Daniel explained the dream, though its fulfilment unfolded over centuries. That is a sentence given and later carried out, not a clock stopped.
examples: 539 BC: Babylon falls to Cyrus (Daniel 5:30-31). 331 BC: Persia falls to Alexander at Gaugamela.
63 BC: Pompey takes Jerusalem, and Judea comes under Rome, the fourth kingdom.
questions.other: Dispensationalists see Daniel 2's stone as striking the toes at Christ's second coming. In their view the toes stand for a future, revived form of the fourth empire, which requires a long gap after ancient Rome. Many other interpreters accept continuity but differ on whether the fourth kingdom is Rome or Greece.

questions.q: When a volcano or a great earthquake strikes, is it a sign that the end of the world is near?
questions.short: Not by itself. Great disasters have struck every century. People who lived through them often felt the end had come, yet the world went on.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, a disaster is not a prophetic clock. In June 1991 Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted. Some who lived near it said they thought it was the end of the world. In January 1995 the Kobe earthquake in Japan killed more than 6,000 people, and some survivors said the same. But Pinatubo had erupted before, about five centuries earlier, and people then surely felt the same fear. Solomon reminds us that there is nothing new under the sun. Jesus also said that wars and earthquakes are 'not yet the end' (Matthew 24:6). The signs he gave were tied to his own generation. So a disaster today is a real warning to repent, but it is not a sign that fixes the date of Christ's return.
examples: Mount Pinatubo, June 1991: one of the largest eruptions of the 20th century. Geologists date its previous large eruption to about 500 years earlier.
Kobe (Great Hanshin) earthquake, 17 January 1995: about 6,400 dead. Some survivors told reporters they thought the world was ending.
Ecclesiastes 1:4, 9: one generation goes and another comes; what has happened will happen again.
questions.other: Many futurist teachers agree that one disaster proves nothing. But they say the rising number and strength of disasters, like birth pains (Matthew 24:8), shows the end is close. Historicists see a long series of judgments through church history. Idealists see such events in every age as reminders of a fallen world awaiting Christ.

questions.q: If disasters are not end-time signs, do they still carry a message from God?
questions.short: Yes. Scripture shows God sometimes uses earthquakes and plagues as judgment or warning. Every disaster reminds us that the world is fallen and that we must repent.
questions.answer: This reading keeps a moral meaning for disasters while denying that they date the end. In Numbers 16 the ground opened and swallowed Korah's rebels. That was a direct judgment. In Amos 4 God sent famine, drought and plague so that Israel would return to him. But Scripture also warns us not to read every disaster as a verdict on its victims. Jesus said the men killed by the tower in Siloam were no worse sinners than others (Luke 13:4-5). He said the man born blind did not suffer because of his own sin or his parents' sin (John 9:1-3). So the right response to a disaster is humble repentance and mercy to the suffering, not date-setting. Eighteenth-century preachers like John Wesley saw earthquakes as calls to repent, not as timetables.
examples: John Wesley's sermon on the causes and cure of earthquakes (1750) followed tremors felt in London. He called hearers to 'prepare to meet' God (Amos 4:12).
In 1756 the colonial preacher Gilbert Tennent saw frequent earthquakes as a hint of great changes, not as proof of Christ's soon return.
Luke 13:1-5: the Galileans killed by Pilate and the eighteen killed at Siloam.
questions.other: Most Christians of all views agree with this moral reading. Some charismatic and futurist teachers go further. They name specific disasters as God's response to specific national sins, for example policies about Israel. Others warn that such claims go beyond Scripture and can wound victims.

questions.q: Why does each generation tend to think that its own troubles are uniquely prophetic?
questions.short: Because we know little of the past. We read our own news as unique when history shows the same troubles again and again.
questions.answer: This reading calls the problem 'generational provincialism'. It is the belief that nothing has prophetic meaning unless it happens to us. Most people know their own decade far better than past centuries. So the wars, plagues and moral decline of today feel unique. But wars, famine and disease have been part of human life since the fall (Genesis 3:17-19). Ecclesiastes says one generation goes and another comes, and there is nothing new under the sun. The cure is to study history and to read prophecy in its own time frame. When we do this, we find that many past generations were just as sure as we are that they were the last. All of them were wrong.
examples: About AD 1000, and again around 1260 and 1500, many in Europe expected the end. Each date passed.
During the Black Death (1347-51) many believed Jesus' words about pestilence were being fulfilled in their day.
Columbus wrote in his Book of Prophecies (about 1501) that the world had only about 150 years left.
questions.other: Futurists reply that some things really are new: the return of Israel in 1948, global communication and weapons of mass destruction. They argue these make our age different from all earlier ones. Historicists also hold that later generations stand nearer the end of a long prophetic sequence.

questions.q: Does a mood of decline and pessimism in society prove that the end is near?
questions.short: No. Europe around 1492 was gloomy and felt it was shrinking. Yet the Reformation, new learning and the spread of the gospel to new lands followed.
questions.answer: On this reading, gloom is a feeling, not a prophecy. A historian of Columbus described Western Europe at the end of 1492 as deeply pessimistic. Christendom was divided, Islam was advancing, the universities were weak, and many escaped into the pagan past. That picture could describe many later ages too. Yet within a generation came the Reformation (1517), a rediscovery of Scripture, and the spread of the gospel to new continents. God often works most when hope seems least. The kingdom is like yeast that slowly fills the dough (Matthew 13:33). Christians should not mistake a dark season for the final hour. Isaiah promised that the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD (Isaiah 11:9).
examples: Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453. Many in Europe felt Christendom was in retreat.
Martin Luther posted his 95 Theses in 1517, 25 years after 1492.
Matthew 13:31-33: the mustard seed and the yeast show slow, steady growth.
questions.other: Premillennial teachers often expect things to grow worse before Christ returns. They cite 2 Timothy 3:1-5 and Luke 18:8 ('will he find faith on the earth?'). Amillennialists expect good and evil to grow side by side until the end. Postmillennialists, like this reading, expect the gospel to triumph widely in history.

questions.q: How can we tell whether an event is a prophetic sign, since generations come and go but the end has not come?
questions.short: This reading offers four keys: find the time frame, check the historical record, study the historical context, and separate fulfilment from application.
questions.answer: Many earlier Christians were sure that the signs fitted their times. They were wrong. To avoid their mistake, this reading uses four keys. First, notice the time frame. Many prophecies say when they will happen, such as 'this generation' (Matthew 24:34) or 'near' (Revelation 1:3). Second, check history. If a 'sign' has happened in every century, its appearance today proves little. Third, study the historical context. When the time text is clear, look for fulfilment in that period before looking to the future. Fourth, separate fulfilment from application. A prophecy may be fulfilled once, but its lessons apply in every age. The normal rules for reading Scripture still apply. These four are simply the ones most often ignored when prophecy is the subject.
examples: Key 1 applied: Daniel read Jeremiah's 'seventy years' and knew the exile was nearly over (Daniel 9:2).
Key 4 applied: Babylon's fall is fulfilled, yet it still warns proud nations (Psalms 2:10-12).
questions.other: Futurists also use time texts but read them differently. 'Near' may mean 'certain' or 'next on God's calendar'. 'This generation' may mean the generation that sees the signs. Historicists read prophecy as a continuous outline of church history. Idealists stress the fourth key and say the main purpose of prophecy is timeless application.

questions.q: Does the Bible give prophecies with fixed time frames, and what do they teach us?
questions.short: Yes. Many prophecies give exact periods: 400 years, seven years, forty years, seventy years. Each was fulfilled within its time frame, not in later periods of the same length.
questions.answer: Read with the first key, these prophecies show that God means what he says about time. God told Abraham that his offspring would be oppressed in a foreign land for four hundred years (Genesis 15:13). Exodus 12:40-41 records that Israel left Egypt at the end of 430 years, 'on that very day'. Joseph foretold seven years of plenty and seven of famine (Genesis 41:29-30). Later famines are not fulfilments of that word. Israel wandered forty years, a year for each day the spies explored the land (Numbers 14:34). Judah's exile lasted seventy years to repay the land's missed sabbaths (2 Chronicles 36:21). Daniel trusted that number and prayed (Daniel 9:2). Later seventy-year spans do not fulfil Jeremiah. In the same way, prophecies tied to 'this generation' belong to that generation.
examples: Genesis 15:13 and Exodus 12:40-41: 400 years foretold (a round number); 430 years recorded, 'to the very day'.
Jeremiah 25:11-12 and 29:10: seventy years for Babylon. Cyrus allowed the return in 538 BC (Ezra 1:1-4).
Numbers 14:33-34: forty days of spying became forty years of wandering.
questions.other: Everyone agrees these periods were literal and fulfilled. Futurists add that some prophecies contain gaps or have a near and a far fulfilment, for example Daniel's seventieth week. Some also see 'day-year' patterns that historicists extend to long church-age periods, such as 1,260 years.

questions.q: Were people in Jesus' day expecting the Messiah because of Daniel's timetable?
questions.short: Very likely. Simeon, Anna and many others were waiting. False messiahs arose too. Even Roman writers report a common belief that rulers from Judea would arise.
questions.answer: On this reading, Daniel's seventy weeks (Daniel 9:24-25) gave Israel a time frame for Messiah the Prince. The Gospels show a nation on watch. Simeon waited for 'the consolation of Israel' (Luke 2:25). Anna spoke to all who looked for Jerusalem's redemption (Luke 2:38). Crowds wondered if John might be the Christ (Luke 3:15). Gamaliel mentioned Theudas and Judas the Galilean, who drew followers (Acts 5:36-37). Magi from the east came looking for a newborn king (Matthew 2:1-2). Daniel had been a chief of Babylon's wise men (Daniel 2:48), so his writings may have been known in the east. Paul says Christ came 'when the fullness of the time had come' (Galatians 4:4). Jesus himself announced, 'The time is fulfilled' (Mark 1:15).
examples: Tacitus (Histories 5.13) and Suetonius (Vespasian 4) both mention an old, widespread belief that men from Judea would rule the world.
Josephus (Jewish War 6.5.4) says an 'ambiguous oracle' in the Scriptures about a world ruler from their country stirred the Jews to war.
Acts 5:36-37: Theudas and Judas the Galilean led failed movements.
questions.other: Most interpreters agree that messianic hope was high in the first century. They differ on how exact the calculation was. Some scholars doubt that ordinary people computed Daniel's weeks. They think the hope came from many texts and from Roman oppression. Dispensational writers like Robert Anderson used Daniel 9 to date Palm Sunday to the day.

questions.q: Did Israel's statehood in 1948 start a prophetic clock, as the 'fig tree' teaching claims?
questions.short: On this reading, no. Matthew 24:32 says nothing about Israel becoming a nation again. The 1948-1988 timetable built on it has already failed.
questions.answer: Futurist writers saw the need for a time marker. Hal Lindsey taught that the fig tree's new leaves in Matthew 24:32 picture Israel's rebirth in 1948. He then took 'this generation' as the generation that saw it, about forty years, so roughly 1988. The fulfilled reading answers in three ways. First, the text does not mention Israel's nationhood. Jesus used the fig tree as a simple seasonal lesson: when leaves appear, summer is near. Luke adds 'and all the trees' (Luke 21:29). Second, the New Testament never predicts a restored Jewish state. Third, the Old Testament promises of return were fulfilled after the Babylonian exile (Ezra 1:1-4; Nehemiah 1:8-9). So 1948 is a real and important historical event, but Matthew 24 does not date it.
examples: Luke 21:29-31: 'Look at the fig tree, and all the trees.' The lesson is about seasons, not one nation.
1988 passed without the rapture. Edgar Whisenant's book '88 Reasons' used the same 1948 starting point.
Jeremiah 29:10-14: the promised gathering came 'when seventy years are completed'.
questions.other: Many futurists still see 1948 as the major prophetic event of the modern era. They point to Ezekiel 37, Isaiah 11:11 ('a second time') and Romans 11:25-26. Some now say a generation may be 70, 80 or 100 years. Many amillennial and covenant writers agree that Matthew 24:32 is not about 1948.

questions.q: If 'this generation' meant Jesus' hearers, what does that mean for wars and earthquakes in our day?
questions.short: It means the signs in Matthew 24:4-34 were for AD 30-70. Today's wars and earthquakes are real evils, but they are not those prophetic signs.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, the phrase 'this generation' in the Gospels always points to the people Jesus was speaking to (Matthew 11:16; 12:41-45; 23:36). Jesus said all these things would happen before that generation passed away (Matthew 24:34). So the false christs, wars, famines, earthquakes, persecution and the gospel to the nations all came in the forty years before Jerusalem fell in AD 70. Israel may still have a future role in God's plan. But that role does not rest on Matthew 24, because Jesus said nothing there about Israel becoming a nation again. When we hear of wars and earthquakes now, we should pray and help. We should not treat them as a countdown.
examples: Matthew 23:36 and 24:34 use the same phrase. The first clearly means Jesus' hearers.
Famine under Claudius (Acts 11:28), about AD 46; earthquake at Philippi (Acts 16:26).
Colossians 1:6, 23: Paul says the gospel had reached 'all the world' by about AD 60.
questions.other: Dispensational writers often read 'generation' as the generation alive when the end-time signs begin. Others read it as 'race', meaning the Jewish people will survive. Many evangelical scholars (for example R. T. France) agree verse 34 refers to AD 70. They see a shift to the final coming in verse 36.

questions.q: Was the Black Death a fulfilment of Jesus' words about pestilence?
questions.short: Many who lived through it thought so. But on this reading Jesus' signs were for his own generation. The Black Death was a terrible event, not the fulfilment of Matthew 24.
questions.answer: The Black Death of 1347-1351 was perhaps the deadliest disaster in recorded history. Modern historians estimate that between a third and a half of Europe's people died, perhaps 25 to 50 million. Survivors felt they were the generation Jesus spoke about. The poet Petrarch wrote in 1349 that later readers would hardly believe that cities were emptied and fields filled with the dead. If any plague could claim to be 'the' sign, it was this one. Yet the end did not come. This shows the danger of reading our own crisis as unique. On the fulfilled reading, Jesus told his disciples to watch for signs within their own lifetime (Luke 21:11, 32), and they saw them. Later plagues are reminders of a fallen world, not prophetic dates.
examples: Petrarch, letter from Parma, 1349: 'Will posterity believe' that the earth was emptied without war or flood?
Plague hit China in the early 1330s before reaching the Black Sea and Italy in 1347.
A popular claim says 'Ring a Ring o' Roses' describes the plague. Folklorists reject this. The rhyme is first printed in 1881 and the plague link appears only in the 20th century.
questions.other: Futurists agree the Black Death did not fulfil the end-time prophecies. They hold the true fulfilment is still ahead, perhaps in the seal judgments (Revelation 6:8). Historicists have often placed great medieval plagues within the trumpet and bowl visions. Idealists see such events as typical of the whole age.

questions.q: Are modern epidemics such as AIDS or COVID-19 worse than past plagues, and so signs of the last days?
questions.short: In share of population, no. Modern epidemics are tragic, but the Black Death killed a far larger part of humanity. Size alone does not make an event prophetic.
questions.answer: This reading compares by proportion, not by headlines. When the Black Death struck, world population was perhaps 400 to 500 million. Scholars suggest 75 million or more died, around one person in six worldwide. AIDS has killed about 42 million people since 1981, out of a world population of 5 to 8 billion. That is a little over half of one percent. COVID-19 had about 7 million reported deaths by 2024, with estimates of excess deaths much higher. Each death is a real loss. But the numbers show our age is not unique. On this reading, even such comparisons are beside the point. The signs of Matthew 24 were limited by Jesus' time text to the generation before AD 70.
examples: Black Death: perhaps 75 to 200 million dead worldwide, out of roughly 450 million people.
AIDS: about 42 million deaths from 1981 to 2023 (UNAIDS estimates).
The 1918 influenza killed perhaps 50 million out of about 1.8 billion people.
questions.other: Some futurist teachers say the key sign is not size but the combination of many signs at once, together with Israel's return and global technology. Others link pandemics to the fourth seal of Revelation 6:8. Many Christians of every view simply see disease as part of the curse that Christ will finally remove (Revelation 21:4).

questions.q: Are earthquakes really increasing in our time, as some prophecy writers claim?
questions.short: No good evidence shows it. Seismologists say the number of large earthquakes is fairly steady. We simply detect and report far more of them.
questions.answer: In 1980 Hal Lindsey wrote that the number of earthquakes per decade had roughly doubled since 1950. He gave no data. The United States Geological Survey says the rate of magnitude 7 or larger earthquakes has stayed fairly constant over the last century. More quakes are recorded because there are many more seismograph stations and faster global news. In the early 1900s the French scholar Count Montessus de Ballore catalogued about 171,000 earthquakes from recorded history. Great killers came long before our day. The Shaanxi earthquake of 1556 killed perhaps 830,000. On the fulfilled reading, Jesus spoke of earthquakes 'in various places' before AD 70, and his time text limits that sign.
examples: Lisbon, 1 November 1755 (All Saints' Day): earthquake, tsunami and fire. Estimates range from 30,000 to 50,000 or more deaths.
Shaanxi, China, 1556: the deadliest recorded earthquake.
USGS: about 15 earthquakes of magnitude 7 or more occur per year on average, with no long-term rise.
questions.other: Some futurists now grant that frequency is not rising. They say the sign is the overall 'birth pains' pattern, or that quake deaths and damage are rising because of crowded cities. Others look to a future great earthquake (Revelation 16:18). Few careful scholars of any view now rely on frequency statistics.

questions.q: Were there earthquakes in the first century to fulfil Jesus' words before AD 70?
questions.short: Yes. Ancient writers report many. Seneca, who died in AD 65, spoke of whole cities destroyed by earthquakes in Asia, Achaia, Syria and Macedonia.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, Jesus' sign of earthquakes 'in various places' (Matthew 24:7) was met in the years AD 30-70. The New Testament records an earthquake at the crucifixion (Matthew 27:51), at the resurrection (Matthew 28:2), and at Philippi (Acts 16:26). Roman sources add more. Laodicea was destroyed by an earthquake in AD 60 (Tacitus, Annals 14.27). Pompeii was badly damaged in AD 62 or 63 (Seneca, Natural Questions 6.1). Seneca also wrote of how often cities in Asia and Achaia had been laid low, and of Paphos on Cyprus collapsing. He wrote this only a few years before Jerusalem fell. So the disciples did not need to wait centuries to see this sign.
examples: Tacitus, Annals 14.27: Laodicea rebuilt itself from its own resources after the AD 60 quake.
Seneca, Natural Questions 6.1: the Campanian (Pompeii) earthquake.
Josephus, Jewish War 4.4.5: a violent storm and earthquake at Jerusalem in AD 68 seemed to men a sign of disaster.
questions.other: Futurists agree such quakes happened but say they were only the 'beginning of birth pains' (Matthew 24:8). The full sign is still future, with a great global earthquake (Revelation 16:18). Some partial preterists apply the earthquake sign to AD 70 and the bowl judgments to a later time.

questions.q: How could 'wars and rumors of wars' be a sign during the Roman peace?
questions.short: Because the Pax Romana made war unusual. When revolts and civil war broke out in the 60s, they stood out. In AD 68-69 Rome itself almost fell.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, the sign makes sense because it came in a time of general peace. Under the Roman peace, large wars were rare. So reports of war were noticed. In the 60s, unrest grew. Britain rebelled under Boudica (AD 60-61). Judea revolted in AD 66. After Nero died in June 68, civil war broke out. Four emperors ruled in about a year: Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian. Tacitus called it a year that was almost the last for the state (Histories 1.11). Jesus told his disciples not to be alarmed, because 'the end is not yet' (Matthew 24:6). His time text (24:34) places these wars before AD 70. In an age of constant war, wars would not be much of a sign.
examples: Tacitus, Histories 1.2: a period 'rich in disasters, frightful with battles, torn by civil strife'.
AD 69: the Capitol in Rome burned during fighting between Vitellius's and Vespasian's men.
Josephus, Jewish War 4.9.2: news of Rome's civil war reached Vespasian in Judea.
questions.other: Futurists say the sign is war on a world scale, nation against kingdom, and see this in the World Wars. Some say the wars of the first century were a partial or near fulfilment. Others, like many amillennialists, see wars as marks of the entire age between Christ's comings.

questions.q: Are the wars of the last century so terrible that they must be a prelude to the end?
questions.short: Not on the historical record. Earlier wars killed huge shares of their populations. Each age has thought its wars were the last.
questions.answer: This reading compares the 20th century with earlier ones. World War II was terribly destructive. Perhaps 70 to 85 million died, and atomic bombs were used. But earlier wars were also catastrophic. The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) may have killed a fifth to a third of the German population. The Manchu conquest of China in the 1600s and the Taiping Rebellion (1850-1864) each killed tens of millions. The Paraguayan War (1864-1870) killed perhaps half or more of Paraguay's people. After the Goths defeated Rome at Adrianople in 378, Ambrose of Milan linked them with Ezekiel's Gog and felt the end had come. The key, on this reading, is that Jesus' wars were limited to forty years after his death. With so many wars in history, the sign would mean nothing without a time limit.
examples: Battle of Adrianople, AD 378: Emperor Valens killed. Ambrose (On the Faith 2.16) identified the Goths with Gog.
Taiping Rebellion, 1850-1864: estimates of 20 to 30 million deaths.
Napoleonic Wars, 1803-1815: perhaps 3.5 to 6 million deaths.
questions.other: Futurists answer that modern war is unique in being truly global and in having weapons that can end human life, as Matthew 24:22 might suggest ('no flesh would be saved'). Others note that the share of people dying in war has fallen since 1945. Amillennialists see wars in every age as part of the 'birth pains'.

questions.q: If these signs are fulfilled, what should Christians do when disasters happen today?
questions.short: Repent, pray, help the suffering and keep working. Fulfilled prophecy still teaches lessons that apply to every age.
questions.answer: On this reading, past fulfilment does not make the Bible silent about today. It changes what we do with the news. Instead of building charts, Christians should do what Jesus commanded. He told his hearers to repent when they heard of disaster (Luke 13:5). The early church sent famine relief to Judea (Acts 11:28-30). Paul told believers to do good to all people (Galatians 6:10). God still rules over nations and nature (Psalms 46:1-3). Disasters remind us that creation groans and waits for redemption (Romans 8:22). They also show how short life is (James 4:14). So the right response is faith, love and good works, not fear or date-setting.
examples: Acts 11:28-30: Agabus foretold a famine; the disciples sent help to Judea.
During the Plague of Cyprian (AD 250s), Christians in Carthage cared for the sick of every faith (Pontius, Life of Cyprian 9).
Martin Luther's letter 'Whether One May Flee from a Deadly Plague' (1527) urged care for neighbours.
questions.other: Christians of every view largely agree on this practical response. Futurists add that today's signs should also stir urgency in evangelism, because the Lord's coming may be very near. Some warn that a fully past reading could weaken watchfulness. Fulfilled readers reply that Christ's final coming is still future and still calls us to watch.

questions.q: Have confident predictions about Russia and Bible prophecy come true?
questions.short: No. Writers in 1916, 1928, 1948, 1980 and 1991 said Russia would soon invade Israel. Each forecast passed without fulfilment.
questions.answer: This reading asks readers to notice the dates. In 1916 Arno Gaebelein wrote that Russia's millions would soon be thrown into Palestine. A 1928 Pentecostal article said the conflict would come 'very shortly'. In 1948 a magazine said World War III might start in ninety days. In 1980 Hal Lindsey said the Soviets would use Afghanistan as a springboard to seize Iran. Instead, the Soviet Union left Afghanistan in 1989 and broke apart in 1991. In January 1991 a newsletter said Russia would attack Israel and Europe. The same writer later admitted he had 'jumped the gun'. Scripture gives a test for prophets: if the word does not come true, the LORD did not speak it (Deuteronomy 18:22). Christians should not build their lives on such guesses.
examples: Soviet troops left Afghanistan in February 1989. The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.
Russia did not take part in the 1991 Gulf War, but the Soviet Union backed the UN resolutions against Iraq.
Dwight Wilson's 'Armageddon Now!' (1977) collects decades of such Russia forecasts.
questions.other: Many futurist teachers agree that date-setting is wrong and that some predictions were careless. But they hold that the core teaching, a northern coalition attacking Israel in the last days, remains true even if timing guesses failed. They point to Russia's alliances with Iran and its role in Syria since 2015 as fresh signs.

questions.q: Are many prophecy 'predictions' just current trends read back into the Bible?
questions.short: On this reading, yes. Writers take what is already happening in politics, project it forward, and then find verses to support it.
questions.answer: This reading argues that much prophecy writing begins with the newspaper, not the text. A writer sees a trend, such as European unity or a Russian arms build-up. He forecasts that it will continue. Then he looks for a verse that seems to fit. When the trend changes, the book is revised. The prophets, by contrast, did not take their message from the news of their day. Peter says prophecy never came by human will. Holy men spoke from God as the Spirit carried them along (2 Peter 1:20-21). Jeremiah condemned prophets who spoke visions from their own minds (Jeremiah 23:16). Prophecy must be read in its own words, time and setting first.
examples: George Orwell noted that political forecasters usually predict 'a continuation of the thing that is happening'.
In the 1970s many books tied prophecy to oil and the Arab world. In the 1990s, to the New World Order. In the 2000s, to terrorism.
2 Peter 1:20-21: no prophecy comes from the prophet's own interpretation.
questions.other: Futurists answer that Jesus told us to read 'the signs of the times' (Matthew 16:3) and to watch. They say comparing news with Scripture is obedient watchfulness, as long as one avoids dates. Some admit past excesses but say real fulfilments, such as Israel's rebirth, show the method works.

questions.q: Did the prophets describe modern weapons with ancient words because they could not imagine tanks and missiles?
questions.short: This reading says no. The prophets spoke from God, and God can describe any weapon. If they spoke of swords and bows, they meant a war fought with swords and bows.
questions.answer: Some writers say a prophet 'could not describe' machine guns, so he wrote of bows and arrows instead. The fulfilled reading replies that modern weapons were not beyond God's imagination. Prophets did not speak from their own understanding but from God (2 Peter 1:21). Ezekiel names horses, swords, shields, bows, arrows, clubs and spears (Ezekiel 38:4; 39:9). He says Israel would burn the wooden weapons for seven years (39:9-10). The simplest reading is that the prophet described a war of his own world. That war lay in his future but is in our past. Futurists cannot have it both ways. They cannot claim a literal reading while turning swords into missiles.
examples: Ezekiel 39:9-10: the people will make fires of the weapons and need no wood from the field.
Daniel 11 describes horses, chariots and ships in wars of the Persian and Greek periods (Daniel 11:40).
Some writers have read Ezekiel's horses as 'horsepower' in engines.
questions.other: Some futurists hold that the battle will literally use primitive weapons, perhaps after a global collapse. Others say the prophet used the words of his time for weapons he saw in vision, as John may describe helicopters as locusts. Others read Ezekiel 38-39 as symbolic or apocalyptic, so weapons are not the point.

questions.q: Does 2 Peter 3:10 describe a nuclear war?
questions.short: This reading says no. Peter used Old Testament judgment language. Reading his words as atomic physics adds modern ideas the text does not contain.
questions.answer: Some writers say Peter's elements melting with fervent heat is a precise description of a nuclear blast. But this is the same writer group that says Ezekiel could not describe modern weapons. Both cannot be true. Peter uses the fire language of the prophets. God's judgments on Sodom, on Edom and on Jerusalem are described with fire and melting (Isaiah 34:4; Micah 1:4; Zephaniah 1:18). The Greek word stoicheia ('elements') can mean basic parts of a system, as in Galatians 4:3, 9 and Colossians 2:8. On the fulfilled or covenantal reading, Peter speaks of the passing of the old covenant world. Other readers see the final renewal of creation. Neither reading needs nuclear physics.
examples: Micah 1:4: mountains melt like wax before the fire. This describes God's judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem.
Galatians 4:3, 9 uses stoicheia for the 'elementary principles' of the old order.
Hiroshima, 6 August 1945, often cited by mid-century writers as a picture of 2 Peter 3.
questions.other: Most futurist and amillennial scholars also reject a nuclear reading. They see 2 Peter 3 as God's direct final judgment and renewal of the cosmos at Christ's return, not a human war. Some popular writers still see nuclear weapons as one way such fire could come. Full and partial preterists differ on whether 2 Peter 3 is past or future.

questions.q: Was Saddam Hussein's Iraq a fulfilment of Isaiah 13 and the fall of Babylon?
questions.short: On this reading, no. Isaiah said Babylon's day was near and named the Medes as God's instrument. That judgment came in Isaiah's own era of history, not in 1990.
questions.answer: In 1991 one writer argued that Iraq's invasion of Kuwait was a step toward the end-time Babylon of Isaiah 13. He said the 'day of the LORD' there is a future tribulation. The fulfilled reading sees three problems. First, the theory rests on a gap of nearly 2,000 years between Daniel's sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks. Second, Isaiah says the day of the LORD is 'near' (Isaiah 13:6). Third, Isaiah names the attackers: 'I will stir up the Medes against them' (13:17). Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians in 539 BC. Daniel records that Belshazzar was killed that night and Darius the Mede received the kingdom (Daniel 5:30-31). Babylon then slowly became a ruin, as Isaiah said (13:19-22).
examples: Nabonidus Chronicle: Cyrus's army entered Babylon in October 539 BC.
Strabo (Geography 16.1.5), about the time of Christ, said Babylon was largely deserted.
Charles Dyer, 'The Rise of Babylon' (1991), proposed the Iraqi link.
questions.other: Some futurists hold that Babylon never suffered the total, sudden destruction of Isaiah 13:19 and Jeremiah 50-51. So they expect a rebuilt literal Babylon to be destroyed in the future (compare Revelation 18). Others see a near fulfilment in 539 BC and a far fulfilment at the end. Many scholars see Isaiah's language as typical judgment poetry.

questions.q: When Isaiah says 'the day of the LORD is near,' can 'near' mean thousands of years away?
questions.short: On this reading, no. If 'near' does not mean close at hand, it means nothing. A literal reading should take the time word plainly.
questions.answer: This reading presses the literal method on its own users. Dispensational writers insist on reading Scripture plainly. Yet they read 'near' in Isaiah 13:6 as 2,500 years or more. Isaiah also says Babylon's 'days will not be prolonged' (13:22). The prophets often said a day of the LORD was near for their hearers. Obadiah said it was near for Edom (Obadiah 15). Ezekiel said it was near for Egypt (Ezekiel 30:3). Zephaniah said it was near for Judah (Zephaniah 1:7, 14). Each came within history. The same rule applies to the New Testament. When Revelation says 'the time is near' (Revelation 1:3; 22:10), it means near for its first readers.
examples: Ezekiel 30:3-4: the day is near; a sword comes on Egypt. Nebuchadnezzar invaded Egypt about 568 BC.
Zephaniah 1:14: the great day is near and hastens. Jerusalem fell in 586 BC.
Compare Daniel 8:26 ('seal up the vision, for it refers to many days') with Revelation 22:10 ('do not seal... the time is near').
questions.other: Futurists answer that 'near' can mean 'imminent' or 'next in God's plan'. They cite 2 Peter 3:8 ('a day is like a thousand years'). Others see a near historical fulfilment that also previews a final, far one. Some scholars say prophets often saw future events without time gaps, like mountain peaks.

questions.q: Does 'the day of the LORD' always mean the final end of the world?
questions.short: No. In the Old Testament it often means any time God comes in judgment on a nation, such as Babylon, Edom, Egypt or Judah.
questions.answer: On this reading, the day of the LORD is any day when God acts decisively in history. Isaiah used it for Babylon (Isaiah 13:6, 9) and for Edom (Isaiah 34:8). Ezekiel used it for Egypt (Ezekiel 30:2-4). Joel used it for a locust plague and invasion (Joel 1:15; 2:1). Amos used it for Israel's fall to Assyria (Amos 5:18-20). Zephaniah used it for Judah's fall to Babylon (Zephaniah 1:7-18). Each 'day' came in history. So it is a mistake to assume that every use points to one future tribulation period. A small correction: the book's link to 'the Lord's day' in Revelation 1:10 is weak. There John uses a different Greek phrase (kyriake hemera), which the early church used for Sunday.
examples: Amos 5:18-20: 'darkness, not light'. Israel fell to Assyria in 722 BC.
Isaiah 34:8-10: a day of vengeance on Edom, described as never-ending smoke.
Didache 14.1 (about AD 100) uses 'the Lord's day' for the day of Christian worship.
questions.other: Most scholars agree the phrase has many historical uses. Futurists add that these past days preview a final Day of the LORD at Christ's return (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10). Many see a pattern of near and far fulfilment. Some dispensationalists define the end-time Day of the LORD as including the tribulation and millennium.

questions.q: How does Daniel's statue of four kingdoms help us understand Babylon's fall?
questions.short: Daniel showed Babylon (gold) giving way to Medo-Persia (silver), Greece (bronze) and Rome (iron). God's stone kingdom then came and outlasts them all.
questions.answer: This reading uses Scripture to interpret Scripture. Nebuchadnezzar saw a statue of gold, silver, bronze and iron (Daniel 2:31-35). Daniel told him that he was the head of gold (2:38). Another kingdom would follow. Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians in 539 BC (Daniel 5:28-31). Greece under Alexander defeated Persia in 331 BC. Rome took the eastern lands by 63 BC. 'In the days of those kings' God set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed (2:44). On this reading, that is Christ's kingdom, which came in the days of Rome (Mark 1:15). It defeats every rival kingdom (Psalms 2). So Babylon's prophecies are fulfilled. Modern states are not new versions of these ancient empires.
examples: Daniel 5:28: 'Peres': your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians.
Battle of Gaugamela, 331 BC: Alexander defeated Darius III.
Pompey entered Jerusalem in 63 BC, bringing Judea under Rome.
questions.other: Most futurists agree on the four kingdoms. But they see the feet and ten toes as a future revived Roman Empire, crushed by the stone at Christ's second coming. Some critical scholars read the four as Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece. Amillennialists generally agree with the reading given here.

questions.q: Did Saddam Hussein's rebuilding of ancient Babylon fulfil prophecy?
questions.short: On this reading, no. It was a nationalist project to attract tourists and honour Iraq's past. Copying the past does not fulfil prophecy.
questions.answer: From the 1980s Saddam Hussein rebuilt parts of Babylon. He put his own name on new bricks, as Nebuchadnezzar had done. Some prophecy writers saw this as the rise of end-time Babylon. Historian Edwin Yamauchi judged it as a matter of national pride and tourism, like the Shah of Iran's 1971 celebration at Persepolis. If any past glory inspired Saddam, it was the Abbasid caliphate of Baghdad (AD 750-1258). The fulfilled reading sees no prophetic link. If anything, Saddam's fall in 2003 illustrates a principle: rulers who exalt themselves like Babylon are brought low (Isaiah 14:12-15; Daniel 4:37). This is application, not fulfilment. Isaiah said Babylon would never be inhabited again as a great city (Isaiah 13:20).
examples: Saddam's bricks bore the words 'built in the era of Saddam Hussein'.
In 2019 UNESCO listed Babylon as a World Heritage Site. It remains a ruin and tourist site, not a capital.
Daniel 4:30-37: Nebuchadnezzar boasted of 'great Babylon which I have built' and was humbled.
questions.other: Some futurists still expect a literal rebuilt Babylon as a world economic center (Revelation 18). They saw Saddam's work as possible preparation and point to Zechariah 5:5-11 (the woman in the basket taken to Shinar). Others think Babylon in Revelation means a future world system, not the Iraqi site.

questions.q: Was Saddam Hussein's 1990 invasion of Kuwait a step toward attacking Israel, as some prophecy writers said?
questions.short: The facts point elsewhere. Iraq invaded Kuwait over oil, debts and border claims. It fired missiles at Israel only later, to break up the coalition against it.
questions.answer: John Walvoord said the invasion was a move to set up a base from which to attack Israel. This reading answers with the historical record. Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990. The main motives were war debts, oil prices and old claims to Kuwaiti land. Iraq did not attack Israel until 18 January 1991, after the coalition began bombing. It fired Scud missiles from western Iraq, which is much closer to Israel than Kuwait is. The aim was to provoke Israel and split the Arab members of the coalition. Israel did not respond. So the events do not fit a prophetic plan in which Iraq moves to destroy Israel. Jesus warned against being led astray by rumours (Matthew 24:4-6).
examples: About 40 Scud missiles struck Israel between January and February 1991.
Kuwait was liberated on 26-28 February 1991.
Iraq owed Kuwait billions of dollars from the Iran-Iraq War (1980-1988).
questions.other: Futurist writers reply that Saddam's hostility to Israel was real and public, and that he paid families of attackers. They see the Gulf War as a 'preview' of end-time hostility from Babylon's region. Most now admit it was not the fulfilment some expected in 1991.

questions.q: Who is 'Babylon the great' in Revelation 17-18?
questions.short: Christians have named four main candidates: first-century Rome, a future revived Roman Empire, a rebuilt literal Babylon, or first-century Jerusalem. This reading argues for Jerusalem.
questions.answer: There are four common answers. Many scholars say Babylon is pagan Rome, the city on seven hills (Revelation 17:9). Futurists often say it is a future revived Rome or a world system. Some expect a literal rebuilt Babylon in Iraq. The fulfilled reading that this group follows says it is apostate Jerusalem of the first century. It begins with the time texts. Revelation says its events 'must soon take place' (1:1) and that 'the time is near' (1:3; 22:10). That rules out a distant future. It then compares Scripture with Scripture. Babylon is 'the great city' (14:8), and so is the city 'where their Lord was crucified' (11:8). The guilt for the blood of prophets (18:24) matches what Jesus said about Jerusalem (Matthew 23:34-37).
examples: Revelation 11:8 and 16:19: 'the great city' is split into three parts.
1 Peter 5:13: 'she who is at Babylon' is often read as Rome, about AD 64.
Josephus, Jewish War 5.1.4: Jerusalem was divided into three warring factions during the siege.
questions.other: Most commentators, including many preterists, identify Babylon with Rome: the seven hills, 'the kings of the earth' (17:18), and maritime trade (18:11-19). Futurists see a future city or system. Idealists see Babylon as the world's seductive power in every age. The Jerusalem view is held by a minority of scholars.

questions.q: Why do Revelation's time statements matter for identifying Babylon?
questions.short: Because John said repeatedly that his visions would 'soon' happen and that 'the time is near'. So Babylon must be a power of his own day.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, Revelation itself sets the time frame. It opens by saying these things 'must soon take place' (1:1) and 'the time is near' (1:3). The risen Christ says 'I am coming quickly' several times (2:16; 3:11; 22:7, 12, 20). The book ends by repeating that the time is near (22:6, 10). John is told not to seal the book (22:10), unlike Daniel, who was told to seal his vision because it was far off (Daniel 8:26; 12:4). If Revelation was written before AD 70, then Babylon is a first-century power: Rome or Jerusalem. Without these time texts, the book can be made to fit any era, which is what many writers have done.
examples: Revelation 22:10 compared with Daniel 12:4: one book sealed, the other open.
Many preterists date Revelation to about AD 65-68, during Nero's reign. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.3) placed it late, near the end of Domitian's reign (about AD 95).
questions.other: Futurists say 'soon' means suddenly or certainly. They also hold that most of the book is about the end. Most scholars date Revelation about AD 95 based on Irenaeus. For them, a Jerusalem identification is impossible, since the city had already fallen. Idealists say 'near' means each generation must be ready.

questions.q: Why does the charge of shedding the blood of prophets point to Jerusalem?
questions.short: Because Jesus laid the blood of all the prophets on Jerusalem and that generation. Revelation lays the same charge on Babylon.
questions.answer: Revelation says the harlot is drunk with the blood of the saints and of Jesus' witnesses (17:6). It also says that in her was found the blood of prophets and saints and of all who were slain on the earth (18:24). This reading compares Jesus' words in Matthew 23. He told the leaders of Jerusalem that all the righteous blood shed on earth, from Abel to Zechariah, would come on 'this generation' (Matthew 23:35-36). He added, 'Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets' (23:37). In Luke he said a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem (Luke 13:33). Stephen accused the council of killing those who foretold the Righteous One (Acts 7:51-52). Paul said the same (1 Thessalonians 2:14-16). The parallel is strong.
examples: Matthew 23:35-36 and Revelation 18:24 both speak of 'all' the righteous blood shed on the earth.
Stephen was killed about AD 34 (Acts 7:58); James the brother of John about AD 44 (Acts 12:2).
Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.1: James, the brother of Jesus, was stoned in Jerusalem in AD 62.
questions.other: Those who see Rome reply that Rome also killed many saints. Nero's persecution in AD 64 (Tacitus, Annals 15.44) is a key example, and later emperors added more. They note that Revelation 17:6 speaks of 'martyrs of Jesus', suggesting imperial persecution. Futurists see an end-time persecution. The harsh words in these texts are about leaders in one generation, not the Jewish people as a whole.

questions.q: Why would a 'harlot' fit unfaithful Jerusalem better than pagan Rome?
questions.short: In the prophets, only a covenant wife can be called a harlot. God called Israel and Jerusalem a faithless wife many times. Rome was never God's bride.
questions.answer: On the fulfilled reading, the image of a harlot is covenant language. The prophets often pictured Israel's idolatry as adultery against God her husband. Ezekiel 16 tells the long story of Jerusalem as an unfaithful bride. Ezekiel 23 does the same for Samaria and Jerusalem. Isaiah says, 'How the faithful city has become a harlot!' (Isaiah 1:21). Jeremiah and Hosea use the same picture (Jeremiah 3:1-8; Hosea 2:2-5). A pagan city cannot break a marriage covenant it never had. Revelation also sets the harlot against the bride. The harlot falls, and the new Jerusalem comes down as a bride (Revelation 21:2). Paul contrasts 'the present Jerusalem', in slavery, with 'the Jerusalem above' (Galatians 4:25-26).
examples: Isaiah 1:21: the faithful city has become a harlot.
Galatians 4:25-26: present Jerusalem in slavery; Jerusalem above is free.
Hebrews 12:22: believers have come to the heavenly Jerusalem.
questions.other: Others note that the prophets also called pagan cities harlots. Nineveh is a harlot (Nahum 3:4) and Tyre is a forgotten harlot (Isaiah 23:15-17). So the image alone does not prove a covenant wife. They see the harlot as Rome's seductive trade and idolatry, or a world system in every age.

questions.q: If Babylon is Jerusalem, why is the harlot riding the beast, which looks like Rome?
questions.short: On this reading, riding the beast shows alliance, not identity. Jerusalem's leaders partnered with Rome against Jesus and his followers.
questions.answer: The beast has seven heads, which John links with seven hills (Revelation 17:9). Many see Rome there. The fulfilled reading agrees that the beast is Rome. But the woman is distinct from the beast she rides. So she is not Rome. She is a city in league with Rome. The Gospels show such an alliance. The chief priests brought Jesus to Pilate because they could not legally execute him (John 18:28-32). They cried, 'We have no king but Caesar' (John 19:15). In Thessalonica opponents accused Paul's friends of acting against Caesar's decrees (Acts 17:7). In the end the beast and ten horns turn on the harlot and burn her (Revelation 17:16), as Rome burned Jerusalem in AD 70.
examples: John 19:12-15: 'If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend.'
Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-7: the temple burned in August AD 70; the city followed in September.
Revelation 17:16: the ten horns hate the harlot and burn her with fire.
questions.other: Those who see Rome reply that the woman is 'the great city that rules over the kings of the earth' (Revelation 17:18). That fits Rome far better than Jerusalem. They read 17:16 as Rome destroyed from within, or as a world system turning on itself. Futurists see a future religious system destroyed by the Antichrist's empire.

questions.q: Can an Old Testament name like Sodom, Egypt or Babylon be used for a different city?
questions.short: Yes. Scripture often gives a city a symbolic name to show its character. Revelation itself calls the city where Jesus was crucified 'Sodom and Egypt'.
questions.answer: On this reading, these names are a kind of prophetic shorthand. Revelation 11:8 says the great city is called 'spiritually' (or 'mystically') Sodom and Egypt, 'where also their Lord was crucified'. That is clearly Jerusalem. Isaiah called Judah's rulers 'rulers of Sodom' (Isaiah 1:10). He said they paraded their sin like Sodom (3:9). Ezekiel said Jerusalem's harlotry began in Egypt (Ezekiel 23:3, 8, 19). Revelation also calls a false teacher at Thyatira 'Jezebel' (Revelation 2:20). So 'Babylon' need not mean the city on the Euphrates. It names a city that acts like Babylon: proud, rich, idolatrous and a persecutor of God's people. The Old Testament Babylon prophecies themselves are fulfilled.
examples: Revelation 11:8: Sodom and Egypt, 'where their Lord was crucified'.
Isaiah 1:9-10: 'rulers of Sodom... people of Gomorrah' addresses Jerusalem.
Revelation 2:20: 'that woman Jezebel' at Thyatira, a symbolic name.
questions.other: Most interpreters agree that 'Babylon' in Revelation is symbolic. They disagree about the target. Many early Christians and modern scholars apply it to Rome, as in 1 Peter 5:13. Reformation writers often applied it to the papacy. Some futurists hold that Revelation 18 requires a literal rebuilt city.

questions.q: Do Bible scholars agree that Gog, 'prince of Rosh,' is the leader of Russia?
questions.short: No. Many leading scholars, including evangelicals, reject the link. It rests on similar sounds, not on Hebrew grammar or ancient geography.
questions.answer: Some popular books say 'Bible scholars agree' that Gog of Ezekiel 38-39 is Russia's leader. They do not. The theory works like this. The Hebrew word rosh is taken as a nation's name. It sounds like 'Russia'. Meshech sounds like 'Moscow'. Tubal sounds like 'Tobolsk', a Siberian city. The fulfilled reading, with many evangelical scholars, rejects this. The historian Edwin Yamauchi wrote that rosh can have nothing to do with modern Russia. He added that informed studies call the Moscow and Tobolsk links untenable. Even some dispensational scholars now agree. Sound-alike word games are not a sound way to read any text. We must ask what the words meant to Ezekiel and his first hearers.
examples: Moscow is first mentioned in 1147 AD. Tobolsk was founded in 1587 AD.
Edwin Yamauchi, 'Foes from the Northern Frontier' (1982), studies the steppe peoples and rejects the Russia link.
questions.other: Many popular futurists still hold the Russia view. Some scholars defend 'Rosh' as a proper name, citing the Greek Septuagint ('Rhos') and possible ancient place names such as Rashu. They usually do not equate it with modern Russia by sound alone. Some say it is a people of the far north, and Russia now holds that territory.

questions.q: What does the Hebrew word rosh mean in Ezekiel 38:2?
questions.short: Rosh normally means 'head' or 'chief'. Many translations read 'chief prince of Meshech and Tubal'. 'Russia' comes from 'Rus', a medieval name.
questions.answer: The word rosh appears hundreds of times in the Hebrew Bible. It means 'head', 'top', 'first' or 'chief'. The high priest is the kohen ha-rosh, the chief priest (2 Kings 25:18). In Ezekiel 38:2 the phrase can be read as 'Gog... the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal'. The King James Version, the ESV and the NIV read it this way. The name 'Russia' comes from the Rus, Scandinavian traders who settled around Kiev in the 9th century AD. That is fifteen centuries after Ezekiel. The fulfilled reading also notes that Rosh never appears as a people's name anywhere else in the Old Testament. The 19th-century scholar Hengstenberg said the Russians had been placed among God's enemies unjustly.
examples: 2 Kings 25:18: 'Seraiah the chief priest' uses rosh for 'chief'.
The Russian Primary Chronicle dates the coming of the Rus leader Rurik to about AD 862.
King James Version, Ezekiel 38:2: 'the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal'.
questions.other: Some scholars argue that the Hebrew accents and grammar favour a place name: 'prince of Rosh, Meshech and Tubal'. The Greek Septuagint, NASB and NKJV read it so. They link it to ancient peoples called Rashu or Rosh. But most do not say that sound alone proves Russia.

questions.q: Where were Meshech and Tubal in Ezekiel's day?
questions.short: In Anatolia, modern Turkey. Assyrian records name them Mushku and Tabal. They were not in Russia.
questions.answer: On this reading, ancient records settle the question. Assyrian inscriptions from the 12th to 7th centuries BC name Mushku and Tabal. They were peoples of central and eastern Anatolia, in today's Turkey. Mushku is linked with the Phrygians of King Midas (Assyrian 'Mita'), about 700 BC. In the Bible, Meshech and Tubal are sons of Japheth (Genesis 10:2). Ezekiel names them as traders with Tyre in slaves and bronze (Ezekiel 27:13). He also names them among the fallen nations in the grave (32:26). So these are real peoples Ezekiel's hearers knew. Herodotus mentions the Moschoi and Tibarenoi near the Black Sea (Histories 3.94; 7.78). They are not modern cities with similar sounds.
examples: Assyrian annals of Sargon II (about 715 BC) mention Mita of Mushku.
Herodotus 7.78: the Moschoi and Tibarenoi served in Xerxes' army in 480 BC.
Ezekiel 27:13: Javan, Tubal and Meshech traded slaves and bronze with Tyre.
questions.other: Many futurist scholars now accept that Meshech and Tubal were in Anatolia. They say Ezekiel names ancient peoples whose lands are today occupied by Turkey and nearby states. These nations could join a future coalition led from the far north. Some older writers still cite Moscow and Tobolsk.

questions.q: Where did the idea that Rosh means Russia come from?
questions.short: It grew in the 19th century. The lexicographer Wilhelm Gesenius suggested it, John Cumming popularized it in 1864, and the Scofield Reference Bible spread it widely in 1909.
questions.answer: The Rosh-Russia link is fairly recent. Some Byzantine writers in the 10th century linked the Rus with Ezekiel's 'Rhos' after Rus raids on Constantinople. But the modern form grew in the 1800s. The German scholar Wilhelm Gesenius suggested in his Hebrew lexicon that Rosh might refer to the Russians. In 1864 the Scottish preacher John Cumming wrote that the 'king of the north' was the Russian ruler. He claimed nearly all expositors agreed. The Scofield Reference Bible (1909) said 'all agree' that Russia is meant. Later writers repeated this through the Cold War. The fulfilled reading notes that a claim of total agreement was never true. Many expositors, such as Hengstenberg, rejected it.
examples: Scofield Reference Bible (1909), note on Ezekiel 38:2.
Crimean War (1853-1856): Britain fought Russia, and many British preachers read Russia into prophecy.
Hal Lindsey, 'The Late Great Planet Earth' (1970), quoted Cumming.
questions.other: Futurist defenders reply that the identification is older than Gesenius in some sources. They also argue that a doctrine's history does not decide its truth. The question is whether the Hebrew supports 'Rosh' as a place. Some cite a 2nd-millennium BC Egyptian or Ugaritic name as evidence.

questions.q: Doesn't 'the remote parts of the north' in Ezekiel 38 point to Russia?
questions.short: Not necessarily. In the Bible 'north' is often the direction from which invaders came, not their homeland. Babylon, in the east, is called a foe 'from the north'.
questions.answer: Ezekiel says Gog will come from the remote parts of the north (Ezekiel 38:6, 15; 39:2). Russia does lie north of Israel. But the fulfilled reading points out how the Bible uses 'north'. Jeremiah warned of disaster from the north (Jeremiah 1:14; 4:6; 6:1, 22). That was Babylon, which lies to the east. Armies from Mesopotamia did not cross the Arabian desert. They followed the Fertile Crescent and entered Israel from the north. Zephaniah places Assyria in the north (Zephaniah 2:13). Isaiah says Cyrus of Persia came from the north as well (Isaiah 41:25). The Bible atlas writer Barry Beitzel notes that 'north' marks the direction of approach. The far north of Ezekiel's day was the region of the Black and Caspian seas.
examples: Jeremiah 4:6: 'I am bringing evil from the north.' This came true when Babylon took Jerusalem in 586 BC.
Isaiah 41:25: one 'from the north' and 'from the rising of the sun' (Cyrus).
Psalms 48:2: Mount Zion is described as 'in the far north'. 'North' can carry symbolic meaning.
questions.other: Futurists answer that 'remote parts' or 'uttermost north' means the farthest north, and Moscow lies almost directly north of Jerusalem. They argue this is stronger than the ordinary 'from the north'. Some scholars treat the 'north' as symbolic of chaos and hostile powers.

questions.q: Do the nations listed with Gog (Persia, Cush, Put, Gomer, Togarmah) describe a modern coalition?
questions.short: On this reading, they describe the known world of Ezekiel's day. If Rosh means Russia because of sound, why do the other names not sound like modern nations?
questions.answer: Some futurists give three reasons for a modern Russian-led attack. Some of Ezekiel's nations lived in lands now in Russia. The armies come from the far north. Many of the nations are today allies of Russia. The fulfilled reading answers that these are ancient names of ancient peoples. Persia, Cush (south of Egypt), Put (Libya), Gomer (the Cimmerians) and Beth-togarmah (eastern Anatolia) all existed in the Persian era. Political alliances change every few years. Ezekiel's list also points to the edges of the Persian Empire, which stretched 'from India to Cush' (Esther 1:1). Finally, if sound-alike names reveal modern nations, then Gomer and Put should also sound like modern countries. They do not.
examples: Esther 1:1 and 8:9: 127 provinces from India to Cush.
Gomer: the Cimmerians (Assyrian 'Gimirrai') invaded Anatolia in the 7th century BC.
Soviet relations with Israel shifted: arms deals were offered by 1991 and full relations restored in October 1991.
questions.other: Futurists reply that Ezekiel used the names of his day for the lands that modern nations occupy. Persia is Iran; Cush is Sudan; Put is Libya; Gomer and Togarmah are Turkey. They see current ties between Russia, Iran and Turkey as a striking match. Others read the list as symbolic of all nations from the earth's edges.

questions.q: Is the Gog and Magog battle of Revelation 20 the same as Ezekiel 38-39?
questions.short: On this reading, no. Revelation places its Gog and Magog after the thousand years, and the details differ. John uses the old name for a new event.
questions.answer: Many futurists place Ezekiel's battle in a future seven-year tribulation. But the fulfilled reading notes that Gog, Magog, Meshech and Tubal are never named in Revelation 4-19, where futurists place the tribulation. Revelation 20:7-9 names Gog and Magog only after the thousand years. The details also differ. In Ezekiel, Gog comes from the north with named nations. In Revelation, the nations come from the four corners of the earth. In Ezekiel, the dead are buried over seven months (39:12). In Revelation, fire comes down and consumes them (20:9). So John uses Ezekiel's name as a type, just as he uses Jezebel (2:20), Sodom and Egypt (11:8) and Babylon (14:8). Ezekiel's event is past. Revelation's is a new event.
examples: Ezekiel 39:12: seven months to bury Gog's dead.
Revelation 20:9: fire comes from heaven and devours the attackers.
Revelation 20:8: 'the four corners of the earth', not only the far north.
questions.other: Some amillennialists hold that Revelation 19:17-21, 20:7-10 and Ezekiel 38-39 all describe the same final battle at Christ's return. They note that Revelation 19:17-18 quotes Ezekiel 39:17-20. Some premillennialists see Ezekiel 38-39 fulfilled before or at the start of the millennium, and Revelation 20 as a separate later revolt.

questions.q: Do 'the latter years' and 'the last days' in Ezekiel 38:8, 16 mean the end of the world?
questions.short: Not necessarily. The Hebrew phrase means 'in the days to come'. Scripture uses it for events in Israel's history, such as the time of the judges and the exile.
questions.answer: The Hebrew phrase acharit ha-yamim literally means 'the after part of the days'. On this reading, it simply means 'in the future', since Hebrew had no single word for that idea. Moses warned that evil would come on Israel 'in the latter days' (Deuteronomy 31:29). Judges 2:20 shows Israel breaking the covenant soon after Joshua's death. Jeremiah said Judah would understand God's judgment 'in the latter days' (Jeremiah 30:24). He promised to restore Moab and Elam 'in the latter days' (48:47; 49:39). Modern versions often translate these 'in days to come'. Jacob also used the phrase for the future of his sons' tribes (Genesis 49:1). Nothing in the phrase itself requires thousands of years.
examples: Genesis 49:1: Jacob tells what will befall his sons 'in the last days'.
Jeremiah 48:47 and 49:39: Moab and Elam restored 'in the latter days'. Many versions translate 'in days to come'.
Numbers 24:14: Balaam's oracle 'in the latter days', often linked to David's victories over Moab.
questions.other: Futurists agree the phrase can mean 'the future'. But they say that in many prophetic texts it points to the messianic age or the end (Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5; Daniel 10:14). In Ezekiel 38 it follows the promise of the Spirit and national restoration (Ezekiel 36-37). New Testament writers say the 'last days' began with Christ (Hebrews 1:2; Acts 2:17).

questions.q: Doesn't Ezekiel 38:8 require Israel to be regathered from many nations, which only happened after 1948?
questions.short: On this reading, no. Israel had already been scattered among many nations by Ezekiel's time. God promised to gather them after seventy years, and he did.
questions.answer: Futurists teach that Israel was scattered among the nations only after AD 70. So they place the regathering in modern times. The fulfilled reading answers from Ezekiel and Jeremiah. Ezekiel, writing in exile, says God scattered Israel among the nations (Ezekiel 12:15; 6:8-9). The northern tribes had been deported by Assyria in 722 BC. Judah went to Babylon and Egypt. Jeremiah promised that God would gather his people 'from all the nations' (Jeremiah 29:14). He gave the time: after seventy years in Babylon (29:10). Ezra and Nehemiah record that return, beginning in 538 BC. Ezekiel 37 promises a united people in the land. Ezekiel 38 then pictures them living securely in unwalled villages (38:11), as in the Persian period before Nehemiah rebuilt the walls.
examples: Ezekiel 12:15: 'I scatter them among the nations.'
Jews lived across the Persian Empire. Esther 3:8 speaks of 'a certain people scattered abroad' in all provinces.
Ezekiel 38:11: 'unwalled villages... without walls, bars or gates.' Jerusalem's walls were rebuilt in 445 BC (Nehemiah 6:15).
questions.other: Futurists reply that the return from Babylon was small and from few lands. They see Ezekiel 38:8, 12 and Isaiah 11:11 ('the second time') as requiring a worldwide return. They hold this began in the 19th and 20th centuries. They also say Israel has not yet 'dwelt securely', so the battle is still future.

questions.q: Why does Ezekiel describe horses, swords, bows and wooden weapons if the battle is in our future?
questions.short: On this reading, because the battle is ancient. Attempts to fit wooden weapons into modern warfare become strained.
questions.answer: Ezekiel describes horsemen (38:4, 15), shields, swords, bows, arrows, war clubs and spears (39:9). The weapons are burned as firewood for seven years (39:9-10). These point to a war in a pre-industrial age. Futurists who read the text literally must explain this. Some say armies will return to old weapons. One writer claimed the Russians had made a wooden rifle of compressed wood, harder than steel and lighter. No source was given. Compressed wood is heavy, and modern light weapons use plastics and composites. In 1940 Harry Rimmer guessed that new rays would make metal weapons useless. The fulfilled reading sees these as signs of a forced literalism. The plain reading is that Ezekiel described a battle with weapons of his own era.
examples: Ezekiel 39:9-10: weapons used as fuel for seven years.
Harry Rimmer, 'The Coming War and the Rise of Russia' (1940), proposed wooden weapons for a future war.
Some writers read Ezekiel's 'horses' as engine 'horsepower'.
questions.other: Some futurists say God may use ancient language for modern arms, or that wooden weapons will be literal after a global collapse. Others see the battle as apocalyptic and symbolic. Its weapons and seven years show total victory, and no literal timing is meant. Many amillennialists take this symbolic view.

questions.q: If Ezekiel 38-39 is not a future war, when was it fulfilled?
questions.short: One proposal places it in the days of Esther. Haman plotted to destroy and plunder the Jews across the Persian Empire. The plot backfired, and the Jews defeated their enemies.
questions.answer: This reading follows the order of Ezekiel. Ezekiel 34-37 promises a shepherd, a new heart and a revived people in the land. That fits the first return under Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest (Ezra 3; Zechariah 3). Ezekiel 38-39 then describes enemies from all over the empire attacking a peaceful people. Ezekiel 40-48 describes a restored temple order in figurative terms. The writer James B. Jordan proposed that Gog's attack matches Haman's plot (Esther 3:8-15). Haman's decree let enemies attack the Jews in all 127 provinces, from India to Cush (Esther 8:9). Instead the Jews struck their enemies (9:5). God turned the plot back on its maker. The feast of Purim marks this victory (9:20-28).
examples: Esther 9:16: 75,000 enemies killed in the provinces.
Esther's events fall in the reign of Xerxes (Ahasuerus), about 483-473 BC. This was after the temple was rebuilt in 516 BC and before Nehemiah's walls in 445 BC.
Ezekiel 38:5 names Persia and Cush. Esther 1:1 describes an empire 'from India to Cush'.
questions.other: Other fulfilled or historical readers point to the Maccabean wars against Antiochus IV (167-164 BC). Some amillennialists see Gog as a symbol of the final world revolt at Christ's return. Futurists hold the battle is still ahead.
