Critics of the Esther view note that Esther never mentions Gog, and Esther 8:9 actually dates to Xerxes, not Darius.

questions.q: What parallels link Esther and Ezekiel 38-39, and where do they differ?
questions.short: Both describe enemies from across the Persian world planning to destroy and plunder a defenceless people, and God turning the attack back. Some details, such as plunder, differ.
questions.answer: On this reading, the parallels are strong. In both, the enemy plans to seize spoil (Ezekiel 38:12; Esther 3:13). In both, the attackers come from all over the empire, including Persia and Cush (Ezekiel 38:5; Esther 8:9). In both, God's people seem defenceless but win a complete reversal. In both, the nations then see God's hand. Ezekiel says the house of Israel will know the LORD from that day on (39:22). Esther says many from the peoples became Jews, because fear of the Jews had fallen on them (8:17). In both, the victory is remembered: by a valley named for Gog's army (Ezekiel 39:11) and by the feast of Purim (Esther 9:28). An honest note: Ezekiel says Israel will plunder its enemies (39:10). Esther stresses three times that the Jews did not take plunder (9:10, 15, 16).
examples: Esther 8:17: many of the people of the land declared themselves Jews.
Esther 9:10, 15, 16: 'on the plunder they did not lay their hand.'
Ezekiel 39:11: the Valley of Hamon-gog (the multitude of Gog).
questions.other: Critics of the view say the differences are too great. Esther has no birds feasting on the dead, no seven months of burial and no fire from heaven (Ezekiel 38:22). Ezekiel's language is cosmic: mountains overturned and the earth shaking. Futurists and many amillennialists say this points beyond any Persian-era event.

questions.q: Why do prophecy teachers keep revising their books and their lists of end-time nations?
questions.short: Because their identifications follow the news, not the text. When the Soviet Union fell, 'the nations of the north' moved to Muslim republics, and earlier books were quietly updated.
questions.answer: On this reading, frequent revision is a warning sign. When the Soviet Union broke up in 1991, Pat Robertson said he now thought the northern nations might be the Muslim republics, such as Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Azerbaijan. That was a major change. It came from new headlines, not new study of Ezekiel. Many books have had new editions with new villains. John Walvoord's Armageddon, Oil and the Middle East Crisis (1974) was revised in 1990. Billy Graham's Approaching Hoofbeats (1983) became Storm Warning (1992). Few editions admit that the earlier version was wrong. God's word does not change with the news (Isaiah 40:8). If a prophecy reading must be rewritten every decade, the method may be faulty.
examples: Walvoord's 'Armageddon, Oil and the Middle East Crisis' sold over a million copies in its 1990 revision during the Gulf crisis.
Thomas McCall and Zola Levitt, 'The Coming Russian Invasion of Israel' (1974), revised 1987 and 1992.
Isaiah 40:8: the word of our God stands forever.
questions.other: Futurist authors reply that updates are honest attempts to watch events, not changes to Scripture. They say the core picture stays the same: a northern coalition, a revived Rome and a future Antichrist. Only the guesses about who fills each role change. Many also warn against sensational date-setting.

questions.q: Is the European Union the revived Roman Empire with ten kings foretold in Daniel and Revelation?
questions.short: On this reading, no. The 'ten kings' were fulfilled in the first century. The EU passed ten members long ago and does not match Rome's borders.
questions.answer: Many futurists teach that a ten-nation European union will become a revived Roman Empire ruled by Antichrist. They cite the ten toes (Daniel 2:41-42), the ten horns (Daniel 7:7, 24) and the ten kings (Revelation 17:12). The fulfilled reading answers in three ways. First, the theory needs a gap of two thousand years between Daniel's sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks, which Daniel does not mention. Second, Daniel never calls the toes kings. Third, the numbers have not fit. The European Community reached ten members in 1981 and twelve in 1986. The EU later grew to 28 and is now 27, after the UK left in 2020. Its borders still leave out much of the old empire: Syria, Egypt, North Africa and Judea.
examples: Hal Lindsey (1970) taught that ten nations would come 'out of' Rome. The European Community had ten members in 1981.
Jacques Delors spoke in 1992 of a possible future EU of 35 members.
Earlier candidates for 'revived Rome' included Mussolini's empire, the League of Nations, the UN and NATO.
questions.other: Futurists reply that the ten kings may be ten regions or leaders, not ten member states. They say the final empire need not match Rome's exact borders. Some note that the Western European Union had ten full members from 1995 to 2011. Amillennialists and historicists see the ten horns as the many kingdoms that followed Rome's fall.

questions.q: Who were the 'ten kings' of Revelation 17:12 in the first century?
questions.short: On this reading, the rulers of Rome's provinces and client kingdoms. They held power under the emperor and joined Rome's war against Jerusalem and the church.
questions.answer: Revelation 17:12 says the ten horns are ten kings who receive authority 'for one hour' with the beast. Their power is short and borrowed. On the fulfilled reading, these are the provincial rulers and client kings of Nero's day. Dean F. W. Farrar listed ten main imperial provinces: Italy, Achaia, Asia, Syria, Egypt, Africa, Spain, Gaul, Britain and Germany. Under Rome, local rulers were also called kings. Pilate and the crowd called Caesar 'king' (John 19:15). Herod Agrippa II was also 'King Agrippa' (Acts 25:13; 26:2). The commentator David S. Clark saw the ten horns as the kingdoms Rome had conquered. Some writers say there were never ten kings in the Roman Empire. History shows there were many local kings under Rome.
examples: Acts 25:13: King Agrippa and Bernice came to greet Festus.
Client kings who sent troops to Titus in AD 70 included Agrippa II, Antiochus IV of Commagene, Sohaemus of Emesa and Malchus II of Nabataea (Tacitus, Histories 5.1; Josephus, Jewish War 3.4.2).
Revelation 17:12: they rule 'one hour' with the beast.
questions.other: Futurists say these ten kings have 'not yet received a kingdom' (17:12) and fight the Lamb at his return (17:14). So they must be future. Historicists list ten barbarian kingdoms that rose from Rome's fall, such as the Franks and Vandals. Idealists see ten as a symbol of the full power of world rulers.

questions.q: If the prophecies about Babylon, Rome and the ten kings are fulfilled, do they still speak to modern nations?
questions.short: Yes. Fulfilled prophecy shows how God judges proud empires. Any nation that copies Babylon or Rome can expect the same kind of judgment.
questions.answer: The fourth key is to separate fulfilment from application. A prophecy may be fulfilled once, but the principle within it applies in every age. On this reading, the fall of Babylon and Rome gives a fixed point for judging current events. Political unions can be good or evil. Under Napoleon and Hitler, a united Europe was clearly evil, and both rulers fell. Later tyrants who acted like a Caesar or a Nebuchadnezzar met their own ruin. Psalm 2 warns kings to serve the LORD with fear and to honour the Son. Daniel says God's kingdom will crush rival kingdoms and stand forever (Daniel 2:44). Paul says Christ must reign until all enemies are under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25). So Christians watch the news with hope, not panic.
examples: Napoleon's empire fell in 1814-1815. Hitler's Reich, which promised a thousand years, lasted twelve (1933-1945).
Daniel 4:34-37: Nebuchadnezzar learned that the Most High rules the kingdoms of men.
Psalm 2:10-12: 'Be wise, O kings... kiss the Son.'
questions.other: Christians of every view accept this principle of application. Futurists add that Revelation's Babylon and beast are also still future, so the warnings are both principle and prediction. Idealists say application is the main point, since the beast and Babylon appear in every age. Historicists see a continuing fulfilment through church history.

questions.q: If these prophecies are past, what future hope do Christians still have?
questions.short: A great hope. Christ reigns now and will put every enemy under his feet. His kingdom grows until the last enemy, death, is destroyed at his final coming.
questions.answer: On this reading, past fulfilment does not empty the future. It shows that God keeps his word on time. Christ is now seated at God's right hand (Acts 2:33-36). He received the kingdom promised in Daniel 7:13-14. That kingdom is like a stone that becomes a great mountain and fills the earth (Daniel 2:35). Rival kingdoms rise and fall, but his endures. Paul says Christ must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Corinthians 15:25-26). That will happen at the resurrection, when Christ appears (1 Corinthians 15:23, 52). The nations will finally worship him (Psalms 22:27; Philippians 2:10-11). So the believer works and prays with confidence, not fear.
examples: Daniel 2:35: the stone became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.
Psalms 110:1, the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New Testament, promises enemies made a footstool.
Philippians 2:10-11: every knee will bow.
questions.other: Futurists share this hope but place much of it after a future tribulation and a literal millennial reign from Jerusalem. Amillennialists see Christ reigning now with no great golden age before the end. Postmillennialists expect widespread gospel success first. Full preterists, unlike this partial view, place the resurrection in the past as well.

questions.q: Does the time element play only a small part in Bible prophecy?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, no. Time words are part of the message itself. A warning without a real time frame would lose its force.
questions.answer: One futurist textbook said the time element holds only a small place in prophecy. The fulfilled reading answers that timing is often the whole point. Jonah told Nineveh that the city would fall in forty days (Jonah 3:4). The people repented because the judgment was close. If they could have stretched forty days into four hundred years, the warning would have meant nothing. In the same way, Jesus told the crowds that the blood of the prophets would fall "upon this generation" (Matthew 23:36). The disciples asked "when" (Matthew 24:3), and Jesus gave a time frame (Matthew 24:34). Read this way, a prophecy's time words are as binding as its other words. If we ignore them, we change the prophecy.
examples: Jonah 3:4-10: a forty-day warning moved a whole city to repent, and God held back the judgment.
Matthew 24:3 and 24:34: the disciples ask "when", and Jesus answers with "this generation".
questions.other: Futurists reply that God's prophetic timetable can include long gaps the prophets did not see, as with Isaiah 61:1-2, where Jesus stopped reading mid-verse (Luke 4:19). They say the time words show certainty and urgency, not a date limit. Idealists say the words show that every age lives near the end.

questions.q: Does any New Testament verse say Jesus could return "at any moment"?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says no verse uses that idea. The texts say the coming was "near" and "at hand" for the first readers, which is stronger than "could happen".
questions.answer: Dispensational writers define "imminency" as an event that could happen at any time, but may not happen soon. They list texts such as Philippians 4:5, Titus 2:13, James 5:7-9 and Revelation 22:20. On the fulfilled reading, none of these texts uses the language of mere possibility. Paul says "the Lord is at hand" (Philippians 4:5). James says the coming "is at hand" and the Judge "stands at the door" (James 5:8-9). Revelation says "the time is near" (Revelation 1:3). These are statements of nearness, not of an open date. Read this way, the any-moment doctrine weakens the texts. It turns "near" into "possible but perhaps far". The fulfilled reading keeps the plain sense: the event was close for those readers.
examples: Philippians 4:5 says "The Lord is at hand" with no "perhaps" or "if".
Compare a weather forecast. "Rain is near" and "rain could come any day this century" are not the same claim.
questions.other: Pretribulational writers answer that "near" describes the next event on God's calendar. Nothing must happen first, so it is always near in that sense. Historic premillennialists and amillennialists agree the church should always be ready. But they say real signs, such as the man of lawlessness, come first (2 Thessalonians 2:3).

questions.q: What did James mean when he said "the Judge stands at the door"?
questions.short: Read plainly, James told his first readers that the Lord's coming was close for them. "At the door" is the same picture Jesus used for an event within that generation.
questions.answer: James urged patient believers to wait like a farmer waiting for the early and late rains (James 5:7). He then said the Lord's coming "is at hand" and that the Judge "stands at the door" (James 5:8-9). On the fulfilled reading, the picture is of someone already on the step, about to enter. Jesus used the same image: when you see these things, know that it is "near, at the doors" (Matthew 24:33). He then said this generation would not pass until all these things happened (Matthew 24:34). James wrote to Jewish believers who were suffering under rich oppressors (James 5:1-6). Their relief came with the judgment on Judea in AD 66-70. Read this way, the farmer picture fits: one season, not twenty centuries.
examples: A farmer waits for the rains of one season, not of a thousand years (James 5:7).
Matthew 24:33-34 joins "at the doors" with "this generation".
questions.other: Many futurists and amillennialists hold that James spoke of the final return. They say the church in every age lives with the Judge "at the door", because the end could come without warning. Some critical scholars say James simply expected the end soon and was mistaken. Most evangelical futurists reject that answer.

questions.q: If the apostles were unsure about timing, how would they have said so?
questions.short: They would have used words of condition, such as "if the Lord wills". The fulfilled reading notes that they used such words for travel plans, but not for the coming of the Lord.
questions.answer: The New Testament writers knew how to speak with caution. Paul wrote, "I will come to you shortly, if the Lord wills" (1 Corinthians 4:19). At Ephesus he said he would return "if God wills" (Acts 18:21). James taught believers to say "if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that" (James 4:15). Yet when these same writers speak of the Lord's coming, they drop the conditions. They say it is "near", "at hand" and coming "quickly". On the fulfilled reading, this contrast matters. Writers who could easily say "perhaps" chose plain words of nearness. If they had meant "any time in the next two thousand years", they had words to say that. They did not use them.
examples: 1 Corinthians 4:19: "shortly, if the Lord wills" (a condition).
Revelation 22:20: "I come quickly" (no condition).
questions.other: Futurists reply that the authors did not need conditions because the return is certain. The uncertainty is only about the date, which Jesus said no one knows (Matthew 24:36). Amillennialists add that "near" can speak of the last days as one era. That era began at the cross and runs to the end.

questions.q: Does "shortly" (en tachei) describe how fast events happen, not when they begin?
questions.short: Some futurists say it means "suddenly when it comes". The fulfilled reading answers that this cannot work for "near" or "at hand", which plainly describe time.
questions.answer: Some futurist commentators read "things which must shortly come to pass" (Revelation 1:1) as "things that will happen rapidly once they start". On the fulfilled reading, this changes a word of time into a word of manner. It might fit "quickly" on its own. But Revelation 1:3 adds "the time is near", and no one can come "near" in a sudden manner. Also, the same phrase en tachei is used for real soon events. Festus said he would go to Caesarea shortly (Acts 25:4). An angel told Peter to get up quickly (Acts 12:7). God would crush Satan under the Romans' feet shortly (Romans 16:20). One futurist writer even admits that in the Bible such actions all came about soon after the word was given. The fulfilled reading agrees with that admission.
examples: Acts 25:4: Festus would leave "shortly", within days.
A parent says, "Clean your room quickly. I will be back soon." A child who waits a week, then cleans fast, has not obeyed.
questions.other: Futurists answer that tachos can mean speed of action, and that Revelation 1:1 echoes Daniel 2:28-29 ("what shall be in the latter days"). They read it as "things that must happen" with sudden swiftness. Some amillennialists say the events began soon, at the cross and in John's day, but run to the end.

questions.q: Do literal interpreters apply their own rule to the time words?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says they do not. Charles Ryrie defined literal reading as giving each word its normal meaning. But the normal meaning of "near" and "soon" is set aside in prophecy.
questions.answer: Charles Ryrie, a leading dispensational scholar, said his system gives every word the same meaning it has in normal use. He called this consistent literal reading the strength of dispensationalism. On the fulfilled reading, the time texts are a test of that rule. In normal speech, "near" means close, "soon" means not long, and "this generation" means people now living. Yet many futurist writers say these words carry a special sense in prophecy. Read this way, that is not a literal method at all. It holds the beasts and numbers of Revelation literally but treats the time words as flexible. The fulfilled reading claims to be more literal here. It takes the time words plainly and lets the symbols be symbols, as Revelation itself does (Revelation 1:20).
examples: Revelation 1:20 explains that stars are angels and lampstands are churches. The book itself marks its symbols.
Matthew 26:18: "My time is at hand". Jesus was crucified within a day.
questions.other: Dispensationalists reply that literal reading includes figures of speech and the author's viewpoint. They say "near" in prophecy is near from God's side of history, which is still a normal use of language. Amillennialists and postmillennialists agree that symbols matter, but often read both the time words and the visions less tightly than either side.

questions.q: Does Luke 18:7-8 prove that "speedily" can mean a long delay?
questions.short: No, says the fulfilled reading. In the parable the widow gets justice in her own lifetime. Jesus' point is that God will act faster than the unjust judge, not slower.
questions.answer: One futurist commentator argued that "speedily" (en tachei) in Luke 18:8 involves a long delay. So he said "shortly" in Revelation 1:1 can also cover centuries. On the fulfilled reading, the parable teaches the opposite. A widow keeps asking an unjust judge for justice. He gives in so she will stop troubling him (Luke 18:5). Jesus then argues from the lesser to the greater. If a bad judge acts, God will surely act for his chosen ones, and act "speedily" (Luke 18:7-8). The widow received her justice while she was alive. Read this way, the parable promises prompt vindication. It does not teach a delay of two thousand years. It fits the martyrs' cry "how long?" being answered within "a little while" (Revelation 6:10-11).
examples: Luke 18:5: the judge acts because she keeps coming, and she is still alive to receive justice.
Revelation 6:10-11: martyrs cry "how long?" and are told to rest "a little while".
questions.other: Futurists note that Luke 18:8 ends with "when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?" They say this points to a long wait that tests faith. Amillennialists read "speedily" as "suddenly and surely", and say God's justice can seem slow to people even when it is on time.

questions.q: How does the New Testament use "near" and "at hand" elsewhere?
questions.short: Every other use means close in time or place. The fulfilled reading uses this pattern to say the same word in prophecy should mean the same thing.
questions.answer: The Greek word engus ("near") and its verb are common in the Gospels. Jesus says summer is near when leaves appear (Matthew 24:32). He says, "My time is at hand" on the eve of the cross (Matthew 26:18). In the garden he says "the hour is at hand", and Judas arrives while he is still speaking (Matthew 26:45-47). John writes that the Passover was near, so Jesus went up to Jerusalem (John 2:13). The Feast of Tabernacles was near (John 7:2). Early in his ministry Jesus said his time was not yet near (John 7:6). On the fulfilled reading, none of these allows a long gap. So when the same words describe the end of the age, they should keep their meaning.
examples: Matthew 26:46-47: "the betrayer is at hand", and Judas comes that same moment.
John 7:6 versus Matthew 26:18: "not yet near" early on, "at hand" one day before the cross.
questions.other: Futurists agree on the normal meaning but argue that prophetic "near" can mean next in order, with no event standing between. Some amillennialists say the kingdom drew near in Christ's first coming. So the whole last era is "near", including the final return.

questions.q: Why are "a short time" and "a little while" read literally, but "quickly" is not?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading sees a double standard. Futurists keep Revelation 6:11 and 12:12 short to fit their seven-year scheme, but stretch the time words about Christ's coming.
questions.answer: John Walvoord read the devil's "short time" (Revelation 12:12) as no more than three and a half years. He read "the third woe comes quickly" (Revelation 11:14) as events moving fast. Robert Thomas argued that the martyrs' "little while" (Revelation 6:11) must be short. He noted that Jesus used the same phrase for a year or for days (John 7:33; John 12:35). He even said an open-ended delay would be unkind to the martyrs. On the fulfilled reading, this is exactly right, and it should be applied everywhere. If "a little while" means a short time in Revelation 6, then "shortly" in Revelation 1:1 and "quickly" in 22:12 should also mean a short time. Read this way, choosing which time words to take plainly is driven by the system, not by the text.
examples: Revelation 6:11 and John 12:35 use the same phrase "a little while", and the second meant only days.
Revelation 11:14 "quickly" and Revelation 22:12 "quickly" are the same Greek word, tachu.
questions.other: Futurists answer that once the seven-year tribulation begins, its events happen in quick order. So "short time" inside that period is literal. They say the opening and closing time words of Revelation look at the whole program from God's viewpoint. Idealists read all these phrases as describing the church age as a whole.

questions.q: Is time in Revelation measured "from God's point of view"?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says nothing in Revelation tells readers to switch to a divine clock. The book was written for servants who needed to understand it (Revelation 1:1).
questions.answer: Some commentators say "the time is near" is seen from God's side, where a thousand years are like a day. They point to 1 John 2:18, "it is the last hour". On the fulfilled reading, that verse proves the opposite. John told his readers it was the last hour because many antichrists had already appeared. That is a sign they could see in their own day. Revelation was given "to show his servants" what must soon happen (Revelation 1:1). It was sent to seven real churches (Revelation 1:4, 11). It promised a blessing to those who read and keep it, "for the time is near" (Revelation 1:3). Read this way, the time words were meant for the human readers. A divine clock that humans cannot read would defeat the purpose of the book.
examples: 1 John 2:18: John points to visible antichrists as proof it was the last hour.
Revelation 1:4, 11: seven named cities in Asia Minor were the first readers.
questions.other: Futurists answer that God speaks in human words but from his eternal view, so "near" is still true even after centuries. Amillennialists say "last hour" and "last days" name the whole age between Christ's two comings. On that view the church has lived in the last hour ever since Pentecost.

questions.q: Does the temple in Revelation 11 show that the book was written before AD 70?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says yes. John measures a standing temple and calls Jerusalem "the holy city", with no hint that it had already been destroyed.
questions.answer: In Revelation 11:1-2 John measures the temple and its worshippers. The outer court is given to the nations, who will trample the holy city for 42 months. Some futurists say this must be a third temple to be built in the future. The fulfilled reading asks where the New Testament ever promises a rebuilt temple. It finds none. One dispensational scholar dated Matthew before AD 70 because it calls Jerusalem "the holy city" and never mentions its fall. The same reasoning fits Revelation (Revelation 11:2). The premillennial scholar J. Barton Payne also judged that the standing temple and the six kings of Revelation 17:10 suit the reign of Nero (AD 54-68). Read this way, "shortly" makes sense. The Jewish War lasted about three and a half years, from AD 66 to 70.
examples: Matthew 4:5 and 27:53 call Jerusalem "the holy city" before its fall. Revelation 11:2 does the same.
Revelation 17:10: "five have fallen, one is". Counting from Julius Caesar or Augustus, many place the sixth king as Nero.
questions.other: Most scholars date Revelation to about AD 95, under Domitian. They follow Irenaeus, who said John saw the vision near the end of Domitian's reign (Against Heresies 5.30.3). They read the temple in Revelation 11 as a symbol of God's people. Futurists see a future rebuilt temple. Idealists see the church protected while it suffers.

questions.q: If "soon" means soon, was John simply wrong?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says there are only two honest options: John was mistaken, or the events came soon. It holds that the events came soon, in the judgment of AD 70.
questions.answer: Some evangelical scholars admit the problem. One wrote that the things which must shortly happen have taken longer than John expected. Another said the simple meaning of the time words cannot be avoided, and that the prophets always saw the future as near. On the fulfilled reading, these admissions are honest but lead to a hard place. They make the Bible's own time words false. The fulfilled reading offers another option. It argues that Revelation was written before AD 70 and that much of it describes the Jewish War, the fall of Jerusalem and the persecution under Nero. Read this way, John was not mistaken at all. The events came within the lifetime of the first readers, just as promised (Revelation 22:6).
examples: Revelation 22:6: "These words are faithful and true ... things which must shortly be done" (KJV).
Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-7: the temple burned in August, AD 70.
questions.other: Futurists reply that John was not mistaken because God's timescale differs from ours, and the fulfillment is still certain. Critical scholars say the early church did expect a quick end and adjusted later. Amillennialists say the events began soon, at the cross and in Roman persecution, and run to the end.

questions.q: Does 2 Peter 3:8 ("one day is as a thousand years") let us stretch "soon"?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says no. Peter compares, he does not convert. The verse never tells readers to filter other time words through it.
questions.answer: Peter writes that with the Lord one day is "as" a thousand years, and a thousand years "as" one day (2 Peter 3:8). He is answering scoffers who said nothing ever changes (2 Peter 3:4). On the fulfilled reading, three points matter. First, Peter says "as", not "is". He describes God's patience, not a formula. Second, no text says to apply this verse to other time words. If it did, any number could be stretched or shrunk. Three days in the tomb could become three thousand years (Matthew 27:63). The thousand years of Revelation 20 could become a day. Third, Peter's own point is that God is not slow in keeping his promise (2 Peter 3:9). Read this way, the verse shows God's faithfulness, not delay.
examples: John 2:19: "in three days I will raise it up". No one stretches this to three thousand years.
Psalms 90:4 uses a similar comparison to show human frailty, not to change prophetic dates.
questions.other: Futurists and amillennialists both use 2 Peter 3:8 to explain a long delay. They say Peter was answering people who already felt the wait was long. They see God's patience as the reason for the delay (2 Peter 3:9, 15). Most do not say "soon" means "late", only that God's timing differs from human hopes.

questions.q: Why was Daniel told to seal his book, but John told not to seal his?
questions.short: Daniel's vision was far off, so it was sealed. John's was near, so it stayed open. The fulfilled reading sees this contrast as God's own comment on timing.
questions.answer: Daniel was told to shut up the words and seal the book "until the time of the end" (Daniel 12:4). Daniel wrote in the sixth century BC, so the events lay centuries ahead. John received the opposite command. "Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near" (Revelation 22:10). On the fulfilled reading, the contrast is clear. Far events were sealed. Near events were left open. If we stretch John's "near" with 2 Peter 3:8, we turn the pattern upside down. Daniel's time would seem near and John's far. Read this way, the command not to seal tells the first readers to act on the book in their own day. It was a message for them, not a code for a distant age.
examples: Daniel 8:26: "seal up the vision, for it refers to many days from now" (paraphrase).
Revelation 22:10: "seal not ... for the time is at hand" (KJV).
questions.other: Futurists answer that Revelation is unsealed because the church age is the last era before the end. The book is now fully open to readers, even if fulfillment is future. Amillennialists say the time is near because Christ has already begun his reign. The book applies to every generation.

questions.q: What did God say through Ezekiel about people who said "the days are long"?
questions.short: God rejected that saying. He told them the vision was not for distant times and would be fulfilled in their days. The fulfilled reading sees a warning for those who stretch near prophecies.
questions.answer: Ezekiel announced that "the end" was coming on the land and that the day was near (Ezekiel 7:2-7). God would "shortly" pour out his anger (Ezekiel 7:8). Ezekiel even packed baggage and acted out exile in front of the people (Ezekiel 12:3-7). Yet the people had a proverb: "The days are prolonged, and every vision fails" (Ezekiel 12:22). Others said the vision was "for many days" and "times far off" (Ezekiel 12:27). God replied that the days were at hand and none of his words would be delayed any longer (Ezekiel 12:23, 28). Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, within a few years. On the fulfilled reading, this is a clear pattern. God's "near" meant near, and the warning ended in one generation, as in AD 70.
examples: Ezekiel 12:27-28: "none of my words will be delayed any longer" (paraphrase).
586 BC: Babylon burned the temple, within about six years of Ezekiel's warnings (from about 592 BC).
questions.other: All Christian views accept that Ezekiel's near judgment came in 586 BC. Futurists say this proves God keeps his word, and that the end-time prophecies will also be kept in their time. They do not see Ezekiel's timing as a rule for all later prophecy, since some prophecies, like Daniel's, were far off.

questions.q: How do other passages use "quickly" and "shortly"?
questions.short: Each use means a short time. The fulfilled reading points to Genesis 41:32 and many New Testament letters, where "shortly" always came true in the speaker's lifetime.
questions.answer: Joseph told Pharaoh that God would "shortly" bring the seven good years and seven lean years (Genesis 41:32). The good years began at once, while Joseph was still alive (Genesis 41:46-49). In the New Testament, Paul hoped to send Timothy "shortly" (Philippians 2:19). He hoped to come to Timothy "shortly" (1 Timothy 3:14). The writer of Hebrews hoped to visit "shortly" with Timothy (Hebrews 13:23). Peter knew he must "shortly" put off his body (2 Peter 1:14). Mary rose "quickly" to meet Jesus (John 11:29). Jesus told Judas, "What you do, do quickly" (John 13:27). On the fulfilled reading, the pattern holds across the Bible. So when Revelation says "I come quickly", the reader should expect the same sense.
examples: Genesis 41:32 and 41:47: "God will shortly bring it to pass", and the seven plentiful years began.
2 Peter 1:14: Peter's death came "shortly", in Nero's reign (by about AD 64-68).
questions.other: Futurists agree on these normal uses. But they say the coming of the Lord is a special case, because Jesus himself said no one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36). Amillennialists say the Lord's coming is the one event that is always "near" to faith, even when centuries pass.

questions.q: Does the fig tree in Matthew 24:32 point to Israel becoming a nation in 1948?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says no. Jesus gave a simple picture from nature: when leaves appear, summer is near. The text says nothing about a nation or a rebirth.
questions.answer: Many popular books read Matthew 24:32 as a coded sign. The fig tree is Israel, and its new leaves are the state founded on 14 May 1948. Hal Lindsey popularised this in 1970. On the fulfilled reading, the text does not say this. Jesus said, "learn the parable from the fig tree". When its branch is tender and puts out leaves, summer is near (Matthew 24:32). So when you see "all these things", know that it is near (Matthew 24:33). The things are the signs Jesus had just listed for his hearers: false messiahs, wars, persecution and armies around Jerusalem. Luke's version makes the point clear: "look at the fig tree, and all the trees" (Luke 21:29). Read this way, the tree is a seasonal clock, not a symbol of a nation.
examples: Luke 21:29: "the fig tree, and all the trees". All trees cannot all be Israel.
14 May 1948: the State of Israel declared its independence. Lindsey once linked a generation of about 40 years to this date.
questions.other: Many dispensationalists hold that the fig tree is Israel and that 1948 was the start of end-time events. Others, including many dispensational scholars, now treat the fig tree as a simple seasonal sign. They still see Israel's return as important from other texts, such as Ezekiel 36-37. Amillennialists read the fig tree as a lesson about watchfulness.

questions.q: When the Bible uses the fig tree for Israel, is it a sign of blessing or of judgment?
questions.short: In the Gospels it is almost always a sign of judgment. The fulfilled reading says that, if the fig tree is Israel, the image points to the fall of Jerusalem, not to a rebirth.
questions.answer: Lindsey wrote that the fig tree has been a historic symbol of Israel. The fulfilled reading asks how the Bible itself uses that symbol. In the prophets a fig tree can show blessing, as in "every man under his fig tree" (Micah 4:4). But when God judges Israel, he strikes its figs (Hosea 2:12; Joel 1:7; Jeremiah 8:13). Jeremiah saw good figs and bad figs (Jeremiah 24:1-10). In the Gospels, every fig tree tied to Israel is a picture of judgment. Jesus cursed a leafy tree with no fruit (Mark 11:12-14). He told a parable of a barren fig tree to be cut down (Luke 13:6-9). Read this way, a Jesus who used the fig tree for Israel was warning of judgment in that generation.
examples: Jeremiah 8:13: "no figs on the fig tree" is a picture of judgment.
Luke 13:7: "Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?" (paraphrase).
questions.other: Futurists answer that judgment and later restoration often go together in the prophets (Hosea 3:4-5; Romans 11:25-26). They say the fig tree's judgment does not cancel a future blessing for Israel. Many amillennialists and postmillennialists also expect a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ, without linking it to a state.

questions.q: Does the New Testament predict Israel's return to the land and a rebuilt temple?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading finds no such prediction. The New Testament speaks of Jerusalem's coming destruction, but not of a later national restoration or third temple.
questions.answer: The Old Testament clearly predicted a return from exile. Jeremiah said it would happen after seventy years for Babylon (Jeremiah 29:10, 14). Daniel read that promise (Daniel 9:2). The return came under Cyrus from 538 BC, and the temple was rebuilt by 515 BC (Ezra 6:15). Isaiah spoke of a "second time" God would gather his people (Isaiah 11:11). The first time was the exodus from Egypt (Isaiah 11:16). On the fulfilled reading, the second time was the return from Babylon and Assyria. No third gathering is named. The New Testament speaks often of the temple's fall (Matthew 24:2; Luke 21:20-24). But it never says, "after this a temple will be rebuilt". Read this way, a teaching this central would surely be stated plainly, if it were true.
examples: Ezra 1:1-3: Cyrus's decree in 538 BC fulfilled Jeremiah's seventy years.
John 2:20: the second temple, rebuilt and enlarged by Herod, had been "forty-six years" in building.
questions.other: Futurists answer that Luke 21:24 implies an end to Gentile control of Jerusalem. They read Romans 11:26 and Acts 1:6-7 as expecting a restored Israel. They hold that Ezekiel 36-37 and Isaiah 11:11-12 ("from the four corners of the earth") go beyond the return from Babylon, since that return was small and from the east.

questions.q: Was God's land promise to Israel already fulfilled?
questions.short: Joshua says it was: God gave all the land he swore, and not one good promise failed. The fulfilled reading therefore sees no unfinished land promise awaiting the end.
questions.answer: Joshua 21:43-45 says the LORD gave Israel all the land he had sworn to their fathers. They took it and lived in it. Not one of his good promises failed; all came to pass. Joshua repeats this before he dies (Joshua 23:14). Nehemiah praises God for keeping his word to Abraham (Nehemiah 9:8). Under Solomon, Israel's rule reached the river Euphrates (1 Kings 4:21). Some futurist scholars reply that the borders of Numbers 34 were not reached, citing Joshua 13:1-7. On the fulfilled reading, Joshua 13 and Judges 3 speak of land still to be possessed by each tribe. The gift was given; the people's obedience lagged. Read this way, God kept his land promise in full. Later the New Testament widens the inheritance to the whole world (Romans 4:13).
examples: 1 Kings 4:21: Solomon ruled "from the river to the land of the Philistines".
Romans 4:13: Abraham's heirs will inherit "the world", not only Canaan.
questions.other: Many futurist scholars say the land promise was eternal (Genesis 17:8) and only partly fulfilled. They point to later promises of return made after Joshua's day (Amos 9:14-15). They expect a final, permanent possession in the millennium. Covenant theologians agree the land was given, but see its fullness in the new creation.

questions.q: Why did Jesus curse the fig tree, and how is it linked to the temple?
questions.short: Mark places the curse around the temple scene. On the fulfilled reading, the leafy tree with no fruit pictures the temple system: impressive outside, but fruitless, and so under judgment.
questions.answer: Mark tells the story in three steps. Jesus enters the temple and looks around (Mark 11:11). The next morning he sees a fig tree in leaf, finds no fruit, and curses it (Mark 11:13-14). He then drives out the traders from the temple (Mark 11:15-17). The next day the disciples see the tree withered from the roots (Mark 11:20). On the fulfilled reading, the two stories explain each other. The temple had leaves: a grand building and busy worship. But it lacked the fruit of repentance that John the Baptist had demanded (Matthew 3:8-10). The leaders began seeking to destroy Jesus (Mark 11:18). Read this way, the curse was an acted prophecy. The temple would fall within a generation, as Jesus said soon after (Mark 13:2).
examples: Mark 11:13: "it was not the season for figs". The lesson is about outward show, not the tree.
Isaiah 5:1-7: God looked for good grapes in his vineyard and found wild ones, so he judged it.
questions.other: Most scholars of all views agree that the cursed fig tree is linked to the temple's judgment. Futurists accept this but say it pictures a judgment on that generation, not a final rejection of Israel. Many point to Romans 11:23-24, where branches cut off can be grafted in again.

questions.q: What does the parable of the barren fig tree (Luke 13:6-9) teach?
questions.short: A tree that bore nothing for three years was given one more season, then cut down if still fruitless. The fulfilled reading sees Jerusalem's final period of grace before AD 70.
questions.answer: A man came for three years looking for fruit on his fig tree and found none. He said, "Cut it down." The vinedresser asked for one more year to dig and feed it. If it still bore no fruit, it would be cut down (Luke 13:6-9). On the fulfilled reading, the parable fits Jesus' ministry to Israel. Just before this, Jesus warned, "unless you repent, you will all likewise perish" (Luke 13:3-5). Soon after, he wept over Jerusalem. He said enemies would surround it and leave not one stone on another, "because you did not know the time of your visitation" (Luke 19:41-44). Read this way, the tree pictures a nation given extra time, then judged when the time ran out.
examples: Luke 13:4-5: those killed by the tower of Siloam are a warning to repent.
Luke 19:43-44: siege banks, encirclement and ruin, fulfilled when Titus besieged Jerusalem in AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 5.12.2).
questions.other: Many interpreters of all schools agree that the parable warns Israel of coming judgment. Some reject linking the three years exactly to Jesus' ministry. Futurists add that the judgment of that generation does not end God's future plan for the Jewish people (Romans 11:1-2, 28-29).

questions.q: Does Matthew 24:32 say the fig tree bears fruit or blossoms again?
questions.short: No. Jesus speaks only of a tender branch and leaves. The fulfilled reading notes that leaves without fruit were exactly what Jesus cursed days earlier.
questions.answer: Some writers say Jesus called the cursed tree to mind and said, "watch it; when it blossoms again, all these things will happen". An older writer spoke of the tree putting out buds. On the fulfilled reading, the text says neither. Matthew 24:32 mentions only a tender branch and leaves. It says nothing of fruit, blossom or new life after death. And days before, Jesus had said to a fig tree, "Let no fruit grow on you ever again" (Matthew 21:19). Read this way, the futurist reading has Jesus contradict his own curse. The fulfilled reading sees no contradiction. The leaves of Matthew 24:32 are simply spring leaves, a sign that summer is near. The fruitless tree of Matthew 21 is a separate picture of judgment.
examples: Matthew 21:19: "Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever" (KJV).
Song of Songs 2:13: fig leaves and fruit as a sign of spring. Seasonal images are common in Scripture.
questions.other: Futurists who link the fig tree to Israel answer that the leaves picture national revival, not yet spiritual fruit. They say fruit comes later when Israel turns to the Messiah (Zechariah 12:10). Other futurists reject the Israel link entirely and read Matthew 24:32 as a simple seasonal lesson.

questions.q: Does "withered from the roots" (Mark 11:20) mean the roots stayed alive?
questions.short: No. The fulfilled reading says "from the roots" includes the roots. The tree died completely, unlike Nebuchadnezzar's tree, whose stump was kept alive on purpose.
questions.answer: Some prophecy writers argued that only the trunk, branches and leaves died, while the roots stayed alive for a later revival. On the fulfilled reading, the phrase means the opposite. A tree withers "from the roots" because the roots have died. In normal Greek and English, "from" includes the starting point. The generations "from Abraham to David" include Abraham (Matthew 1:17). Herod killed boys "from two years old and under" (Matthew 2:16). Compare Daniel 4. There God ordered a tree cut down but told them to leave "the stump of its roots in the earth" with a band of iron (Daniel 4:15). That tree was kept for a later restoration (Daniel 4:26). Read this way, Mark gives no such hint for the fig tree.
examples: Daniel 4:15, 26: the stump is left on purpose, and Nebuchadnezzar's kingdom is restored.
Job 18:16: "his roots shall be dried up beneath" (KJV). Withering roots mean full death.
questions.other: Most futurist scholars do not use the "living roots" argument. They ground a future for Israel in Romans 11 instead, where Paul speaks of a root and branches that can be grafted back (Romans 11:16-24). They read the fig tree curse as a judgment on that generation, not on the people forever.

questions.q: Does "no fruit from you ever again" really mean never, or only for an age?
questions.short: In Greek the phrase stacks negatives with "to the age". Standard grammars call this a strong, emphatic "never". The fulfilled reading says it was a final curse.
questions.answer: Some writers say the Greek word aion means an age. So, they argue, Jesus only cursed the tree for a period. On the fulfilled reading, this ignores the rest of the sentence. Matthew 21:19 joins the strong negative "ou me" with "no longer" and "to the age". Mark 11:14 has "no longer", "to the age" and "no one". Grammars describe this piling up of negatives as a very strong denial. The same phrase "eis ton aiona" with a negative appears when Jesus says the believer will "never" die (John 11:26) or thirst (John 4:14). Read this way, Jesus' words to the tree were a full curse. If the fig tree is Israel's temple order, that order would never bear fruit again.
examples: John 11:26: "shall never die" uses the same negative with "to the age".
John 10:28: the sheep "shall never perish". No one reads this as "only for a period".
questions.other: Futurists answer that the curse applies to the tree and the temple order of that day, not to the Jewish people's future. They point to Romans 11:11, "did they stumble so as to fall? By no means". Many covenant theologians agree that the curse was on the old temple system, not on Jewish people as such.

questions.q: If the fig tree is cursed, does that mean no Jewish person can bear fruit for God?
questions.short: No. The fulfilled reading applies the curse to the old covenant order and its leaders. Individual Jews, like Gentiles, can bear good fruit through faith in Christ.
questions.answer: The fig tree pictures the nation's leaders, temple and system in that generation. It does not say anything against Jewish people as persons. Jeremiah saw both good figs and bad figs among the exiles (Jeremiah 24:1-10). John the Baptist told the crowds that every tree, Jew or not, would be judged by its fruit (Matthew 3:7-10). Jesus praised Nathanael as "an Israelite in whom is no guile" (John 1:47). The first church was almost wholly Jewish, and it bore great fruit (Acts 2:41; Acts 21:20). Paul, a Jew, said God had not rejected his people (Romans 11:1). On the fulfilled reading, the curse ended a covenant order, not God's love for a people. Every person, of any nation, is welcomed by faith in Christ (Romans 10:12).
examples: Acts 21:20: "many thousands of Jews" believed in Jerusalem.
Romans 11:1: Paul calls himself an Israelite to prove God has not rejected his people.
questions.other: All Christian views agree on this point. Dispensationalists go further and say God has a distinct national future for Israel. Many covenant theologians expect a large future turning of Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11:25-26). Others read "all Israel" as the full number of Jewish and Gentile believers.

questions.q: Should a metaphor be the key sign for all end-time prophecy?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says no. A central doctrine should rest on plain statements, not on a picture whose meaning Jesus himself explained as seasonal timing.
questions.answer: Popular futurism has made Israel's rebirth the starting point of end-time events. Yet the New Testament never says plainly that Israel would become a state again. So the fig tree verse is asked to carry the weight. On the fulfilled reading, this is a weak base. Jesus explained his own picture. Leaves mean summer is near; "so also" these signs mean the end is near (Matthew 24:32-33). He then gave the time frame: "this generation" (Matthew 24:34). Read this way, using the image to point to 1948 adds a meaning the text does not give. It also produced failed dates. Some writers used 1948 plus a forty-year generation to set the end near 1988. When 1988 passed, the scheme had to be revised.
examples: 1988: Edgar Whisenant's booklet predicted the rapture that year, partly by counting a generation from 1948.
Matthew 24:33: "so likewise ye". Jesus himself states what the picture means.
questions.other: Many futurist scholars agree that the fig tree should not be used to set dates. They say Israel's return rests on Old Testament texts, such as Ezekiel 37 and Zechariah 12. Historic premillennialists and amillennialists also reject date setting, but differ on whether modern Israel has any prophetic meaning.

questions.q: Does the Bible predict a future "bloodbath" for Israel?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says the predicted great suffering of Jerusalem already happened in AD 66-70. Jesus warned that generation to flee, and there is no further holocaust to wait for.
questions.answer: In a 1976 book Charles Ryrie wrote of a coming time of Israel's greatest bloodbath. He saw the Bible as history written in advance. The fulfilled reading agrees that Jesus predicted terrible suffering for Jerusalem (Matthew 24:21; Luke 21:23-24). But it holds that this judgment has already happened. Jesus told the people of Judea to flee to the mountains when they saw the signs (Matthew 24:16). Many Christians did leave before the siege. Josephus records famine, civil war and great loss of life (Jewish War 5.12.3; 6.9.3). His total of 1,100,000 dead is probably too high, but the scale was vast. Read this way, the Bible does not foretell another slaughter of Jews. Placing that suffering in the future can make it seem fated, which is dangerous.
examples: Luke 21:20-21: "when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies ... flee".
Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3: Jerusalem's Christians moved to Pella before the war.
questions.other: Dispensationalists hold that Zechariah 12-14 and Daniel 12:1 describe a future time of trouble for Israel. They stress that it ends in rescue and national conversion (Zechariah 12:10; Romans 11:26). They do not welcome suffering; they see Christ coming to save Israel. Many amillennialists apply these texts to the church's trials.

questions.q: Is it antisemitic to deny that the Bible predicts a restored national Israel?
questions.short: No. The fulfilled reading says antisemitism is hostility or prejudice toward Jews as Jews. A disagreement about how to read prophecy is not hatred of any people.
questions.answer: Some writers have said that anyone who denies a future national restoration of Israel is antisemitic. The fulfilled reading answers that this confuses theology with prejudice. Antisemitism means hostility, hatred or discrimination against Jewish people because they are Jewish. A person can read Old Testament restoration texts as fulfilled and still love and defend Jewish neighbours. On this reading, the restoration promises were kept in two stages. First came the return from Babylon (Ezra 1:1-4). Then came the gathering of Israel's faithful remnant into the Messiah's people, starting with thousands of Jews at Pentecost (Acts 2:41; Acts 15:15-17). Gentiles were grafted into that Jewish root (Romans 11:17-18). Read this way, the church is not anti-Jewish. Its foundation stones are Jewish apostles (Ephesians 2:20).
examples: Acts 15:15-17: James applies the rebuilding of David's tent to Gentiles joining the Jewish church.
Romans 11:18: "you do not support the root, but the root supports you" (paraphrase).
questions.other: Many Christian Zionists say that "replacement" readings have fed contempt for Jews in church history, and that a future for national Israel guards against this. Many Jewish scholars also see "supersession" as harmful. Most covenant theologians reject the label "replacement" and say the church is Israel enlarged, not Israel replaced.

questions.q: Has dispensationalism itself changed on Israel and the church?
questions.short: Yes. Since the late 1980s, "progressive dispensationalism" has softened the sharp split between Israel and the church. The fulfilled reading sees this as evidence that the older system was weak.
questions.answer: Classic dispensationalism, spread by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) and Dallas Theological Seminary, taught two peoples of God with two programs. In the late 1980s and 1990s, scholars such as Craig Blaising, Darrell Bock and Robert Saucy developed "progressive dispensationalism". It sees more unity between Israel and the church. It accepts that Christ's Davidic reign has already begun in part (Acts 2:30-36). It is less focused on land and future dates. The fulfilled reading sees these changes as a move toward its own position. On this reading, the older system needed revision because its texts would not support the sharp divide. Peter, for example, says David's throne promise was fulfilled when Christ rose and sat at God's right hand (Acts 2:30-31).
examples: Acts 2:30-36: Peter links David's throne to Christ's resurrection and ascension.
1993: Blaising and Bock published "Progressive Dispensationalism", and Saucy published "The Case for Progressive Dispensationalism".
questions.other: Progressive dispensationalists say their changes refine the system, not abandon it. They still hold a future for national Israel in the land. Classic dispensationalists think the progressives gave up too much. Covenant theologians welcome the move toward unity but say it does not go far enough.

questions.q: Where are the Old Testament promises to restore Israel fulfilled, on this reading?
questions.short: In the return from exile, and then in Christ and the Jewish church he gathered. Gentile believers were later added into that same people.
questions.answer: The fulfilled reading sees two stages. First, God brought Judah back from Babylon as Jeremiah promised (Jeremiah 29:10). The temple and walls were rebuilt (Ezra 6:15; Nehemiah 6:15). Second, the deeper promises of a new heart and new covenant came true in Jesus (Jeremiah 31:31-34; Hebrews 8:8-13). The first church was almost all Jewish (Acts 2:5, 41). Gentiles were later grafted into this existing tree (Romans 11:17). The New Testament then calls all believers in Christ Abraham's seed (Galatians 3:7, 29), the true circumcision (Philippians 3:3), and members of "the commonwealth of Israel" (Ephesians 2:12, 19). Read this way, Israel was not discarded. Its faithful remnant became the core of a renewed Israel, open to all nations.
examples: Hebrews 8:8-13 quotes Jeremiah's new covenant and applies it to the church.
Acts 2:5-11: Jews "from every nation under heaven" were gathered at Pentecost.
questions.other: Dispensationalists say the new covenant was made "with the house of Israel" and still awaits a national fulfilment. The church shares only its spiritual blessings. Many covenant theologians agree with the fulfilled reading here but also expect a future mass conversion of Jewish people (Romans 11:25-26), as Charles Hodge and John Murray taught.

questions.q: Does Zechariah 13:8-9 predict that two-thirds of Jews in Israel will die in the future?
questions.short: Many futurists say yes. The fulfilled reading says the prophecy follows the striking of the Shepherd (13:7) and was fulfilled in the first century, so no future slaughter is foretold.
questions.answer: Zechariah 13:8-9 says two parts in the land will be cut off and die, and a third will be refined like silver. Some futurist writers apply this to a future tribulation. They have said two-thirds of the Jews in Israel will be killed. Israel has over seven million Jewish citizens today, so that would mean millions of deaths. On the fulfilled reading, the context places the text in the past. Zechariah 13:7 says "strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will scatter". Jesus applied this to his own arrest (Matthew 26:31). The refining that follows fits the generation after the cross, ending in AD 70. A refined remnant called on God's name and became his people (Zechariah 13:9; Romans 11:5). Read this way, no future holocaust is required by Scripture.
examples: Matthew 26:31: Jesus quotes Zechariah 13:7 on the night he was arrested.
Josephus, Jewish War 6.9.3: huge loss of life and 97,000 taken captive during the war.
questions.other: Dispensationalists hold that Zechariah 12-14 forms one future scene. In it the nations attack Jerusalem, Israel mourns for the pierced one (12:10), and Christ returns (14:4). They stress that the surviving third is saved, and that God, not believers, brings the trial. Some amillennialists read the two-thirds and one-third as a picture of judgment and remnant in every age.

questions.q: Does the "parenthesis" view mean God has no dealings with Israel today?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading argues that the classic view, by pausing God's program for Israel until the rapture, logically leaves present Israel without special prophetic status. Dispensationalists strongly reject that conclusion.
questions.answer: Classic dispensationalism teaches that God's prophetic clock stopped after 483 years of Daniel's seventy weeks (Daniel 9:24-27). The church age is a "parenthesis". The final seven years, "the time of Jacob's trouble" (Jeremiah 30:7), will begin after the rapture. One Scofield companion said God is not dealing with Israel as a nation during this age. The fulfilled reading draws out an implication. If Israel's promises are postponed, then Jewish people today stand before God like everyone else. Their hope is in Christ (Romans 10:12-13). Read this way, the fulfilled reading is not saying anything harsher than the parenthesis view. Both agree that salvation for Jew and Gentile is in Christ alone. The difference is about the future of a nation.
examples: Romans 10:12: "there is no difference between Jew and Greek".
Daniel 9:24-27: the seventy weeks, read with a gap by dispensationalists and without one by the fulfilled reading.
questions.other: Dispensationalists answer that Israel remains "beloved for the fathers' sake" and that God's gifts and calling cannot be revoked (Romans 11:28-29). They say the Abrahamic promise to bless those who bless Israel (Genesis 12:3) is still in force. They see the regathering of Jews to the land as God preparing for the coming week.

questions.q: Did end-times expectation make some Christians passive during the Nazi persecution of Jews?
questions.short: A historian from within premillennialism found that many premillennial writers in the 1930s saw the persecution as expected and said little against it. Others, from many traditions, did help Jews.
questions.answer: In 1977 Dwight Wilson, a lifelong premillennialist, studied American premillennial writing on Russia and Israel since 1917. He found that many premillennial writers saw European antisemitism in the 1930s as a forerunner of "Jacob's trouble". Some treated it as part of God's plan. Wilson judged that this led to a fatalistic "hands off" attitude, with little moral protest. Some writers even blamed Jews for their own suffering. Wilson also said premillennialists were, in theology, more pro-Jewish than any other Christian group. On the fulfilled reading, this history shows the danger of treating persecution as a fixed future event. Read this way, the Bible calls Christians to resist injustice, not to watch it (Proverbs 24:11-12). Fairness requires adding that wider society also failed refugees then.
examples: 1939: the ship St. Louis, carrying over 900 Jewish refugees, was turned away by Cuba, the United States and Canada.
Proverbs 24:11-12: "rescue those being led away to death" (paraphrase).
questions.other: Defenders note that apathy toward refugees was widespread among Christians and governments of every view. They point to premillennialists who aided Jews, and to the strong support for Israel among dispensationalists since 1948. Historians such as Timothy Weber and David Rausch differ on how much fundamentalists shared the antisemitism of their time.

questions.q: Did some prophecy teachers accept the forged "Protocols of the Elders of Zion"?
questions.short: Yes. Historians record that a few leading dispensational teachers in the 1920s-30s gave credit to the Protocols, a forgery exposed in 1921. Others in the same movement rejected it.
questions.answer: The Protocols claimed to reveal a Jewish plan for world control. In 1921 The Times of London showed that much of it was copied from an 1864 French satire about Napoleon III. Henry Ford spread it in his newspaper, the Dearborn Independent, in the early 1920s. In 1927 Ford publicly apologised. Historian Timothy Weber records that James M. Gray, president of Moody Bible Institute, defended parts of Ford's claims in 1927. He was criticised by Jewish groups and by Hebrew Christians. Arno C. Gaebelein, a Scofield Bible editor, treated the Protocols as genuine in his 1933 book. He also led a mission to Jews in New York. On the fulfilled reading, this shows how prophecy speculation can mix with prejudice. The Bible forbids false witness against any neighbour (Exodus 20:16).
examples: August 1921: The Times (London) exposed the Protocols as plagiarised from Maurice Joly's 1864 satire.
1927: Henry Ford issued a public apology and closed the series.
questions.other: Defenders of dispensationalism point out that the system's founders were strongly pro-Jewish, and many teachers condemned the Protocols. Historian David Rausch argued that most early fundamentalists were friends of the Jewish people. All Christian traditions today reject the Protocols, and all have their own history of antisemitism to repent of.

questions.q: Why could a teacher love Jewish evangelism yet repeat harmful ideas about Jews?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says the system expected both future Jewish suffering and future Jewish salvation, so both attitudes could live side by side. Historians also point to the wider prejudice of that era.
questions.answer: Some early twentieth-century teachers ran missions to Jewish people while repeating damaging claims about Jews in world events. Historians have asked why. One answer is that their prophecy system expected Jews to pass through a terrible tribulation before turning to Christ. This could make persecution seem both expected and part of God's plan. The fulfilled reading argues that this is a built-in risk of placing "Jacob's trouble" in the future. Read this way, a past fulfilment removes that risk. The great tribulation is over, so no modern suffering is "prophesied". Jews today should be treated like any neighbour: with love, honesty and respect (Romans 13:10). Paul's own longing for his people is the model (Romans 9:1-3; Romans 10:1).
examples: Romans 9:2-3: Paul's "great sorrow" for his Jewish kin.
Romans 10:1: "my heart's desire and prayer ... for Israel is that they might be saved" (KJV).
questions.other: Many historians say these men reflected the prejudices of their whole culture, not of one view of prophecy. Antisemitism also appeared among Christians of other eschatologies, and in liberal and secular circles. Dispensationalists today stress that God's love for Israel, not its suffering, is the heart of their view.

questions.q: If futurists expect great suffering in Israel, why do some encourage Jews to move there?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading asks this as a pointed question. It contrasts it with Jesus' warning to leave Jerusalem before its fall (Matthew 24:16).
questions.answer: Some Christian groups have helped Jews immigrate to Israel and have funded settlements. They believe the Bible foretells a regathering in the last days. Yet many of the same teachers expect that two-thirds of Jews in the land will die in a future tribulation (Zechariah 13:8). One commentator also read Zechariah 14:2 as a future defeat of Jerusalem by all nations. The fulfilled reading asks why Jews are not being warned to flee. Jesus told his hearers to flee Judea when the signs came (Matthew 24:16; Luke 21:21). On this reading, the New Testament never urges anyone to gather in Jerusalem for the end. It points to a new worship not tied to that city (John 4:21-24). Read this way, a future-focused system creates a painful tension.
examples: Luke 21:21: "let those in the city depart" (paraphrase).
John 4:21: "neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem" will you worship the Father.
questions.other: Christian Zionists answer that they help Jews because God promised to bless those who bless Abraham's seed (Genesis 12:3). They see the return as God's own act (Ezekiel 36:24). They believe the coming trial ends in the Messiah's rescue (Zechariah 14:3-4). They say they do not cause the tribulation and pray for Israel's peace (Psalms 122:6).

questions.q: Did the guilt of "all the righteous blood" (Matthew 23:35-36) rest on Jews of every age?
questions.short: No. Jesus limited it to "this generation". On the fulfilled reading that judgment fell in AD 70 and ended. No later Jew carries it.
questions.answer: Jesus told the leaders of his day that the blood of the righteous, from Abel to Zechariah, would come "upon this generation" (Matthew 23:35-36). The fulfilled reading stresses the limit. It was that generation, which rejected its visitation (Luke 19:44). The judgment fell in AD 66-70 and was complete. Sadly, church history shows Christians blaming Jews of later centuries as if the guilt never ended. The fulfilled reading says this is a misuse of Scripture. Ezekiel taught that a son does not bear his father's guilt (Ezekiel 18:20). Read this way, placing Jesus' judgment in its own generation actually protects Jewish people from a false charge. It leaves no room for treating Jews today as cursed.
examples: Ezekiel 18:20: "the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father" (KJV).
1965: the Catholic document Nostra Aetate stated that Christ's death cannot be charged against all Jews then living, or against Jews today.
questions.other: Most Christians of every view now agree that Jews of later ages carry no guilt for the crucifixion. Futurists also limit the judgment of Matthew 23 to that generation. But some apply the larger "times of the Gentiles" (Luke 21:24) to the long dispersion that followed, and expect a future end to it.

questions.q: How has "His blood be on us and on our children" (Matthew 27:25) been misused?
questions.short: It was used for centuries to call Jews "Christ-killers". On the fulfilled reading, the cry touched only that crowd and their children in AD 70, and Peter offered that same generation forgiveness.
questions.answer: In Matthew 27:25 a crowd in Jerusalem cried that Jesus' blood would be on them and their children. Through the centuries some Christians used this verse to blame all Jews for Jesus' death. This fed hatred and violence. The Passion play at Oberammergau, Germany, first performed in 1634, was criticised for this theme. It was revised in later decades. On the fulfilled reading, "our children" were the next generation, who lived through AD 70 (Luke 23:28). The words do not reach further. Even so, Peter told Jerusalem's people that the promise of forgiveness was "for you and your children" (Acts 2:38-39). Jesus prayed, "Father, forgive them" (Luke 23:34). Read this way, the gospel answers that cry with mercy, not a lasting curse.
examples: Luke 23:28: "weep for yourselves and for your children". Jesus' warning about that generation.
Acts 2:39: "the promise is unto you, and to your children" (KJV).
questions.other: Christians of all views now reject the deicide charge. Many teachers stress that all humanity, Jew and Gentile, put Christ to death (Acts 4:27). They note that Roman authority carried out the execution. Some scholars also point out that the crowd was small compared to the whole nation.

questions.q: Is it right to call the Holocaust God's punishment on the Jewish people?
questions.short: No. On the fulfilled reading, the covenant judgment Jesus foretold ended in AD 70. Scripture gives no warrant for calling later atrocities divine punishment.
questions.answer: In 1990 a leading Israeli rabbi suggested the Holocaust was a punishment for sin. Many in Israel were outraged, including survivors. One survivor said the remark turned the killers into God's messengers. Some Christian writers have also said that Israel remains under divine discipline until it turns to Christ. On the fulfilled reading, such claims misuse prophecy. Jesus' warning of judgment had a time limit, "this generation" (Matthew 24:34), and it was fulfilled. Jesus also warned against reading disaster as proof of special guilt (Luke 13:1-5; John 9:2-3). Read this way, the murder of six million Jews was a monstrous evil by human beings. It was not the fulfilment of a prophecy. Its authors bear full guilt before God (Genesis 9:6).
examples: Luke 13:4-5: those killed when the tower fell were not worse sinners than others.
1941-1945: about six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust.
questions.other: Christians of all views condemn the Holocaust as great evil. Some futurists hold that Israel as a nation is under discipline until it believes (Romans 11:25), but most firmly deny that this excuses or explains the Holocaust. Jewish thinkers have debated the question deeply, and most reject the idea of punishment.

questions.q: Is sharing the gospel with Jewish people antisemitic?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says no. The apostles, who were Jews, preached to Jews first. Respectful witness is love, though coercion and contempt are wrong.
questions.answer: In 1989 an evangelical gathering issued the Willowbank Declaration, urging Christians to share the gospel with Jewish people. A rabbi with the American Jewish Committee called it a blueprint for spiritual genocide. Jewish concern is understandable. In history, Jews were sometimes forced to convert, as in Spain in 1391 and 1492. The fulfilled reading draws a line. Forced conversion and contempt are sins. But a free, kind invitation is not hatred. Peter, Paul and the other apostles were Jews who preached first to Jews (Acts 3:25-26; Romans 1:16). Paul longed for his people's salvation (Romans 10:1). Read this way, both the fulfilled reading and dispensationalism agree that Jews, like all people, are welcome in Christ.
examples: Acts 3:25-26: Peter says God sent his servant "to you first".
1492: the Alhambra Decree forced Spain's Jews to convert or leave.
questions.other: Some Christians hold a "two-covenant" view, that Jews are saved through God's covenant with Israel apart from Christ. They avoid evangelism for that reason. Most evangelicals, dispensational or not, reject this view (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). Many Jewish leaders see targeted missions as a threat to Jewish survival after the Holocaust.

questions.q: Is criticism of the State of Israel's policies the same as antisemitism?
questions.short: Not in itself. Disagreeing with a government is different from hostility to a people. But criticism can become antisemitic when it uses double standards or old hatreds.
questions.answer: The fulfilled reading says opposing policies of Israel's government is not the same as opposing Jews. In the Cold War, many Christians opposed the Soviet state while respecting the Russian people. Christians can ask whether any state acts justly, including its treatment of Christians and Arabs. But care is needed. Criticism becomes antisemitic when it blames all Jews for a government's acts. It does so when it uses old stereotypes, or holds Israel to standards applied to no other nation. On this reading, the Bible calls for just weights for everyone (Proverbs 11:1; Leviticus 19:15). Read this way, a Christian may be neither a blind supporter nor an enemy. He can pray for peace for all who live in the land (Psalms 122:6-8).
examples: Leviticus 19:15: judge the poor and the great alike, without partiality.
Micah 6:8: do justice, love mercy and walk humbly with God.
questions.other: Christian Zionists often say God's promises give the State of Israel special status, so opposing its existence opposes God's plan (Genesis 12:3). Many Jewish groups warn that anti-Israel rhetoric often hides antisemitism. Other Christians, including many Palestinian Christians, say biblical justice requires honest critique of all governments.

questions.q: What is the real Christian answer to antisemitism?
questions.short: Love of neighbour. The fulfilled reading says the issue is ethics, not end-times charts: every Jewish person bears God's image and must be treated with justice and love.
questions.answer: Minority groups of many kinds have been mistreated in history. In the United States, enslaved Africans suffered terribly, and Irish immigrants faced job barriers. Jewish people have faced hatred in nearly every century. On the fulfilled reading, no view of prophecy can protect them by itself. The answer is obedience to God's moral law. Every person is made in God's image (Genesis 1:27). We must love our neighbour as ourselves (Leviticus 19:18). Jesus taught that a neighbour can be of any race or faith (Luke 10:29-37). Paul warned Gentile believers not to boast against Jewish branches (Romans 11:18-20). Read this way, Christians of every eschatology must stand against hatred of Jews. Here all the views agree.
examples: Luke 10:33: the hero of the parable is a Samaritan, from a despised group.
Romans 11:18-20: Gentile believers must not be proud, but fear.
questions.other: Christian Zionists add that standing with Israel as a nation is part of this love (Genesis 12:3). Many Jewish and Christian scholars say churches must also face the history of anti-Jewish teaching in sermons and texts. Most traditions now teach respect for Judaism and reject the contempt of the past.

questions.q: Should the views of the early church fathers settle questions of prophecy?
questions.short: No. On the principle of Scripture alone, the fathers are helpful witnesses but not final judges. If the Bible says something happened in the first century, it happened.
questions.answer: Both futurists and preterists quote the early church writers. Some futurists argue that writers only a generation or two from the apostles must have known the truth. The fulfilled reading accepts that history is useful. But it says the Bible alone is the rule of faith. Godly teachers have often been wrong about prophecy. Even in the apostles' day some believers misread Jesus' words (John 21:22-23). The Bereans checked even Paul against Scripture (Acts 17:11). Paul warned against traditions of men (Colossians 2:8). Read this way, the fathers show how early Christians read prophecy. But their views must be tested by the text. A long list of names can never override what the Bible states plainly.
examples: John 21:22-23: a saying spread among believers that John would not die, but Jesus never said that.
Acts 17:11: the Bereans examined the Scriptures daily to test Paul's teaching.
questions.other: Most Protestants of every view agree that Scripture alone is the final authority. Futurists still value the fathers as early witnesses to how the apostles' teaching was understood. Catholic and Orthodox Christians give a larger role to tradition, while still seeing it as faithful to Scripture.

questions.q: Did the early church writers link the beast or antichrist to Nero or Rome?
questions.short: Several did. Some linked the beast's number to "Lateinos" (Latin), and Victorinus and others saw Nero in Revelation 17. Others expected a future antichrist.
questions.answer: A futurist pastor once asked: if Nero was the beast, why did the fathers not say so? The fulfilled reading answers that some did connect the beast with Rome or Nero. Irenaeus suggested that 666 might spell "Lateinos", meaning a Latin or Roman (Against Heresies 5.30.3). Victorinus, about AD 300, saw Nero as one of the kings in Revelation 17. Tertullian said Nero was the first to stain the rising faith with blood (Scorpiace 15). Augustine reported that many believed Nero would rise again as antichrist (City of God 20.19). Fairness requires adding that most of these writers still expected an antichrist in the future. They mixed past and future. Read this way, the fathers do not give a clear futurist witness either.
examples: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.30.3: "Lateinos" in Greek letters adds up to 666.
Tacitus, Annals 15.44: Nero's cruel punishment of Christians after the fire of Rome in AD 64.
questions.other: Futurists point out that Irenaeus clearly expected a future antichrist who would rebuild the temple and reign three and a half years (Against Heresies 5.25.4; 5.30.4). They note that he placed John's vision in Domitian's reign (5.30.3). They argue that the fathers saw Nero, at most, as a type of a later antichrist.

questions.q: Are writers close to the apostles' time always reliable on prophecy?
questions.short: No. Nearness in time does not guarantee accuracy. Irenaeus, for example, also wrote that Jesus lived to nearly fifty, which almost no one accepts.
questions.answer: One futurist argument says the fathers' own fathers and grandfathers would have told them about the antichrist. The fulfilled reading answers that second- and third-hand reports can be wrong. Irenaeus, a strong early witness, claimed that Jesus was nearly fifty when he died (Against Heresies 2.22.5). He also passed on a saying, from Papias, about vines with ten thousand branches in the coming kingdom (Against Heresies 5.33.3). Few accept these today. Popular myths spread even in modern times. Many people still believe medieval scholars thought the earth was flat. Historians have shown that educated people knew it was round. Read this way, the plain words of Scripture, written by eyewitnesses, outweigh later reports. "This generation" (Matthew 24:34) is firmer ground than tradition.
examples: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5: Jesus said to be past forty, against Luke 3:23.
Jeffrey Burton Russell, Inventing the Flat Earth (1991), shows the flat-earth belief was a later myth.
